# WILHELM ROETHER’S

## PREFACE.

While the tireless zeal with which learned men of our time handle all the finest and most elegant Greek writers—for the true benefit of literature—is worthy of the highest praise and should be received with gratitude, almost no one of learning would criticize or disapprove of the effort as being poorly spent if the writers of "Later Greek" <note>original: *Graecitatis*</note> (who cannot be numbered among the very best) were either brought to light from the libraries where they still hide, or if those already published were edited with greater care and correction. 

Among these writers, those who seem especially worthy of more diligent critical attention are the ones whom some call "compilers" <note>original: *compilatores*—a term Roether notes is not strictly classical Latin</note>. These figures either drew directly from original sources that have since been destroyed by the "injury of time" <note>A common scholarly phrase referring to the loss of ancient texts due to neglect, war, or decay.</note>, or they composed their *Excerpts* <note>Selected passages or summaries from larger works.</note> with the help of manuscripts <note>original: *codicum*</note> that were superior to the ones preserved in our libraries today. And among these compilers, [the author] certainly holds not the least place—

<summary>In this preface, Wilhelm Roether defends the scholarly value of "later" Greek writers and compilers. He argues that these authors are essential because they preserve fragments of ancient texts that are now lost and were often based on manuscripts superior to those currently known.</summary>

<keywords>Wilhelm Roether, Greek literature, compilers, textual criticism, manuscripts, excerpts, historiography</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, specifically identifying John Lydus as the subject of the previous page's praise and critiquing the existing editions of his work. It maintains the academic yet introductory tone of Wilhelm Roether.</meta>

...is held by ***John Lydus***. For although he himself suffers from all the flaws that afflict other writers of "declining Greek" <note>original: *cadentis Graecitatis* — a term used by older scholars to describe the Byzantine style, which they viewed as less "pure" than the language of Classical Athens.</note>, he nevertheless managed his particular field much more accurately than most of the others; thus, a significant portion of antiquity is illuminated by his work.

· This being the case, those who brought this author’s short works into the light have certainly earned great gratitude from lovers of antiquity. I speak of *Niels Schow*, who in the ninety-fourth year of the previous century <note>1794</note> published his treatise **On the Months**; *Jean-Dominique Fuss*, who in the year 1812 published his books **On the Magistracies**; and ***Karl Benedict Hase***, who very recently brought the treatise **On Omens** out from the hiding places of libraries—where it lay mutilated in many parts—and restored it <insert>~~from~~</insert> with a critical skill that is plainly wonderful and almost incredible. The more we are delighted by the work of this most learned man <note>Hase</note>, the more we must lament that the treatise **On the Months**, when it was first published, did not receive the same care and diligence from its editor. For I believe it will not escape anyone who has even lightly touched that work just how much *Schow* left behind for a future editor of the same treatise, both to be corrected and to be explained. Indeed, there is hardly a page—to put it this way—in which we are not hindered, once and again, by the most foul defects with which the text suffers, preventing us from immediately understanding the meaning of a writer who is otherwise not at all difficult.

Therefore, I did not think I should refuse when, more than three years ago, *Friedrich Creu-* <note>The text cuts off mid-name; the editor is referring to the scholar Friedrich Creuzer.</note>

<summary>Roether identifies John Lydus as a vital source for ancient history and praises editors like Hase and Fuss, while harshly criticizing Niels Schow’s earlier, error-ridden edition of "On the Months."</summary>
<keywords>John Lydus, John the Lydian, On the Months, On the Magistracies, On Omens, Niels Schow, Jean-Dominique Fuss, Karl Benedict Hase, Friedrich Creuzer, textual criticism, Byzantine Greek</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, completing a reference to Friedrich Creuzer and acknowledging the influence of Karl Benedict Hase. It outlines the scope of the current edition of John Lydus’s "On the Months."</meta>

[Creu]zer <note>The text completes the name of Friedrich Creuzer (1771–1858), a German philologist and archaeologist who was a mentor to the editor, Wilhelm Roether.</note>, whom I recently had as a teacher and now enjoy as a friend, was the authority who encouraged me to undertake the preparation of a new critical edition of this short work. In this task, I believe I have reached a point where I need not fear that learned men will accuse me of excessive haste in publishing my edition; I now hand over this study <note>original: *lucubrationem* — literally "work produced by lamplight," a common scholarly term for a work of intense study.</note> of mine to those who care for this branch of literature. It remains for me to provide some introductory remarks concerning the plan of the whole work and how I have striven to achieve my goals. I need not do what editors of ancient writers usually do—namely, discuss the life of the writer at the start of their editions, the history of his books, the manuscripts they used, the testimonies of the ancients regarding any given writer, and so forth—since ***Hase***, in that commentary prefixed to **John Lydus's** work *On the Magistracies*, has already pursued all those matters so thoroughly that I would seem to be "doing work already done" <note>original: *actum agere* — a Latin idiom for performing a task that is already finished or redundant.</note> if I set out to explain those things. Therefore, I refer those readers who desire to learn such things to paragraphs V, XVI, XVII, XVIII, and XXIII of the commentary I have praised.

Now, regarding this edition of mine, my first priority was to use, in part, the **Paris manuscript** number 3084, which alone had not yet been previously collated, *) and in part from the readings of the **Roman manuscript**...

---

*) ***Hase*** took care to have this manuscript collated with the ***Schow*** edition through *A. Cherbuliez*, a minister of the Divine Word <note>original: *verbi divini [minister]* — a common title for a clergyman or pastor.</note>...

<summary>The editor explains that he was encouraged by Friedrich Creuzer to produce this edition and clarifies that he will not repeat the biographical details of John Lydus already covered by Karl Benedict Hase. He identifies the Paris and Roman manuscripts as his primary sources for correcting the text.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, detailing his methodology for correcting the text. He explains how he incorporated previous scholarly work by Nicolaus Schow and Karl Benedict Hase while applying his own editorial judgment to address scribe errors and corrupted passages.</meta>

VIII

[variet]y of readings, which Schow <note>Nicolaus Schow (1754–1830), a Danish philologist who produced an earlier edition of Lydus.</note> noted; I have inserted his complete annotations into my own, distinguished by the symbol: **SCH.** Partly from the sources which Lydus either had before his eyes or seems to have had while writing his book, and finally partly from conjecture—by consulting those writers who treated the same subject—I have purged the text of faults as far as possible, making it more accessible to readers.

In this task, I exercised such caution that I rarely accepted any reading unless it was supported by the authority of either the manuscripts or the sources from which Lydus drew. Where it was manifest that a scribe had made an error, I restored the reading that seemed true to me, even at my own risk <note>original: *meo periculo* — a philological term meaning the editor is making an educated guess (conjecture) not found in the original manuscripts.</note>; however, I did this in such a way that I gave an account of all my changes in the notes. I made a few exceptions for minor corrections, such as where an omega (ω) was placed instead of an omicron (ο) in comparative forms, or where the "movable nu" <term>ν ἐφελκυστικόν (*nu ephelkustikon*): a letter 'n' added to the end of Greek words to avoid two vowels clashing or to fit a poetic meter.</term> was missing, and similar instances.

In other places, I was not ashamed to use the little word *sic* <note>Latin for "thus"; used in editing to indicate that a strange or incorrect word is exactly as it appears in the original source.</note>, common in critical notations, to indicate that I did not understand the meaning of a corrupted passage, even though I might sometimes have a way to heal it through conjecture. Furthermore, I have adapted the spelling and the system of punctuation to the style that is currently most prevalent. Moreover, it was my intention that the Planudean Excerpts <note>Summaries written by the 13th-century scholar Maximus Planudes, which help preserve parts of Lydus's work that are otherwise lost.</note>, which Schow inserted into the Barberini text <note>The *Codex Barberinianus*, a significant manuscript once owned by the Barberini family.</note>—though not all in their proper places—especially those which [are found] in Part III...

---

...a Genevan minister, who at that time was pursuing literary studies at the University of Paris as one of Hase's <note>Karl Benedict Hase (1780–1864), a German-born Hellenist and professor in Paris who was a leading authority on Byzantine Greek.</note> students.

<summary>The editor describes his critical method for reconstructing the text of John Lydus, balancing manuscript evidence, previous scholarship by Schow, and his own careful conjectures. He also notes his modernization of spelling and punctuation for the benefit of contemporary readers.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the editor’s explanation of his textual methodology. Having discussed his conservative approach to corrections on the previous page, he now justifies maintaining the structural sequence of the previous edition by Schow to ensure cross-compatibility for scholars, while noting where his own corrections align with other contemporary philologists like Jacobs and Hase.</meta>

IX

contained [within the work], into their proper order: however, I omitted this task, lest my edition differ too much from that of **Schow** <note>Nicolaus Schow (1754–1830), a Danish scholar whose 1794 edition was the previous standard for Lydus’s work.</note>, so that those who did not have his edition readily available might still be able to find those passages which learned men—**Creuzer**, **Hase**, **Jacobs**, and others—cited in their own writings from **Schow's** edition. Therefore, I limited myself to indicating in the annotations which other passages these **Excerpts** should be joined with. With the same purpose, I also placed the chapter and page numbers from **Schow's** edition in the margin: for, as for the fact that I did not follow **Schow's** division (which relied on no certain logic) but instead marked each **Excerpt** with its own number, no one will fail to approve of that.

In this business, it delighted me most whenever I later saw that my own emendations agreed with those of learned men, whose authority serves as manifest proof for me. I have recorded this consensus for the most part in the annotations; however, by some chance, I only happened upon several emendations by others when the greater part of the work had already been printed: *) which I mention so that learned men do not hold it against me as a fault that I did not [mention] their [work]...

---

*) Thus, for example, **Friedrich Jacobs** <note>A prolific German classical scholar (1764–1847) known for his work on the Greek Anthology.</note> in his notes to the *Palatine Anthology*, volume III, page 395, had already changed the words "this man indeed these things" <note>original: οὗτος αὐτὰ μέν (*houtos auta men*)</note>, which are in part I, number 9, page 6 of this edition, into "not so many things indeed" <note>original: οὐ τοσαῦτα μέν (*ou tosauta men*)</note>, just as I have restored based on the conjecture of **Hase** and **Boissonade** <note>Jean François Boissonade de Fontarabie (1774–1857), a French classical scholar.</note>. The words "those from the disciplines" <note>original: οἱ ἀπὸ τῶν μαθημάτων (*hoi apo tōn mathēmatōn*)</note> in part I, number 16, page 20, he—as I do—renders on page 913 of the cited book as *mathematicians*, adding: "lest you think, as the editor did, that something has fallen out." In the same place, page 949, instead of "nodding the reins of the many-starred" <note>original: πολυαστέρος ἡνία νεύων (*polyasteros hēnia neuōn*)</note>, as it is read in part II, number 4, page 42, he wishes it to be written as "steering the reins of the starry night" <note>original: νυκτὸς πολυαστέρου ἡνιοχεύων (*nyktos polyasterou hēniocheuōn*)</note>, which emendation he confirms with a passage from Anacreon (found in **Athenaeus**, book XIII, page 564, section D): "you steer the chariot of my soul." — The same author in the same work on page 321, instead of "but because of him," which is in part II, number 9, page 64, and which **Scho-**

X

...made mention [of them], lest they say I have committed the [theft] of the jackdaw <note>A reference to Aesop's fable where a jackdaw decks himself in the feathers of other birds to appear more beautiful; the editor is saying he does not want to take credit for other scholars' discoveries.</note>, as it is in the fable—an arrogance which is far removed from my character.

Next, it was my chief care to accurately cite the passages of those authors whom **Lydus** <note>Joannes Lydus (6th century CE), a Byzantine administrator and writer.</note> praises, and where necessary, to correct the errors Lydus committed in naming his sources; or, as far as was possible, to track down those authors he passes over in silence and indicate the names of those I discovered. As for the other errors of **John** [Lydus], which he committed in great number, I have noted some of them in his explanations of etymologies <term>etymis</term> <note>Lydus was notorious for imaginative but often linguistically incorrect explanations of the origins of words.</note>, but for the most part I passed them over in silence, as learned men would detect them even without my speaking. For I did not think the writer himself should be subjected to the strict **Rule of Criticism** <term>Criticae regula</term> <note>The scholarly standard of analyzing a text for historical and logical consistency.</note> as much as his booklet should be purged by me of the faults that crept in through the negligence of scribes. To illustrate those points which were less clear, I compared similar passages from **John’s** other remaining writings, so that his style of writing might be better understood, and I also examined ancient writers who touched on the same subjects, and their passages,

---

[Jacobs] corrected "through which also..." <note>original: διὸ δὲ α.</note>, whereas I thought it should be corrected so that "this" <note>original: τοῦτο</note> was placed after "but through" <note>original: διὰ δέ</note>; he thinks "and Zeus himself" <note>original: Δία δὲ αὐτόν</note> should be written. — The **Oracle of Hecate** <note>A mystical text often cited in late antiquity regarding the goddess of magic and crossroads.</note>, which is in part III, number 7, page 94, he emends in the same way as we do on page 615, putting "bearing three things" <note>original: τρισσὰ φέρουσα</note> instead of "taking away thrice" <note>original: τρὶς ἀφαιροῦσα</note>. — Likewise on page 324, "immovable" <note>original: ἀκίνητος</note>, which was in part III, number 30, page 126, which we corrected from **Plato**, he changes to "ever-moving" <note>original: ἀεικίνητος</note>. — On page 875, "reveler" <note>original: βακχευτήν</note>, which is in part IV, number 38, page 200, before the words "and running up" <note>original: καὶ ἀνατρέχοντα</note>, he says is corrupted, and after the words "up through the heaven" <note>original: ἀνὰ τὸν οὐρανὸν</note> before "from the [number] seven" <note>original: ἐκ τῆς τ. ἑπτ.</note>, he supplies "the heaven" <note>original: τὸν δὲ οὐρανόν</note>, for which I myself have put "where" <note>original: οὗ</note>, which amounts to the same thing. — On page 611, he himself also changes "remains" <note>original: μένει</note>, which is read in part IV, number 48, page 228 (and which **Schow** had wrongly removed), into "part" <note>original: μέρει</note>.

<meta>This page continues the editor’s explanation of his scholarly apparatus. Having discussed his efforts to trace Lydus's sources, the editor now describes how he incorporated the work of modern scholars and the practical limitations—such as his teaching duties and the timing of new publications—that affected the scope of his annotations.</meta>

XI

...as far as they were able, I have added notes either to correct **Lydus** or to make him easier to understand. Finally, I also consulted the books of more recent authors, especially those who have frequently read **John’s** little work—who are not few in number—and I noted what seemed relevant to our purpose. In this task, if I have perhaps omitted much that learned men might desire, I would wish them to consider: first, that I had to be careful not to exceed the proper limit of annotation; second, that during the time I was composing these notes, I was hindered by the school duties <note>The editor likely held a teaching position that occupied his primary time.</note> I then held, which prevented me from gathering every resource that might exist in the books of learned men; and finally, that some books which could assist our **Lydus** in some part have appeared only very recently, when a large part of my manuscript pages had already been sent to the bookseller. *)

---

*) There are many things which I could even now add and supplement, were I not prevented from writing them by urgent business. **Additions and Supplements**. At another time, when I have collected more, a supplement <term>mantissa</term> <note>original: "mantissa"; a traditional scholarly term for an addition or appendix thrown in to "fill the measure."</note> will follow my little work, in which I intend to correct and supplement it to the best of my ability. At this point, I cannot help but add what the most learned man, **L. Chr. Zimmermann**, noted on the proof-sheets he corrected:
Regarding page 198: "the third child of Cabirus, etc." <note>original: "τρίτος Καβίρου παῖς"</note> See **Welcker**, *The Aeschylean Trilogy: Prometheus*, page 164 and following. — Regarding page 224: "Amalthea" <note>original: "Ἀμάλθειαν"</note> See **Welcker**, *On a Cretan Colony in Thebes*, page 6 f., note 12, where our passage is also cited. — Regarding page 228: "that Zeus is Idaean" <note>original: "τὸν Δία Ἰδαῖον εἶναι"</note> On **Zeus** as the son of **Prometheus**, see **Welcker**, *The Aeschylean Trilogy: Prometheus*, page 96, note 112, where our passage is likewise cited. — Regarding page 232: "brought in by others" <note>original: "πρὸς τ. ἄλλων ἐπικομιζομένοις"</note> On the word for "clod of earth" <note>original: "βῶλος"</note> occurring in the masculine gender, see also **Coray** on **Plutarch’s** *Life of Alexander*, 25. **Lobeck** on **Phrynichus**, page 54. **Apollonius Rhodius** also uses it in the masculine gender in Book III, line 1393. — Regarding page 286: "Euphorion says" <note>original: "ὁ Εὐφορίων φησίν"</note> See **Meineke’s** *Euphorion*, page 167.

<meta>This page continues the editor’s preface, detailing the contributions of fellow scholars Hase and Creuzer, and introducing the work of Lewald and Nokk. The editor acknowledges the collaborative nature of this edition and explains the abbreviations used in the footnotes.</meta>

XII

In this entire business of annotating, I have been continuously and exceptionally helped by the handwritten notes of the distinguished men *Hase* and *Creuzer*, which they most kindly allowed me to publish alongside my own. When I consulted the former of these men regarding some of my conjectures and emendations, he sent a very detailed letter on May 27, 1824, <note>original: "d. VI. Kal. Jun. ann. MDCCCXXIV." The editor uses the Roman calendar format.</note> in which he not only resolved my doubts but also added many other observations that had occurred to him while reading. I have translated these notes, originally written in *German*, word-for-word into *Latin* <note>While the editor translated the German notes into Latin for his 19th-century audience, they are here translated into English for the modern reader.</note> as they are now read among my own annotations. For this generosity, I thank this most learned man from my heart; I also ask him that, if any parts have been rendered poorly into *Latin*, he might, with his usual kindness, excuse them along with my other errors. *Creuzer*, on the other hand, had written his notes in the margins of his own copy in such a way that I have seen to it they were transcribed for the press. These notes are marked with these abbreviations: **HAS.** and **CR.**, while mine are distinguished from the others by these letters: **RR.**

Besides these two men, another pair of most learned and dear friends have done a great service to *Lydus*: I mean *Ernest Anton Lewald* and *Lorenz Nokk*. When I consulted *Lewald* regarding two passages from *Aristotle* contained in *John’s* <note>Referring to the author, John Lydus.</note> little work, he discussed them with such skill and insight in an essay <term>excursus</term> <note>original: "excursu"; a detailed discussion of a specific point, often appended to the main text.</note> which I added starting on page 300. He displayed there the same brilliance found in his other writings, as well as in his recent work on the *Aristotelian Cate-* <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely referring to Lewald’s work on Aristotle’s *Categories*.</note>

For indeed, a chapter of **Valens** is titled exactly thus: *On the rising of the zodiacal signs* <note>original Greek: "περὶ ἀναφοράς ζῳδίων"</note> (page 336, at the end of **Johannes Laurentius Lydus**) and this phrase is used very frequently in these fragments. Nor can you learn accurately what it means even from **Estienne’s** *Thesaurus* <note>The "Thesaurus Graecae Linguae," a massive Greek dictionary.</note> in the latest edition by **Valpy** (p. 10010). However, there exists a book by **Hypsicles of Alexandria** [titled] *On Risings* <note>original Greek: "Ἀναφορικός"</note>. Likewise, the terms *rising* <note>original Greek: "ἀναφορά"</note>, or *succession* <note>original Greek: "ἐπαναφορά"</note>, and *ascending* <note>original Greek: "ἀναφορικός"</note>, and *ascensionally* <note>original Greek: "ἀναφορικῶς"</note>, and *setting* <note>original Greek: "καταφορά"</note>, etc., are used in various ways by the ancient astrologers. You should see **Sextus Empiricus**, *Against the Mathematicians* V. 20, p. 341, where you may understand that **J. A. Fabricius** rightly defended the common reading against the conjectures of **Salmasius** <note>Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), a French classical scholar.</note>, as is clear from the passage of **Plotinus** mentioned above. See also **Sextus**, book V, sections 52, 53, and following. **Claudius Ptolemy** uses it no less frequently in his astrological books. See, for example, his *Canon*, or *The Hundred Sayings*, section 25; **Porphyry’s** *Introduction to Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos*, page 201, and everywhere else. Add **Proclus’s** *Sphere* and the notes of **Henisch** there, page 201, Augsburg edition, 1619. — **Cr.** <note>Initials of Friedrich Creuzer.</note>

->THE PUBLISHER GREETS THE READERS.<-

Since this little book had already been fully printed by our presses over a year ago, and lacked nothing except a preface from the editor—a man most famous and highly distinguished for his wealth of learning—who, however, had been called away to other very serious duties and business in his own country <note>Nicolaus Schow (1754–1830) was a Danish philologist who returned to Copenhagen to fulfill academic and administrative roles.</note>, he did not have the leisure to write it, despite our requests by letter. We did not wish to allow this little work to be suppressed in our hands any longer, nor for lovers of literature <note>original: "harum litterarum amatores", referring to students of classical philology and ancient texts.</note> to be deprived of its many and varied benefits. Therefore, with the learned man’s permission, we have reprinted his "Preliminary Remarks" <note>original: "Praemonenda"</note>, which were originally included in the preview of this work inserted in the seventh volume of the *Unpublished Works of Ancient Literature and Art* <note>original: "Bibliothecae veteris litter. et artis Ineditis", a series edited by Schow and others to share newly discovered ancient texts.</note>, page 21 and following:

> “As things now stand, there is scarcely any hope shining forth that any lost fragments or books of the classical writers, especially the Greeks, or of those we already possess, will be found. Some...”

...nevertheless, the category of Greek literature in which new monuments <note>The author uses "monuments" (monumenta) in the sense of written records or literary works.</note>, still lying hidden sporadically in libraries, can be uncovered and brought to light with profit, is that to which the works of the compilers are referred. For these authors either drew from sources that we have lost through the ravages of time, or they transcribed from manuscripts that were more accurate and complete than those preserved in libraries today. Among these compilers, *John Laurence the Philadelphian, known as Lydus* <note>John Lydus (c. 490–560 AD) was a Byzantine civil servant and scholar whose works are vital for understanding the administration and customs of ancient Rome.</note>, deserves no small place; for he seems to have investigated the ancient sources of Greek and Roman religion quite diligently. I willingly subscribe to the opinion of Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893 AD) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who reviewed hundreds of books in his "Bibliotheca" (or "Myriobiblion").</note> in Codex 180, page 407, who judges this work of Lydus with these words: <note>original Greek: "ἡ περὶ μηνῶν πραγματεία, εἰ καὶ πολὺ τὸ ἄχρηστον ἔχει, ἀλλ' οὖν πρὸς τὴν τῆς ἀρχαιότητος μάθησιν ἐπίχαρί τε καὶ λίαν χρειῶδες"</note> "The treatise *On the Months*, even if it contains much that is useless, is nonetheless charming and extremely useful for the study of antiquity." For it must be admitted that by Lydus, no less than by other compilers of a later age, many things are presented that are trite, frivolous, and less than useful. Lydus’s era is known from that same passage of Photius; namely, he lived in the 6th century under the emperors *Anastasius*, *Justin*, and *Justinian* (see *Fabricius, Greek Library, Vol. III, p. 512* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736) was a German scholar whose "Bibliotheca Graeca" remains a foundational bibliography of Greek literature.</note>). Codinus and Suidas <note>The "Suidas" (now known as the Suda) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia; George Codinus was a later Byzantine writer who wrote about the antiquities of Constantinople.</note> had his excerpts *On the Months* <note>original: "περὶ μηνῶν" (peri mēnōn)</note> before their eyes; for this reason, these two also bring light to Lydus’s work and borrow from it. Now, since I have decided to bring to light the complete excerpts of Lydus’s *On the Months*, I wanted a certain sample to precede the edition so that learned men might better recognize the utility of this undertaking; although...

Schow's Edition,
page 1.
</margin>

# I. FROM THE WRITINGS OF JOHN OF PHILADELPHIA. <note>John Lydus, the author, was a native of Philadelphia in Lydia, hence this title.</note>

---

<margin>
Part I.
Chapter I.
</margin>

**1.** — — Rightly, then, do the myth-makers depict Kronos <note>The Titan Cronus in Greek mythology</note> making away with his own children, hinting, no doubt, that Time <note>original: *chronos*; a common ancient wordplay linking the god Kronos with the concept of time, Chronos</note> is both the father and the destruction of all things produced by him.

**I. FROM THE WRITINGS OF JOHN**] The Vatican Codex reads *John Lydus*. SCHOW. <note>Nicolaus Schow, the 18th-century editor of this text.</note>

**1. the myth-makers**] Reading: *the myth-makers certain* <note>original: οἱ μυθικοί τ. (*hoi mythikoi t.*)</note>. SCHOW. See also below in II. 1. and IV. 27. In the same way below in IV. 21. at the end, *mentioning* <note>original: ἐπιμιμνησκόμενα (*epimimnēskomena*)</note> instead of *those mentioning* <note>original: — νοι (*-noi*)</note>, due to the confusion of the letters $\bar{\alpha}$ (alpha) and $\overline{οι}$ (oi). Although Hase, in his Commentary on our author’s book *On the Magistracies* <note>original: *De magistratibus*; another work by Lydus regarding the Roman civil service</note> page LII, brings these words from Leo Allatius’s index of *Miscellanies* thus: *Rightly then do those concerned with mythic...*, from which you might suspect the reading should be *those concerned with mythic matters*. RUHNKEN. <note>David Ruhnken, a 18th-century classical scholar.</note> Reading: *those who wrote down mythic accounts*. (Furthermore, it is quite ridiculous that in Photius’s *Library* <note>A 9th-century collection of book summaries by the Patriarch Photius</note> codex 189, page 470, *Acestorides’s four books of MYTHIC accounts of cities* <note>original: ’Ακεστορίδου τῶν κατὰ πόλιν ΜΥΘΙΚΩΝ λόγοι δ</note> is translated—whether by Schott or his associates is not clear—thus: *Acestorides' four books of

<column-break/>

political mythology*). Although among writers of the time of Theodosius and Justinian <note>Emperors of the 4th through 6th centuries AD</note> that specific phrasing using "mythic" <note>original: *μυθικὰ*</note> is not so frequent; you may more easily find: *according to the... MYTHOLOGISTS* (See John Chrysostom <note>An influential 4th-century Archbishop and preacher</note>, *Exposition on Psalm 48*, 664 line 4—these passages are cited according to the editions listed in my Notes to Leo, pages 273–280): *poets and philosophers and mythologists*. In the same author's *Oration 92, On those who have fallen asleep*, VI. 863 line 9: *a babbler, or a mythologist, or a joker*. Also in *Oration 106, On repentance and almsgiving*, 923 line 14: *to rebuke the mythologists*. Also *Oration 1, On false prophets*, VII. 221 line 28; in these instances, however, the term is mostly used in a hostile sense, just as Chrysostom uses it in his oration: *What sort of women one ought to lead as wives*

2. The servants of Dionysus <note>The Greek god of wine and theater, also known as Bacchus</note> called the ritual procession a **Triumph** <note>original Greek: *Thriambon*</note>, deriving the name from the *thyrsi* <note>ritual staffs tipped with pine cones</note> and the *iambs* <note>satirical verses or "jests"</note>, as if it were a "thyrsi-iamb." Alternatively, according to Plutarch, the name comes from the word "to shout aloud" <note>original Greek: *throein*</note>.

3. The Lydians <note>An ancient people of western Asia Minor</note>, they say, discovered wine; and not only wine, but also the cultivation of the fig tree.

4. The Romans knew wine as **Must** <note>original Latin: *mustum*</note>, because the people of Sardis <note>the capital of Lydia</note> were the first to call it a "mystery," as if it were an initiate <note>original Greek: *mystēn*</note> into sacred rites.

<margin>page 2.</margin> 5. **Sabinus** was named appropriately after the cultivation of wine; for the name "Sabinus" signifies a sower and a planter of wine.

6. **Messapia**, which is Calabria <note>the "heel" of Italy</note>, is named after Messapus.

7. <margin>chapter II.</margin> 8. The myth that **Erylus**—who lived in Italy and whose land was seized by Evander, the son of the prophetess Carmentis—was born with three souls, is a most philosophical riddle; for it suggests the soul has three distinct powers...

### EXCERPTS 2–8.

2. The attendants of Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine</note> called the ritual procession a **Triumph** <note>original: *thriambon*</note>, a name derived from the *thyrsos* <note>a ritual staff tipped with a pine cone</note> and the *iambs* <note>satirical or mocking verses</note>, as if it were a "thyrsi-iamb." Alternatively, according to Plutarch, the name comes from the word "to cry out aloud" or "to make a commotion" <note>original Greek: *throein*</note>.

3. They say the Lydians <note>an ancient people of western Anatolia</note> discovered wine; and not only wine, but also the cultivation of the fig tree.

4. The Romans knew wine as **Must** <note>fresh, unfermented grape juice; original: *mustum*</note> because the people of Sardis <note>the capital of Lydia</note> were the first to call it a "mystery," as if it were an "initiate" <note>original Greek: *mystēn*</note>, meaning something steeped in sacred rites.

5. The name of the **Sabines** <note>an ancient Italic tribe</note> was derived from the cultivation of the vine, a name perfectly suited to the reality; for this name signifies a "planter of the vine."

6. **Messapia**, or Calabria <note>the "heel" of the Italian peninsula</note>, is named after Messapus.

7. They call **Lucania** "the most wooded"; for the Romans call a grove a *lucus* by way of "privation" <note>the linguistic practice of naming something for a quality it lacks; literally "a grove [of light] that lacks light"</note>, because it **lacks light**, just as in Greek a forest is called "timberless" <note>original Greek: *axylos*</note>.

8. The myth says that **Erylus** the Italian—who was defeated by Evander, the son of the prophetic Carmenta, who then held the region—possessed three lives <note>original: *animas*</note>. This story has a very philosophical meaning: for Socrates states that there are three powers inherent in the soul—

Socrates in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phaidoni"; the text likely means the *Phaedrus*, as noted in the commentary below</note> teaches that the mind is a charioteer, and the powers of the soul are the horses. In this same way, the oracles decree that the soul must be bridled:

->A mortal being, a creature of thought, must bridle the soul,<-
->Lest it strike against the shapeless earth, but instead be saved.<-

For since the nature of the universe is composed of opposing powers, it is necessary for the soul, which permeates all things, to be fitted with these opposing principles. ### EXCERPTS 8—9.

...in the *Phaedo* <note>original: "Phaedone"; the author likely refers to the *Phaedrus*, which contains the famous Chariot Allegory</note> he teaches that the mind is a charioteer, while the powers of the soul are the horses. For this reason, the oracles also command that bridles be cast upon the soul:

> It is necessary for a person endowed with reason to cast bridles
> upon the soul, lest it fall into the unlucky earth, but instead
> be preserved safe.

For since the nature of the universe arose from contrary powers, it is necessary that contrary principles also meet within the soul that is poured through all things. For that part of the soul which participates in the mind is contained by the **Monad** <note>the principle of "oneness" or pure intellect</note>, that is, the mind; however, that part which belongs to the soul’s lower nature and is nourished by pleasure is contained by the **Dyad** <note>the principle of "twoness" or matter and division</note>, as if it were matter. Nevertheless, the oracle teaches that the entire soul is a divine **Triad** <note>a "three-fold" unity</note>. For the same author says:

> After he mixed the spark of the soul with two harmonies,
> reason and divine power, to which he added a third:
> pure Love, which has the power of joining and
> fertilizing all things, a venerable thing.

9. **Evander** <note>a culture-hero from Arcadia who, according to Roman legend, founded a city on the site of the future Rome</note> was the first to bring the so-called "Cadmean letters" from Greece into Italy. # I. VARIOUS SUBJECTS

...[xi and zeta, as well as] **phi** (φ) and **chi** (χ) instead of the rough breathings, and **eta** (η) and **omega** (ω) instead of the long vowels, were invented later. For in the old days there were only five vowels, with the letter **epsilon** (ε) serving the purpose of **eta**, and **omicron** (ο) serving for **omega**. This is still the case even now among the Romans <note>referring to the Latin language</note>, where the sound changes its power only by its "time" <note>vowel quantity; Latin uses the same character for both long and short vowels, like the 'a' in 'father' vs. 'fat'</note>. Later, Marcus Flavius, an Italian grammarian following the Greeks' example, ascribed the remaining characters to the Romans. For time loves to change things.

### EXCERPTS 9—12.

...[so that] long vowels might later be found in addition. For in ancient times there were only five vowels; the letter **E** served the purpose of **Eta** <note>the Greek long 'e'</note>, and **O** served for **Omega** <note>the Greek long 'o'</note>. This practice still holds among the Romans today, where the sound changes its value only by "time" <note>original: *tempore*; referring to "vowel quantity," where the length of time a vowel is held determines the meaning of a word</note>. But later, Marcus Flavius, an Italian Grammarian, followed the Greeks and added the remaining characters to the Roman letters. For time is accustomed to change all things.

10. Since the Phoenicians were the first bankers and sordid moneylenders, they devised letters, weights, and the entire art of making a profit; for this reason, the poets even call them *kapelous* <note>original: καπήλους; meaning petty traders or retail brokers</note>. But let us return to the point from which we departed.

They say that Geryon had three bodies—not because he actually possessed that many bodies, but because three islands located in the Ocean were his allies in war. <note>This is a "Euhemerist" explanation, a common ancient practice of interpreting myths as exaggerated accounts of real historical events.</note>

# I. VARIOUS SUBJECTS

...on the first of the Kalends of May <note>the first day of May</note>, during the third year of the sixth [Olympiad] <note>754/753 BCE</note>, or (as others say) during the second year of the eighth [Olympiad] <note>747/746 BCE</note>. ***

Writers on rural matters regarding the *Parilia* <note>original: *Parilia*; an ancient Roman festival on April 21st celebrating the foundation of Rome</note>. — **of the sixth**, understand this to mean the "Olympiad" <note>the four-year period used by Greeks for dating</note>. # I. OF VARIOUS ARGUMENTS

Romulus gives the beginning of the year to the month of March in honor of Mars; for the story goes that he was born from him—a year consisting of only ten months.

15. The decad <note>the number ten</note> is a complete number, which is why it is also called "perfect fullness" <note>original Greek: "panteleia"</note>, containing all the forms of the other numbers, ratios, proportions, and harmonies. For the decad is a measuring rule <note>term: "gnomon" — originally a tool for measuring right angles, here used to mean a fundamental standard of reality</note> among existing things, characterizing everything and uniquely defining the infinite within each thing. It is the gatherer, collector, and fulfiller of all that is contained within both the intelligible nature <note>the realm of pure thought or the divine</note> and the sublunary realm <note>the physical world beneath the Moon</note>. For thus Parmenides <note>a pre-Socratic philosopher</note> hands down to us: first, the intelligible things; second, those found in numbers; third, the cohesive; fourth, the perfecting; fifth, the divisive; sixth, the life-giving; seventh, the demiurgic <note>the creative or building forces</note>; eighth, the assimilative; ninth, the absolute; and tenth, the worldly. Rightly, then, Philolaus <note>a Pythagorean philosopher</note> addressed it as the "decad," as it is receptive <note>original: "dektikēn" — a pun on the word "dekas" (ten)</note> of the infinite, while Orpheus called it...

<margin>page 7.</margin>

...I see. Finally, this inscription is also found in Edmund Figrelius <note>*On the Statues of Illustrious Romans*, published in Stockholm, 1656</note> as follows: **TO TARRUTENIUS MAXIMILIANUS, A MAN OF SENATORIAL RANK, MOST ELOQUENT, CONSULAR OF PICENUM. ANICIUS ACILIUS GLABRIO FAUSTUS [etc. GAVE] THIS.** — Our Tarutius Firmanus is written as *Taroutios* by Plutarch in the passage cited; on which point see especially the notes by Leopold [RR].
   **The beginning of — only months]** I have provided "The beginning of the year" based on the conjecture of Schow <note>Nicolaus Schow, an 18th-century Danish philologist</note> in place of "The beginning of March" which his text has [RR]. These words are mutilated, and for the sake of the sense, they should perhaps be read thus:

<column-break/>

Romulus gives the beginning of the year to the month of March in honor of Mars, for the story goes that he was born from him; and the year consisted of only ten months. [Schow]. Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* Book I, chapter 12: *who (Romulus) dedicated the first month of the year to his father Mars*, and our own author below in section III. 15. [RR]. See Plutarch’s *Roman Questions*, chapter 19, where you may consult the passages cited by Wyttenbach on page 27 and following. [Cr].

   15. **The decad is complete, etc.]** *The Great Etymological Dictionary* under the word *dekas* (ten), page 253: "that which contains every number within itself." *The Theology of Arithmetic*, page 63 in the Ast edition: "It is called power and perfect fullness, since it limits every number." In a similar way, see Macrobius, *On the Dream of Scipio*, Book I, chapter 6.

The decad <note>the number ten</note> is a full number, which is why it is also called "perfect," since it embraces all the patterns <note>original: "ideas/species"</note> of the remaining numbers, ratios, proportions, and harmonies. For the decad is a standard <note>term: "gnomon" — a tool used to determine right angles or measure shadows; here used to mean a fundamental rule of reality</note> among things that exist, marking everything with its character and defining what is infinite in each thing by its own logic. It possesses the power of joining, gathering, and perfecting everything encompassed by nature, by reason, and by the world beneath the Moon <note>term: "sublunary" — the physical world of change and decay, as opposed to the eternal heavens</note>. For thus Parmenides <note>an influential early Greek philosopher</note> teaches us: first are those things belonging to reason and mind; second, those contained in numbers; third, those having the power of containment; fourth, those of perfecting; fifth, those of separating; sixth, those of generating; seventh, those of perfecting something through art; eighth, those of making things similar; ninth, those that are absolute; and tenth, those pertaining to order. Rightly, then, Philolaus <note>a Pythagorean philosopher who argued that the Earth moved around a "central fire"</note> named it the "decad" <note>from the Greek "dechesthai," meaning to receive or contain</note>, since it is capable of 

<margin>He calls the number ten the most perfect number. Compare: *Etymologicum Gudianum* p. 137; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* I. 3; *Theology of Arithmetic* 58; and Boeckh on Philolaus. **Rr.** <note>"Rr." likely refers to the editor David Ruhnken</note></margin>

<margin>"For it is a standard among existing things etc." from *Theology of Arithmetic* 59: Reasonably, the Creator used it as a measure for all things, and like a standard or a straight-edge, harmonizing it with his purpose; through the consonant ratios within it, things from heaven to earth are found to be arranged both as a whole and in part according to its design. **Rr.**</margin>

...saying: “The words *and from* <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐκ</note> cannot be omitted. For the marvelous nature of the number twelve is confirmed by two principal arguments: first, since it is composed of the most elementary... right-angled triangle...; and (this is the second reason, because it is composed) of a doubled six. For first, $12 = 3 + 4 + 5$; second, $12 = (1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3) + (1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3)$. Now, the number six is perfect, being ‘completed from its own parts.’ What our mathematicians call factors, the Greeks called ‘parts’ <note>original Greek: Μέρη</note>; hence *merismos* <note>original: μερισμὸς</note> is our division, and *merizein* <note>original: μερίζειν</note> is to divide, that is, to break into factors. Psellus, in *On the Four Mathematical Sciences* (Basel edition by Xylander, 1554, p. 7), says: ‘A part is a number belonging to a number, the smaller of the larger, when it measures <note>This means the smaller number divides the larger without a remainder.</note> the larger.’ Therefore, a number ‘completed from its own parts’ is one which arises from the sum of its individual factors, or one whose sum of factors is equal to the product of those same factors. In truth, $6 = 1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 = 1 + 2 + 3$.” — From these points, I have altered the punctuation of the whole passage 

<column-break/>

# I. VARIOUS TOPICS

...[the name of] Venus according to the Phoenicians <note>original: "φροδίτης ἐστὶ κατὰ τοὺς Φοίνικας"</note> calling that garment in the ancestral manner a **trabaia** <note>The *trabea*, a ceremonial toga worn by kings and augurs</note>, which it is said **Agathocles the Sicilian** was the first to invent. It is called *trabaia* as if it were "triply-dyed" <note>original Greek: "τρίβαφος" (tribaphos)</note>; for it is composed of three colors: purple, scarlet, and the so-called **isatis herb** <note>original: "ἰσάτιδος βοτάνης"; likely woad, used for blue dye</note>, which is sacred to Mars. Then he <note>King Numa</note> established the guardian of the city—whom we now address as the **Prefect**, or as some say, the **City-Ruler** or **City-Judge**—whom they formerly called the **Urban Praetor**. He also clearly takes precedence over the Roman Senate; this is evident from his shoes, upon which a small **crescent** <note>original: "σεληνίσκος" (selēniskos)</note> is embossed in the shape of the letter **sigma** <note>The lunate sigma, shaped like a 'C'</note>, by which the Romans designate the number **one hundred** <note>original: "ἑκατὸν ἀριθμὸν"; the 'C' stands for *Centum*, representing the original 100 members of the Roman Senate</note>...

**tan** <note>The suffix of the word "Aphroditan" from the previous page</note> That Venus is called this by the Phoenicians is likely; **Baaltis**, the Phoenician goddess, is signified by him. See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* (which Creuzer praises in *Symbols* vol. II p. 9 note 13) Book I, chapter 10, p. 38 of the Cologne edition, who says she is also called *Dione*. **Rr.** <note>Initials of the commentator, likely Reiske</note>

**trabaia** Codinus, in *On the Origins of Constantinople* p. 16 of the Paris edition, says the "trabeas" are **costly cloaks**. To illustrate these, Lambecius in his *Observations* p. 154 included our passage starting from the words **"Now Numa..."** up to the words **"which is of Mars"**, in which he omitted the article **the** before **ancestral garment**, and for **trabaia** he writes **Trabea**, and below **trabea**. Regarding this garment, see our author [Lydus]

**isatis herb** It had been written as *isatis thunder* <note>original: "ἰσ. βρόντης"; a scribal error swapping 'herb' for 'thunder'</note> [sic]. Furthermore, *isatis* is a plant called *vitrum* <note>woad</note> by the Romans, concerning which see Pliny.

# I. VARIOUS SUBJECTS

...and they used both bark and linden-wood tablets for writing, which is why even now the official known as the **scribe of the praetor** <note>original: "tou praitōros skribas"</note> precedes the consuls. [Later in time, **Ptolemy** <note>Likely Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the Pharaoh of Egypt</note>—following the advice of **Aristarchus** the grammarian to embrace the protection of the **Romans**—was the first to send **paper** <note>original: "chartēn", referring to papyrus made in Egypt</note> to Rome as a gift of hospitality. However, he was out-rivaled in reputation by **Attalus** of Pergamon, under the direction of the grammarian **Crates**, who took up the effort out of rivalry with his professional competitor Aristarchus. For Attalus had sheepskins scraped <margin>p. 11.</margin> until they were thin and sent the Romans what they call **membrana** [parchment]; in memory of the sender, the Romans still call these membranes **Pergamenian** <note>original: "Pergamenē", the root of the word 'parchment'</note>.] But it was **Ptolemy** who discovered paper.

# Part II. II. CONCERNING THE DAY <note>original: ΠΕΡΙ ΗΜΕΡΑΣ (*Peri Hemeras*)</note>.

The Egyptians, however, count the following day from the evening until the evening again, because the cosmographers <note>Ancient writers who described the origins and structure of the universe</note> suppose that darkness existed before the ordering of the whole universe, and they name Night the mother of all things. ## II. CONCERNING THE DAYS.

---

1. **The** natural day is counted from the rising of the Sun until its setting, but not in the same way among all peoples. For the Babylonians establish that it extends from the rising of the Sun until the very setting of the same, making no mention of the night at all, as if it did not exist according to its primary substance, but rather occurred by chance. The Egyptians, however, starting from the evening, add the coming day until the following evening, because the cosmographers <note>Ancient scholars who described the physical and mythical origins of the universe</note> establish that there was darkness before the arrangement of the Universe, and they name Night the mother of all things. Whence the myth-tellers [say] that Diana <note>The Roman name for Artemis, goddess of the moon</note> and Apollo <note>The god of the sun</note> [were born] from Latona <note>Leto, a goddess associated with the darkness that precedes light</note>...

<columns>2</columns>

In the matter of causes, Joannes Lydus <note>A 6th-century Byzantine administrator and scholar</note> rarely departs [from his sources]; one should write, for instance, "not." <note>original Greek: οἷον μή (*hoion me*)</note> **Has.** <note>Reference to the editor, Charles Benedict Hase</note>

*The Egyptians [count] from the evening.*] Julius Caesar relates the same thing regarding the Gauls in *The Gallic War*, Book VI, chapter 18. Compare Creuzer, *Symbols*, volume I, page 393, note, where our passage is mentioned. **Rr.** <note>Reference to the editor, Friedrich Roether</note>

*Because of the — assuming darkness*] The Paris manuscript reads: *on account of the arrangement before this universe,* etc. <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸ τῆς πρὸ τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς διακοσμήσεως (*dia to tes pro toude tou pantos diakosmeseos*)</note> To this belongs the quote in the Orphic Fragments <note>Mystical poems attributed to the legendary Orpheus</note>, Fragment X, page 471, concerning the deliberation of the creator god with Night (from Proclus), where these things are found:

<column-break/>

*Maia, highest of the gods, immortal Night,* etc. <note>original Greek: Μαῖα, θεῶν ὑπάτη, Νὺξ ἄμβροτε (*Maia, theon hypate, Nyx ambrote*)</note> **Rr.**

*And to name the night...*] The Paris manuscript reads: *the night however,* etc. **Rr.** The Vatican manuscript reads: *and to consider night the mother of all things.* It comes back to the same meaning. **Sch.** <note>Reference to the editor, Nicolaus Schow</note>

*Whence the myth-tellers from Latona, etc.*] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, chapter 23, page 616 in the edition of Moser and Creuzer: *The second* (Diana) *is better known, whom we have received as born from the third Jove and Latona.* Compare Apollodorus, *The Library*, Book I, chapter 4, page 20 in Heyne’s edition, and Joannes Lydus in a larger fragment of the book *On the Months* at the end of the short work *On Omens*, page 266. **Rr.**

# ON THE DAY IN GENERAL.

<margin>1</margin> [they] make those who were born [twins], and indeed the first Diana (<note>original: *Ἄρτεμιν* (Artemin)</note>, as if she were the "air-cutting Moon" <note>original: *ἀερότεμιν Σελήνην* (aerotemin Selēnēn)</note>, that is, the Moon that cuts the air), and afterwards the Sun. Leto (<note>Latona</note>) would be Night; for through her, forgetfulness (<note>original: *λήθη* (lēthē)</note>) and sleep come to men. The Umbrians, however, an Italian people, reckoned the day from one midday to the next, just as astrologers do when casting birth charts.

2. All musical tones are produced by the movement of the planets: for Saturn moves in the Dorian mode, Jupiter in the Phrygian, Mars in the Lydian, and the others are moved by the remaining tones, according to the opinion of Pythagoras, following the sound of the vowels: for the star of Mercury produces *a* <note>alpha: $\bar{\alpha}$</note>, Venus *e* <note>epsilon: $\bar{\epsilon}$</note>, the Sun *ē* <note>eta: $\bar{\eta}$</note>, the star of Saturn *i* <note>iota: $\bar{\iota}$</note>, Mars *o* <note>omicron: $\bar{o}$</note>, and the Moon *u* <note>upsilon: $\bar{\upsilon}$</note>; while the star of Jupiter produces the tone of *ō* <note>omega: $\bar{\omega}$</note>. However, the sound of these tones does not reach us because of the immense distance.

---

*distance*) [The author notes that] *seven tones are produced (according to the Pythagoreans), which they call the diapason harmony, that is, the totality of the concert. In this, Saturn is moved by the Dorian, Mercury by the sound, Jupiter by the Phrygian, and so forth.* See Achilles Tatius, *Introduction to Aratus's Phenomena*, chapter 17, page 80 (Petavius edition, Verona) and Macrobius, who discusses this matter more extensively in *On the Dream of Scipio*, II. 1. page 118 and following (Bipont edition). See also Hermann on the *Orphic Hymns* XXXIV (33), page 296. — Appuleius in *Florida*, Book I, no. 4: *whether you preferred the simple Aeolian, the varied Iasian, the plaintive Lydian, the religious Phrygian, or the warlike Dorian* — on which passage Elmenhorst cites Lucian in *Harmonides*, who writes: "and to preserve the specific character of each harmony, the

<column-break/>

inspired quality of the Phrygian, the Bacchic <note>frenzied or celebratory</note> quality of the Lydian, the solemnity of the Dorian, and the polished nature of the Ionian." Boscha notes in the Index: *Floridus remarks that the Dorian song follows the modes D, La, Re, Sol; the Phrygian E, Mi, La; and the Lydian F, Ut, Fa.* See Thiersch, *Pindar*, vol. I, page 43 and following, and Plutarch, *On the E at Delphi*, page 389 E (from which Lydus seems to have drawn much in this passage) and Wyttenbach's commentary on him, page 284.
*the sound of the rhythms [does not reach] us — because of the distance*] Macrobius provides another reason in *On the Dream of Scipio*, II. 4. page 136: *Nor should we pass this over: we do not perceive the music born from the perpetual revolution of the heavens with a clear hearing because the sound is greater than the narrowness of human ears can receive.* <note>The editor Rr. notes this alternative view that the "music of the spheres" is simply too loud for humans to hear, rather than too far away.</note>

# DAY OF THE SUN.

...would have the power of Reason itself, which is good and excellent, equal and finite, and light and upright and eternal, masculine and on the right. For Reason (as it is said in the mystical word) possesses an essence, remaining once and for all within its own essence, and drawn back into itself, stable and permanent. Furthermore, the Monad <note>The Monad refers to the number "one" as a divine, indivisible principle</note> is referred to Apollo—that is, to the one Sun—who is called Apollo <note>original Greek: Ἀπόλλων</note> precisely because he is removed from the many <note>original Greek: ἄπωθεν τῶν πολλῶν (*apōthen tōn pollōn*). This suggests a Latin etymology where the Sun (*Sol*) is named for being the only (*solus*) star of its kind visible by day</note>.

6. It is known that natural philosophers attribute the second day to the Moon, as she both moistens and moderately warms; that is, she is the overseer of matter. ...composed of equal sides; but the female is oblong <note>original Greek: *heteromēkēs*, a geometric number where one side is exactly one unit longer than the other, such as 2 × 3</note>, possessing night and darkness because of its inequality. For the oblong number has its smaller side less by one, and its greater side more by one. ## II. ON DAYS 6—7.

...of sensible motion, and entirely separated from the intelligible <note>The "sensible" refers to things perceived by the senses, while the "intelligible" refers to things understood by the mind/intellect.</note>.

Finding these things to be so, Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many of the city's religious and legal institutions.</note> forbade the Romans from using the dual number <note>The "dual" is a grammatical category for exactly two things, distinct from singular and plural.</note> during festivals; for the Romans do not count as we do, saying "before four" and "before three," and then "before two"; rather, they omit the two. ...[of the tria]d and its power in perception; for the number belonging to it has granted birth, growth, and nourishment to all created things. And it is not without reason that it is said:

# II. ON THE SEVEN DAYS

According to Theophrastus <note>original: Θεόφραστον; a student of Aristotle and the "father of botany," who also wrote extensively on music and physics.</note>, there are three divisions of the music that moves all things: sorrow, pleasure, and divine inspiration. Furthermore, there are three movements of a body: locomotion, alteration <note>The OCR reads "nomos" (law), but the commentator later notes this is a scribal error for "alloiosis" (alteration/change).</note>, and progression. There are also three compositions of spheres: the center, the diameter, and the circumference. There are also three movements of the stars: forward motion, backward motion, and acronychal rising <note>original: ἀκρωνυχία; this refers to a star or planet rising in the east at the exact moment the sun sets in the west.</note>. There are also three differences among bodies: for some are material, some are airy, and some are fiery, as the Chaldean <note>Likely a reference to the "Chaldean Oracles," a mystical text of the 2nd century AD combining Platonic philosophy with Near Eastern wisdom.</note> teaches. There are also three aspects of every movement...

<margin>Diogenes Laertius, Book 5, Section 18: Aristotle said that education requires three things: nature, learning, and practice. Regarding this passage, see the remarks by Menagius.</margin>

**the music that moves all things]** The Parisian manuscript reads "the music that mingles all things." These remarks seem to be taken from Theophrastus's books *On Music*. Diogenes Laertius is the authority who states that Theophrastus wrote three such books. (Editor's note: Rr.)

**Furthermore — the movements are three]** Macrobius, in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* (Book 1, Chapter 6), says that every body is moved by seven motions: *for there is either approach, or retreat, or turning to the left or right, or movement upward or downward, or rotation in a circle* <note>original Latin: "aut enim accessio est, aut recessio, aut in laevam dextramve deflexio, aut sursum quis seu deorsum movetur, aut in orbem rotatur."</note>. This first type of motion Lydus mentions is what Nicephorus Blemmydes <note>A 13th-century Byzantine scholar.</note>, in his *Epitome of Physics* (Chapter 5), calls "the first and most sovereign." He further says there: "this is divided into the straight, the circular, and the mixture of these." Again on page 48: "For of all changes in place, there are three that are primarily simple: that around the center of the whole, which is circular; that away from the center, which is upward;

<column-break/>

and that toward the center, which is downward."
Nokkius states: "Plato established two kinds of motion: alteration and locomotion. In the *Parmenides* (Chapter 24), he says: 'whatever is moved must either be carried along or altered; for these alone are motions.' Aristotle, however, established a threefold motion. First, change of place (in respect to location) is called locomotion (*phora*); second, change of quality (in respect to kind) is called alteration (*alloiosis*); third, change of quantity (in respect to amount) is called growth and decay. See Aristotle’s *Physics* (Books 5, 7, and 8). Therefore, we do not hesitate to affirm that the corrupted word *NOMOS* [law] in the text was born from *ALLOIOSIS* [alteration], so that it should be written: 'the movements are three: locomotion, alteration, and progression'—that is, there are three changes: motion, variation, and increase." (Editor's note: Rr.)

**forward motion, backward motion]** The Parisian manuscript reads *prodismos* and *hypodismos* [shorthand forms of the Greek words for forward and backward movement]. (Editor's note: Rr.)

**for some are material]** I have restored the word "are" <note>original: ἐστὶν</note> from the Parisian Manuscript. (Editor's note: Rr.)

**as the Chaldean teaches]** See the notes of Boivinus on Nicephorus Gregoras (Paris, 1702) in various places. (Editor's note: Rr.)

-># TUESDAY<-

The three distinctions of music that moves [the soul] according to Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle; he argued that music arises from three emotions: pain, pleasure, and inspiration.</note> are: sorrow, pleasure, and divine inspiration. Indeed, there are also three motions of a body: locomotion, alteration, and growth. There are also three substances of spheres: the center, the diameter, and the circumference. There are also three motions of the stars: forward progress, retreat, and the highest station (or, the zenith). There are also three varieties of bodies; for some are material, some are airy, and some are fiery, as the Chaldean <note>Likely referring to the Chaldean Oracles, a collection of mystical texts used by late Neoplatonists.</note> teaches. Furthermore, there are three [dimensions] of every body—

<note>The following section is a philological commentary on the text above, specifically regarding the three dimensions of a body.</note>

**And three of each — length]** I suspect that instead of "motion" <note>original: κινήματος</note> one should read "body" <note>original: σώματος</note>, as the word "motion" may have arisen because the scribe's eye wandered from the following word "shapes" <note>original: σχήματα</note>. In place of "depth, length," the Parisian manuscript has the reversed order "length, depth." On this matter, see Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, I. 11, p. 550: "A body is that which has three dimensions: width, depth, and length." Compare also Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I. 5, p. 20, Bipontine edition. Nokke's annotation on this passage is as follows: "It is very unusual for width, depth, and length to be called 'motions' <note>original: κινήματα</note>." Plato, in *The Republic* VII, chapter 10, p. 528a, says: "It is correct to take the third [increase] in order after the second." This somehow concerns the increase of cubes and that which partakes of depth; that is, after planes and surfaces, which are extended in length and width (the second increase), <term>Stereometry</term> <note>The mathematical study of three-dimensional objects.</note>, or the doctrine of solids which extend in length, width, and depth (the third increase), must be treated. Hence he says he erred: "for although the method for the increase of depth was next, because it is difficult for investigation (so I read instead of 'ridiculous'), I skipped over it and spoke of astronomy after geometry, which is [the study of] movement 

<column-break/>

of depth." Therefore, what are "increases" <note>original: αὔξεις</note> for Plato are "motions" <note>original: κινήματα</note> for our author. But "increase" is, as we saw a little while ago, a type of "motion." What of the fact that Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, in his commentary on Hesiod, teaches: "the cube is a solid, as it has motion into length, depth, and width"? It seems, therefore, that we should read "and three are the motions of every shape: into width, depth, and length." But if anyone thinks the passage should not so much be corrected as explained, I certainly do not object—on the contrary, I support it with all my strength. For there are three types of motion: in length, width, and depth; and Nicephorus Blemmydes <note>A 13th-century Byzantine scholar and monk.</note>, in his *Epitome of Physics*, chapter 5, expressly says: "Regarding change of place, upward and downward are as in length; to the right and to the left are as in width; forward and backward are as in depth." Yet that word "each" is problematic; for these are not the shapes of "each motion," but only of "local motions" in a straight line, as the same Nicephorus remarks in the place cited.

RR.

### II. ON THE 7 DAYS

...shapes: width, depth, and length. There are also three circles that define the width of the zodiac: the summer tropic, the winter tropic, and the equator. One could say much more regarding the triad as it is perceived by the senses. Indeed, the entire universe is said to be composed of three powers: arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic. For the "intelligible" triad <note>A Neoplatonic concept referring to a higher reality beyond physical reach</note> exceeds the scope of this present investigation. No less is it possible to see this in the sensible realm <note>the physical world perceived by the senses</note> in the generation of animals: first there is the casting of the seed, second the preservation into kinds <note>the development of the species' characteristics</note>, third growth, and fourth perfection <note>reaching full maturity</note>. Because of this, I believe those concerned with agriculture safely sow and plant around the conjunctions or full moons, as the air is then more moist and moved toward the generation of things; but around the half-moons they cut timber, as much as is workable, and gather crops for storage, as the season is then drier.

### WEDNESDAY

...but in a circle: "For this reason, the soul is that which moves itself; it is necessary, however, that there be that which first moves: and this is a circle or a sphere." <note>Original Latin: "Hanc ob causam animus est id quod se ipsum movet... circulus autem hoc vel globus." This reflects the Pythagorean belief that circular motion is the most perfect and identifies it with the soul.</note> And thus it is indeed among things known by the intellect <note>intelligibilia</note>. Nonetheless, one may see the same in the world of the senses <note>sensibilia</note> in the generation of living creatures: for first is the injection of the seed; second, the transition into its kind; third, growth; and fourth, perfection <note>reaching full maturity</note>. Indeed, there are four turnings of the Sun <note>original: "Solis conversiones"</note>, by which all existing things are preserved: two equinoxes, and the summer and winter solstices. There are also four primary appearances of the Moon itself, serving as roots and beginnings: the new moon <note>interlunium</note>, the full moon <note>plenilunium</note>, and the two half-moons <note>dichotomi</note>. Each appearance possesses a different influence: for from the new moon until the first half-moon, it moistens; from there until the full moon, it heats; from there until the second half-moon, it dries; and from this point back to the new moon, it brings cold. Because of this, I believe those who are engaged in agriculture safely sow and plant around the new moons or full moons, as the air is then more moist and stirred for the generation of others; but around the half-moons, they cut timber for building and gather fruits for preservation, as the weather is then

growing as a half-circle, as if the globe were divided, and it is then called **halved** <note>original Greek: διχότομος (dichotomos)</note>: in the second stage, it now fills up by gathering its reviving fires into a whole orb, and it is then called **full**: in the third, it is made **halved** again, when it is contracted by decreasing to a middle point: in the fourth, it is thinned by the final diminishing of its light. — For it is first moist, then hot, then dry, and finally cold. <term>RR.</term> <note>Likely an abbreviation for *Res Rustica*, referring to classical agricultural manuals.</note>

<column-break/>

"From which I believe those concerned with agriculture," etc. <note>This is a Greek translation of the preceding Latin passage.</note> Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, Chapter 37: **"Certain things should be done in the fields while the moon is waxing rather than waning, and some the opposite—such as harvesting grain and cutting wood."** Palladius, *On Agriculture*, Book II, Chapter 22: **"In this month (January), timber for building should be cut when the moon is waning,"** etc. Book III, Chapter 4: **"Sowing is done well up until the twelfth day of the moon."** Compare also Book XII, Chapter 15 and Book XIII, Chapter 1. <term>RR.</term>

<note>The author uses these classical citations to prove that the "four-fold" nature of the lunar cycle was the foundation of ancient scientific and practical life.</note>

## II. CONCERNING THE DAYS. 8—9.

<margin>p. 23.</margin>
And while these matters pertain to the world of the senses and the intellect, regarding the numerical axiom, the fourth number is a square; for it alone is by nature generated as "equally equal" and "equal-membered" <note>original: ἰσάκις ἴσος ἰσομερὴς</note> from the same factors by both addition and power—that is, addition from two and two, and power from twice-two—displaying a most beautiful form of harmony that belongs to no other number. For this reason, it is also called "perfective" <note>original: ἀποτελεσματικὸς</note>; for if the numbers from one to four are added together in order, they complete a decad <note>the number ten; 1+2+3+4=10</note>.

<margin>C. VII.</margin>

If you expressed this thought in mathematical terms, it is 4 = 2 + 2 = 2 × 2 = 2². <term>RR.</term>

## II. CONCERNING THE 9 DAYS. ##

...a fivefold circular essence, from which they say the heavens were formed according to Aristotle. For the pentad <note>the number five</note>, having taken up the tetrad <note>the number four</note>—which holds the place of matter and serves as a substrate for things growing from it—increased it and led it toward that eternal revolution born of growth. For the pentad is the frontier of the decad <note>the number ten</note>, and is, as it were, an image of universal perfection. Aside from the Sun and Moon, there are five "wandering stars" <note>planets</note>, and there are five circles in the celestial sphere, and five zones. Among the philosophers, Zeus <note>Jupiter</note> is called the creator of sensation, and it was natural that the pentad should be dedicated to him according to its nature; for the pentad is kindred to sensation, <margin>p. 24.</margin> which is divided fivefold <note>the five senses</note>. For this reason, Pythagoras says that the number five is dedicated to Fate <note>original: Εἱμαρμένη (Heimarmene)</note>, since the word is that Fate rules over the world of the senses. This is why the oracle says that souls who have been restored surpass Fate:
> "For theurgists <note>practitioners of divine rituals or 'god-workers'</note> do not fall under the herd subject to Fate."

---

...from whatever point it began to turn, it returns to the same; thus, numbers are called "circular" which, when squared, end in themselves—such as five times five, which is twenty-five, ending in the digit five. Theo of Smyrna, page 60: "Certain numbers are called both 'circular-shaped' and 'restoring' <note>original: ἀποκαταστατικοὶ (apokatastatikoi)</note>; these are the ones which, when multiplied either by plane <note>squared</note> or solid <note>cubed</note>—that is, in two or three dimensions—return to the same number from which they began. The circle is such a thing: from whatever point it begins, it is restored to that same point. See Psellus in the same work, page 19." <term>RR.</term> <note>RR refers to the editor, Reinhold Rost.</note>

**from which they say — Aristotle]** These words and those

**and the wandering stars except the Sun etc.]** *Theologumena Arithmeticae* 25, page 24 (Ast edition): "That the wandering stars are five, excluding the sun and moon." <term>RR.</term>

**and the circles etc.]** *Theologumena Arithmeticae* 27, page 25 (Ast edition): "The parallel circles in the heavens are also five, etc." Compare Geminus, *Elements* chapter IV, and Nicephorus Blemmides, *Epitome of Physics* chapter 25, page 200. <term>RR.</term>

## II. CONCERNING DAYS 10–11.

...possessing the nature of both male and female, and <margin>p. 25.</margin> for this reason called "male-female" <note>original: *arrenothēlys*; a term for an androgynous or hermaphroditic nature</note> by the theologians. [The philosopher Plato] taught that the soul consists of seven numbers. ### III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

The number ten turns back upon itself; and for this reason the year was named **eniautos** <note>original Greek: ἐνιαυτός</note>, from "moving within itself" <note>original Greek: en heautō kineisthai</note>.

# 86 III. CONCERNING THE YEAR AND MONTHS

They say that, having surpassed all others in fortune, wisdom, and especially in <term>astronomy</term>, Julius Caesar went up to Rome and added eleven days to the lunar months, and in this way completed the <term>solar year</term>. <note>Julius Caesar’s reform in 46 BCE transitioned Rome from a lunar-based calendar to the solar Julian calendar.</note> [As for why it is called **bisexton** <note>original Greek: βίσεξτον; the origin of "bissextile" or leap year.</note>, it is because every four years the Romans count twice before the sixth <term>Calends of March</term> <note>The Romans did not add a "February 29th" at the end of the month; instead, they doubled the "sixth day before the first of March" (February 24th).</note>, and in doing so they observe the life-generating number; this number belongs to **Aphrodite**, and Aphrodite is the protector of the Romans <note>Venus Genetrix, the goddess Aphrodite, was claimed as the ancestral mother of the Julian family.</note>.] — Since the changeable body <note>Matter in the sublunary world.</note> was poured around the earth according to its own proportion of weight, it was necessary for that which was to approach the earth to share in every power. Therefore, God arranged the <term>lunar sphere</term>, which shares in every power of the active spheres, and placed it near the sensory universe as the overseer of the **elements**. For this reason, the mystical teaching conveys that **Hecate** is **four-headed** because of the four elements. The fire-breathing head of the **horse** clearly refers to the sphere of fire; while the head of the **bull**, bellowing with a certain divine sound, refers to the sphere of air;

---

<margin>p. 31.</margin>

Macrobius, *Saturnalia* Book I, chapter 14, page 268 of the Bipont edition. "That it is called **bisexton** — **Aphrodite** of the Romans." The Barberini manuscript says: "One must count the **bisexton** twice before the sixth Calends of March every four years," omitting the rest. The Paris manuscript agrees with the Barberini, but incorrectly writes **bisekton** <note>original: βίσεκτον</note> for **bisexton**. Regarding the **Bisexto** (or **Bissexto**), Macrobius in *Saturnalia* Book I, chapter 14, page 269 of the Bipont edition, writes: *lest the quarter-day be missing, Caesar decreed that every fourth year the priests, who had charge of the months and days, should intercalate one day in that month and place where, among the ancients, it was accustomed to be intercalated.*
