### III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

...nor being generated, like each of the numbers within the first ten <note>original: "decad"</note>, which is why the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who saw numbers as the fundamental reality of the universe</note> dedicate the number seven <note>original: "heptad"</note> to **Athena**. For they say that by the cycle of the seven-day period <note>original: "hebdomad"</note>, all immortal things are preserved. And for this reason, they call it the "mighty-fathered virgin" <note>original: "ombrimopatra," an epithet of Athena meaning she was born from the head of her father Zeus without a mother</note>, because it is the offspring of the **monad** <note>the number one, representing the source of all things</note>, which alone encompasses and gives substance to all things. For the monad is the cause of all, and the seven is also called "**judgment**" <note>original: "krisis"</note> because, by this number, all things reach their turning point. This is evident from the general span of human life: for in the sixty-third year (which comprises seven sets of nine), the birth is [judged, as the soul-governing power, which is the seventh, and the body-shaping power, which is the ninth, come together.] <note>This refers to the "Grand Climacteric," a year ancient Greeks believed was a major turning point or crisis in a person's life.</note>

<margin>C IV.</margin> 7. **Numa** <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome who organized their religious calendar</note>, honoring the odd number everywhere (but not the even), arranged the festivals of the month into three parts. For the **tripod** <note>a three-legged ritual seat</note> is sacred to **Apollo**, as it is an image of the monad. In this way, he also arranged the festivals <margin>p. 31.</margin> of the month. For as there are said to be three courses of the **Moon**—the swift, the middle, and the relaxed—because of which the poets call **Hecate** (that is, the Moon) "**of the Three Ways**" <note>original: "Trioditis," referring to Hecate's association with crossroads</note>, he divided the month into three festivals.

<column-break/>

...concerning the number seven <note>original: "septenario"</note>, the belief in its virginity became so established that it is also called **Pallas** <note>another name for Athena</note>. For it is believed to be a virgin because, when doubled, it produces no number that is confined within the ten <note>original: "denarium"</note>, which is established as the first limit of numbers. It is called Pallas because it proceeded from the offspring and multiplication of the monad alone, just as **Minerva** <note>the Roman equivalent of Athena</note> is said to have been born from only one parent. **RR.** <note>Likely the initials of the editor/commentator, Christian Gottfried Runge.</note>

<margin>2.</margin> "because the [thing] of the"] I have restored the article *to* from the Paris Manuscript. **RR.**

"and it is also called judgment"] **Olympiodorus** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> in his commentary on **Plato's** *Alcibiades I*, section 17. **Cr.** <note>Likely Friedrich Creuzer, a German philologist.</note> See also Creuzer’s very full note on Olympiodorus, p. 158, where he mentions our passage. Add *Theology of Arithmetic*, 45, p. 42 (Ast edition), where it says: "In illnesses, the seventh day is the day of judgment <note>the "critical day" when a patient either begins to recover or declines</note>." **RR.**

"for in the sixty... together"] The words "is judged" and those following up to "together" are omitted in the Paris manuscript. The parenthesis mark, which was after "birth" in Schow's edition, I have placed after "comprises" following Hase’s advice. Similar things are found in *Theology of Arithmetic*, 54, p. 53 (Ast edition): "For why is it now necessary to speak in detail about the seven-year climacterics <note>critical periods in life</note>..."

# ON THE UNIVERSE 6—7.

...as one who neither generates nor is generated, like each of the numbers within the first ten <note>original: "decade"</note>. Whence the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers were the building blocks of reality</note> call the number seven <note>original: "heptad"</note> the number of **Minerva** <note>The Roman equivalent of Athena, often associated with the number seven because she was born fully formed and did not "reproduce" numbers within the first ten</note>: for they say that by the circuit of the seven, all immortal things are preserved. And for this reason, they say she was a virgin born of a mighty father, since she is the offspring of the **monad** <note>the number one, representing the singular source of all</note>, which alone encompasses and constitutes all things: for the monad is the cause of all things. Moreover, it is called <term>krisis</term> <note>original: κρίσις, meaning judgment or a critical turning point</note> because, by its number, all things reach a turning point in one direction or the other. And this is apparent from the entire span of human life: for from the sixty-third year (which contains seven sets of nine <note>9 x 7 = 63, known as the "Grand Climacteric" or a major life crisis year</note>), the stage of life is judged, as the year which has the power to form the soul (which is the seventh) and that which has the power to shape the body (which is the ninth) coincide at the same time.

### III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

For the Moon is three-formed <note>original: τρίμορφος (trimorphos), referring to the three phases of the moon: waxing, full, and waning</note>, and why this is so can be understood from the oracle, which speaks thus:

> And I am a maiden of many forms, wandering the heavens,
> Bull-faced, three-headed, harsh, with golden arrows,
> Phoebe, mistress of endless arts, light-bringer to mortals, Eileithyia <note>The goddess of childbirth, here identified with the moon</note>,
> Bearing three distinct signs of a triple nature.

For as **Aristotle** says, the Moon makes her journey sharper <note>meaning faster</note> near the winter solstice, slower near the summer solstice, and uniform near the equinox. Therefore, the first festival of the month is called the **Kalends** <note>The first day of the Roman month</note> by the Romans, and the **New Moon** <note>original: Νουμηνία (Noumenia)</note> by the Greeks. The ancients called them "Kalends" based on a Greek meaning, from the high priest "calling out" <note>original: καλεῖν (kalein)</note> the assembly in the place called the **Royal Calabra** <note>A building on the Capitoline Hill in Rome where the priests announced the appearance of the new moon</note>, and announcing whether the festival of the **Nones** <note>The day of the first quarter moon, usually the 5th or 7th day of the month</note> should be observed on the fifth day or when the Moon is halved <note>the seventh day</note>, from which they tracked the middle of the month.

### III. ON THE YEAR AND MONTHS

For in the months that even now preserve the lunar festivals, he <note>The High Priest, mentioned in the previous section</note> indicated the **Nones** on the fifth day. At this time—on the thirteenth day and certain portions of the cycle—it is likely that the midpoint of the lunar *body* itself occurs, rather than the midpoint of its *light*. For the number thirteen is composed of the first two squares: four and nine (one even and one odd). These have as their "sides" <note>In geometry, the side is the square root</note> the number two for the even (representing the material form) and the number three for the odd (representing the active or efficient idea). This number <note>thirteen</note> was, for the ancients, the greatest and most perfect observation for their festivals. 

Indeed, the fifteenth day is properly the "middle of the month" <note>original: μεσομηνία (mesomenia)</note> by six degrees; for that is when the midpoint of the *light* itself occurs. Therefore, they also considered it a festival of **Jupiter** (as if he were the Sun), through whom we agree the Moon is illuminated. However, in the solar months <note>Months where the Nones and Ides fall later</note>, they indicated the **Nones** on the seventh day; for the number seven belongs to the Sun, as has been said before. It is clear that the shortest period of the Moon <note>The sidereal month</note> is twenty-seven days and some hours, while the period of its light <note>The synodic month, from new moon to new moon</note> is nearly thirty days. Thus, the first day is the **New Moon** <note>original: νεομηνία (neomenia)</note>, from which it is the Roman custom to call out the second...

They regarded the **Nones** as entirely unlucky <note>original: *nefastas*. In the Roman calendar, *dies nefasti* were days on which it was religiously forbidden to conduct legal business or public assemblies</note>, sometimes because of the fifth day, sometimes because of the "halved" moon. They did not even permit them to be called by this or that expression, but rather favored the mid-month arriving nine days later—that is, the **Ides**—or perhaps granted them honor for another reason, following the calculation of the lights <note>referring to the celestial bodies, the Sun and Moon</note>. # III. CONCERNING THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

We find that the name of the **Ides** <term>Ides: The midpoint of the Roman month, falling on the 13th or 15th day</term> was introduced among political leaders from the "form" (*eidos*) of the Moon <note>original: *εἴδους τῆς Σελήνης*. The Greek word *eidos* means form or appearance, referring here to the full moon</note>, but among the priests, it came from a type of sacrifice. They used to proclaim the **Nones** <term>Nones: Derived from the Latin word for "ninth," these fell on the 5th or 7th day of the month</term> on the fifth or seventh day after the **Kalends**, because each of these numbers is most appropriate for the celestial lights. From the **Nones** themselves until the **Ides** themselves, they observed exactly nine days in between, because the number nine is most suitable and natural to the Moon. For according to **Xenocrates** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Plato</note>, this number generates itself; for the progression up to the number nine is limitless and dwells within multitude. They called the new moon the **Kalends**; the second day of the month, they called "four days before" or "six days before" the **Nones** (as has been stated); the fourth day they called "one day before the **Nones**," because the number two was considered ill-omened <note>original: *ἀποφράξεσθαι τὴν δυάδα*. The "dyad" or number two was often seen as unlucky in Pythagorean and late antique thought</note>; the fifth day was the **Nones**; the sixth was "eight days before the **Ides**"; the seventh was "seven days before the **Ides**"; the eighth was "six days before the **Ides**"; the ninth was "five days before the **Ides**"; the tenth was "four days before the **Ides**"; the 11th was "three days before the **Ides**"; the 12th was "one day before the **Ides**"; the thirteenth was the **Ides**.

<margin>p. 37.</margin>

If the **Nones** fell on the fifth day and the month consisted of 30 days, then the 14th day was called "18 days before the **Kalends**" of the following month; if the **Nones** fell on the fifth and the month had 31 days, the 14th was "19 days before the **Kalends**" in the same way. But if the **Nones** fell on the seventh and the month had 31 days, then the 15th was "17 days before the **Kalends**." In the case of February alone, the 14th was "16 days before the **Kalends** of March," and so on, following the decreasing order of the number of the **Kalends**. ### IN GENERAL 7.

We find that the name of the **Ides** <term>Ides: The midpoint of the Roman month, typically the day of the full moon</term> was introduced into the language among political figures from the **form** <note>original: *ἐκ τοῦ εἴδους* (ek tou eidous)</note> (that is, from the appearance) of the Moon, but among the priests, it was derived from a type of sacrifice. They used to proclaim the **Nones** <term>Nones: A marker in the Roman calendar falling on the 5th or 7th day</term> on either the fifth or seventh day after the **Kalends**, because both numbers are most fitting for the celestial lights. From the **Nones** themselves until the **Ides** themselves, they placed only nine intervening days for this reason: that the number nine is the most suitable and naturally connected to the Moon. For according to **Xenocrates** <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Plato known for his theories on numbers</note>, this number generates itself; for the progression up to the nine-fold is infinite and linked to multitude. Therefore, they called the new moon the **Kalends**; the second day of the month they called "four days before" or "six days before" (as has been stated) the **Nones**; the fourth day, "the day before the **Nones**" (for the reason that the **dyad** <term>dyad: The number two, which in Pythagorean thought represented division or instability</term> was held to be ill-omened); the fifth day, the **Nones**; the sixth day, "eight days before the **Ides**"; the seventh day, "seven days before the **Ides**"; the eighth day, "six days before the **Ides**"; the ninth day, "five days before the **Ides**"; the tenth day, "four days before the **Ides**"; the eleventh day, "three days before the **Ides**"; the twelfth day, "the day before the **Ides**"; the thirteenth day, the **Ides**; the fourteenth day—if the **Nones** fell on the fifth and the month had thirty days—was "eighteen days before the **Kalends**" of the following month; if the **Nones** fell on the fifth and the month had thirty-one days, it was similarly "nineteen days before the **Kalends**"; but if the **Nones** were on the seventh and the month had thirty days, the fifteenth day was similarly "seventeen days before the **Kalends**." However, in **February** alone, the fourteenth day was "sixteen days before the **Kalends** of March," and thereafter, they decreased the number of days before the **Kalends**. But when there was a **leap year** <term>leap year: Latin *bissextum*, referring to the intercalary day added to the Roman year</term>, the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth days...

# III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

<column-break/>

...somewhat more sparsely. But **Antiphon** <note>a 5th-century BCE Athenian philosopher and orator</note> claims that the **Moon** shines with its own light, but the part of it that is hidden by the striking rays of the **Sun** is obscured; for it is the nature of a stronger light to dim a weaker one, which is exactly what happens with the other stars.

**Thales** <note>often called the first philosopher of the Greek tradition</note> and those following him judged that the **Moon** is illuminated by the **Sun**. **Heraclitus**, however, says that the **Sun** and the **Moon** undergo the same process: for being bowl-shaped in their forms, they are illuminated to our sight by moist exhalations <term>anathumiasis: vapors rising from the earth or sea which many ancient Greeks believed provided the "fuel" for celestial bodies</term>, but the **Sun** is brighter because it appears in clearer air. According to <margin>p. 40.</margin> **Eratosthenes** <note>the Head Librarian at Alexandria who famously calculated the Earth's circumference</note>, the **Moon** is seven hundred and eighty thousand stades <note>a Greek unit of distance; 780,000 stades is roughly 90,000 miles</note> distant from the **Earth**, and the **Sun** is four million and eighty thousand stades away. For the **Moon**, occupying the seventh zone <note>the innermost orbital sphere in the geocentric model of the universe</note>, is closer to the **Earth** than the other stars; for which reason they say it is not a pure compression of ether <note>the "fifth element" that makes up the heavens</note>, but a mixture—

---

The word **"the"** <note>original: "ton"</note> is used instead of **"about the divine,"** as it had been previously. (From **Plutarch**, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book II, 28, page 589, Wyttenbach edition. To be restored by Laurentius: **"the [Sun] undergoes"** instead of **"about the divine."** See also **Stobaeus**, *Extracts*, Book I, page 550, Heeren edition. Compare page 524.) — The word **"says"** after **"Moon"** is omitted — and from the word **"bowl-shaped"** it reads thus: **"for the stars, being bowl-shaped in their forms, receiving the rays from the moist exhalations, are illuminated to our sight, the sun being brighter, for it is carried in clearer air."** Compare Creuzer, *Dionysus*, page 255.

**But Antiphon—the Moon**] Regarding the phrase **"that the moon shines,"** the word **"claims"** <gloss>original Greek: "bouletai," meaning "he wishes to say" or "he maintains"</gloss> must be understood. This **Antiphon** (about whom see **Cicero**, *On Divination*, Book I, 51) was a **dream-interpreter** <term>oneirokritēs: a specialist who provides meanings for dreams</term>, or even a

<column-break/>

**soothsayer** <term>teratoskopos: literally "a viewer of wonders," an observer of portents and prodigies</term>. He wrote a work titled *On Truth*, and even before **Epicurus**, he did away with the concept of Divine Providence. Various scholars have discussed him, such as Taylor in *Lectures on Lysias*, chapter VII; Ruhnken in his *Dissertation on Antiphon* in the *Minor Works*, volume I; and Bergmann's second edition. See further Fabricius, *Greek Bibliography*, volume II, and Reiske’s notes on Artemidorus’s *Interpretation of Dreams*, page 442. — This man is distinct from **Antiphon the Philosopher and Mathematician**, who, in the passage concerning the nature of the moon among philosophers, is called **Antiphantus** in the editions of **Stobaeus** (*Extracts* I. 37). When **Heeren** suspected this name was a corruption, he was able to confidently correct it in that same place and in his Commentary.

# IN GENERAL 8.

<columns>2</columns>

...in a certain way. According to **Antiphon** <note>Antiphon the Sophist, a 5th-century BCE philosopher</note>, however, the **Moon** shines with its own internal radiance, but that part of it which is hidden is obscured by the arrival of the **Sun’s** rays; for it is so arranged by nature that a stronger fire obscures a weaker one, which indeed also happens in the case of other stars.

**Thales** <note>Thales of Miletus, often considered the first Greek philosopher</note> and those who follow his teachings judged that the **Moon** is illuminated by the **Sun**. **Heraclitus**, however, says that the **Moon** is affected in the same way as the **Sun**: for since they have the shape of a bowl <note>original: "scaphae", referring to a shallow boat or basin</note>, they are illuminated by moist vapor <term>anathumiasis: the ancient theory that celestial bodies were fueled by evaporating mists from the earth</term> so that they become visible; but the **Sun** is brighter because it appears in pure air.

The **Moon** is said to be distant from the **Earth** (as it appears to **Eratosthenes** <note>the scholar-librarian famous for measuring the Earth's circumference</note>) by seven hundred and eighty thousand stades <note>roughly 90,000 miles</note>, and the **Sun** by four million and eighty thousand stades. For the **Moon**, which occupies the seventh zone (that is, the seventh circle), is closer to the **Earth** than the other stars: for which reason it is not a pure globe of ether—

### IN GENERAL 8—10.

<columns>2</columns>

...they say it is, but composed of a mixture of ethereal and airy substance: for that part of it which appears dark, which some call the "face," is nothing other than mixed-in air; because air is naturally dark, it extends as far as the Moon itself. This, however, is a point that should not be overlooked. The "new moon" <note>original: *interlunium*</note> is called the head (the beginning) of the month by the ancients. They record ten appearances of the Moon by which the thirty-day cycle is completed; they are as follows: conjunction <note>original: *coitus*</note>, rising, crescent-shaped <note>original: *lunata*</note>, halved, gibbous <note>original: *amphicyrtos*</note>, full, then halved again, then gibbous again, then crescent-shaped again, then.... Others, however, maintain there are eleven appearances: for after the conjunction they also count the "birth," when the Moon is distant from the Sun by one part (that is, by one degree).

9. The Romans, therefore, as we have said, honored the Calends <note>the first day of the month</note> as the new moon, and after these in order the Nones, and in the third place the Ides. Hence Heraclitus does not miss the mark when he calls the month a "generation."

### III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS

11. Following the Calends <note>the first day of the month</note>, we find that time is divided in many ways: into eternity, into time, into season, and into the year. Eternity <note>original: *aiōn*</note>, then, is a kind of infinite circling of the celestial bodies, or the complete and perfect revolution of the entire heaven itself; whereas time <note>original: *chronos*</note> is the indefinite extension proceeding out of eternity. For this reason, Kronos <note>the god of time</note> is said to be the son of Ouranos <note>the god of the sky</note>; for time proceeds from the movements of the heaven. Thus, a "season" <note>original: *kairos*</note> is a specific instance or example of time, and is not time itself.

12. [Note that the Greeks made the beginning of the year from the 25th of December—that is, the solstice <note>original: *tropē*, the "turning" of the sun</note>—while the Romans did so after eight days, on the first of January. The Greeks observed the solstice itself, but the Romans observed the shadow of the sundial <term>gnomon|the vertical part of a sundial that casts a shadow</term> to see when it would first begin to shorten; for until those eight days have passed, the decrease of the shadow is imperceptible.]

-># ON THE UNIVERSE 11—13.<-

11. After the Calends, however, we find that time is divided in many ways: into eternity, into time, into season, and into the year. Eternity <note>original Latin: *aevum* or *aeternitas*</note>, then, is a certain infinite circuit of the celestial bodies (or spheres), or the complete and perfect revolution of the entire heaven itself; whereas time <note>original Latin: *tempus*</note> is an infinite progression proceeding out of eternity. For this reason, Kronos <note>the Greek god of time; associated with the Roman Saturn</note> is also called the son of Uranus <note>the personification of the Sky</note>; for time <note>Greek: *chronos*</note> proceeds from the movements of the heaven: so that a "season" <note>original Latin: *tempestas*, referring to a specific point or quality of time</note> is a specific instance of time, and not time itself.

12. The Greeks used to establish the beginning of the year from the 25th of December—observing, clearly, the turning of the Sun <note>the winter solstice</note>—while the Romans did so eight days later, on the first day of January. The Greeks followed the actual turning of the Sun, while the Romans followed the shadow of the gnomon <term>gnomon|the vertical part of a sundial that casts a shadow</term> to see when it would first begin to shorten; for until that eighth day, the decrease of the shadow is not perceptible.

13. Because of the process of generation <note>the creation and birth of things</note>, the movement of the heavenly bodies was made twofold. For if the movement were simple <note>moving in only one direction or at one speed</note>, nothing would have been procreated by it, as Aristotle also says in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*: "If there were only one movement, both [generation and corruption] could not exist, because they are opposites; for the same thing, while it remains the same and behaves in the same way, is naturally compelled to always do the same thing: so that there would be either constant generation or constant corruption. It is necessary, however, that there be multiple movements and that they..."

...and contrary, either in their direction or their irregularity; for contrary causes produce contrary effects. For this reason, it is not the primary motion <note>the rotation of the fixed stars</note> that is the cause of generation and decay, but rather the motion along the oblique circle <note>the ecliptic, the path the sun appears to follow</note>; for in this path, there is both continuity and the capacity for being moved by two motions.”

14. That they honored the year as a god is evident from the capital city of the Lydians itself. For Xanthus <note>Xanthus of Lydia, a 5th-century BCE historian</note> calls it both Sardis and Xuaris. If someone calculates the numerical value of the name "Sardis" <note>Using Greek isopsephy, where letters serve as numbers: Σ(200) + α(1) + ρ(100) + δ(4) + ι(10) + ν(50) = 365</note>, they will find three hundred and sixty-five units when adding them together. From this it is clear that the city was named Sardis in honor of the Sun, who completes the year in that many days. It is widely agreed even now that "New Sardis" signifies the New Year; indeed, some say that in the ancient Lydian tongue, the year itself was called "Sardis."

### III. ON THE YEAR AND THE MONTHS.

...if the ancient cycle was held in what they call a *lustrum* <note>original: λοῦστρον; a five-year period of purification</note>, that is, a five-year period (for it was a purification, and the mysteries of the Mother <note>Cybele, the Great Mother goddess</note> were performed during it), it seemed best later, in honor of **Mars** <note>original: Ἄρεος (Areos); the ancestral god of the Romans, as they say</note>, to renew the cycle every fifteen years. For the complete restoration of **Mars** is observed in two ways: the minor is fifteen years, and the middle <note>The editor suggests this should read "great"; see the marginal note</note> is seventy-nine years. That the Romans received **March** <note>original: Μάρτιον (Martion)</note> as their ancestral beginning of the year is clear from those they call **matrons** (that is, the noblewomen) feasting the household servants, just as it was the custom for the owners to do during the **Saturnalia** <note>original: Κρονίοις (Kroniois); the festival of Saturn</note>. Of these, some women serve the male servants out of honor for **Mars**, because of his superior nature; while the men (introducing a service to **Saturn** <note>original: Κρόνῳ (Kronō)</note> as a way of averting evil) served their own slaves, so that they might not truly suffer something that provokes divine resentment and fall into slavery under their enemies.

16. The Greeks called this the *Allotment* <note>original: Ἐπινέμησιν (Epinemēsin); the Indiction tax cycle</note> based on the nature of the event. For when the **Sun** enters **Libra** <note>original: Ζυγῷ (Zygō); the Balance</note>, it reveals the quality of the harvest; and at this time, those of old humanely distributed the taxes to their subjects...

# ACROSS THE WHOLE 15—16.

...they call it. For Antiquity, since it held the cycle (that is, the circle) of the *lustrum* <note>original: "lustri"; a five-year period of purification</note>, as it was called by them, which is a five-year period (for it was a purification, and the mysteries of the Mother <note>Cybele, the Great Mother goddess</note> then took place), it later seemed right to renew the cycle every fifteen years in honor of **Mars** <note>original: "Martis"; the ancestral god of the Romans, according to tradition</note>. For the perfect restoration of **Mars** is observed in two ways: the minor, which is fifteen years, and the major, which is seventy-nine years. That the ancestral beginning of the year, **March** <note>original: "Martium"</note>, was accepted by the Romans is also apparent from this: that the **matrons**, as they were called among them (that is, the noblewomen), provided food to the servants, just as the masters were accustomed to do during the **Saturnalia** <note>original: "Saturnalibus"</note>. From these rituals, the women serve the male slaves in honor of **Mars**, due to his superior nature; while the men—instituting a service to **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturno"</note> as a way of averting evil—served their own slaves, so that they might not actually be reduced to slavery by enemies after some blameworthy event had occurred.

16. The Greeks called this the *Allotment* <note>original: "Ἐπινέμησιν" (Epinemēsin); refers to the tax cycle or indiction</note> from the nature of the matter. For when the **Sun** is in **Libra** <note>original: "Libra"</note>, it signifies the condition of the crops, according to which the ancients humanely *allotted* <note>original: "ἐπένεμον" (epenemon); that is, distributed</note> taxes to their subjects (citizens)...

---

# IN GENERAL 23—25.

23. Fabius the senator was condemned by the senate because he was proven to possess more money than the amount established by law. # IN GENERAL 29—31.

...but since he was a maker of arms, so that the shields <note>The *ancilia*, the twelve sacred shields of Mars; one had fallen from heaven, and the others were copies made to protect the original.</note> which had fallen from heaven might not be worn out by always being moved, he made copies of those models. 31. I have changed "to those who sin" into "to those on the wagons," and "of wagons" and "of the wagon" into "of the wagons" and "of the wagon." <term>Rn.</term> <note>Likely David Ruhnken, a 18th-century classical scholar.</note> John [Lydus] plundered Dionysius. # IN GENERAL 32–35.

32. The Egyptians founded Philadelphia in Lydia. <note>Philadelphia was a city in modern-day Turkey; the author here claims an Egyptian origin for its settlers.</note>
33. **A vault** <note>original Greek: *psalis*</note> is a type of architectural feature having the form of a half-cylinder.
34. **Ceres** <note>The Roman name for the Greek goddess Demeter</note> presides over the founding of the city, just as **Earth** does; for this reason, they depict her wearing a crown of towers. She is also called **Cybele**, from the **cubic shape** <note>original Greek: *apo tou kubikou schēmatos*</note> because, according to the principles of geometry, **Earth** is characterized by a solid and stable nature, even though the Stoic philosophers define the earth as being spherical.
35. They say that **Astarte** (the Syrian goddess) is **Venus** <note>The Roman goddess of love, equivalent to the Greek Aphrodite</note>.

---

34. [On the phrase: "Demeter etc."] George Codinus, in *The Origins of Constantinople* (chapter 28, page 14 of the Paris edition): "The ancients call Demeter the 'Earth'; and since the Earth is the foundation of every city, as it supports all cities, she is fashioned as a tower-bearer." For this reason, Ovid in his *Fasti* (Book IV, line 219) calls her *turrita* (**towered**), and in Book VI (line 321) he calls her *turrigera* (**tower-bearing**) and describes her as being "encircled by a crown of towers." See also Creuzer’s *Symbolism* (volume II, page 40, note 56). The scholar Nokkius adds the following remarks to this passage: "Michael Psellus (page 53) writes: 'To the Earth they assigned the cube, as it is the most stable of bases.' Plato in the *Timaeus* (page 55 in the Stephanus edition) says: 'Let us assign the cubic form to the Earth; for of the four elements, Earth is the most immobile and the most easily molded of bodies, and it is necessary that such a body has the most secure bases.' Timaeus of Locris, in *On the Soul of the World* (page 98), states: 'From the square is born the cube, which is the most settled and steady body in every way.' Based on this, we should correct the entry in the *Suda* lexicon under the word 'cube,' which reads: 'square in every direction; a cube: so called from having a base all around'—whereas the original manuscripts show 'cube, every square etc.,' a

<column-break/>

reading that is worthless. The works of Hesychius, Zonaras, Photius, and the various Etymological dictionaries require the same correction. Aulus Gellius correctly writes in his *Attic Nights* (I. 20): 'Such are those things that are square on every side; which the Greeks call *kuboi* (cubes) and we call *quadrantalia*. For a cube is a figure square on every side. Indeed, squares, such as the faces of cubes, are stable and firm.' For this reason, the *Gudian Etymological Dictionary* states: 'the number four [*tetras*] is named from the word for seat [*hedra*]; because it provides (or perhaps contains) within itself the number three.'" [Note by Reiske].

[On the phrase: "even though it is spherical etc."] Plutarch, in *On the Opinions of the Philosophers* (III. 10): "Thales and the Stoics, and those who follow them, say that the earth is spherical." [Note by Reiske].

35. This excerpt is taken from the month of April (IV. 44, page 89 in Schow's edition). Cicero, in *On the Nature of the Gods* (III. 23): "The fourth Venus was conceived in Syria and Tyre, and she is called Astarte." Compare Eusebius in his *Preparation for the Gospel* (I. 10, page 25), whom the scholar Gesenius cites under the word **Ashtoreth** <note>Hebrew: עַשְׁתָּרΕΤ; the Canaanite and Phoenician goddess of fertility and war</note>. See also Creuzer’s *Symbolism* (volume II, page 65). [Note by Reiske].

### IN GENERAL 39—41.

...[one] of the flatterers in the senate had called him "Lord" <note>Latin: *dominum*, a term implying the relationship of a master to a slave</note> as if by way of a title of excellence. Augustus himself stood up and said, "Indeed, I have learned to converse with free men, but not with slaves."

40. On the third day before the Nones of August <note>August 3rd</note>, they used to kill dogs throughout Rome without restriction in honor of the geese. This was because the dogs had betrayed the Capitol by sleeping, whereas the geese had saved it by staying awake <note>This refers to the Gallic siege of Rome in 390 BCE, where the sacred geese of Juno alerted the Romans to a night attack that the guard dogs failed to detect</note>. Others, however, say they were accustomed to do this so that the dogs would not become a nuisance to the sick at night; others say it was so they would not harm men when driven to madness <note>rabies</note>. For at that time Sirius, the Dog Star <note>Latin: *Canicula*</note>, rises, which is also seen to be the cause of their rabies.

41. Comets exist in the hollows below the Moon, displaying a certain star-like nature. For they are not true stars, but "thickenings" <note>condensations</note> produced from the exhalation of the Earth, arising from that air which is caught by contact into the ether. For this reason, they are also carried around together with the ether at the same speed until they dissipate. When the ether, having a flow descending toward the lower regions, is caught, "Bearded Comets" <term>Pogonias: a comet with a tail resembling a beard</term> and "Jar-shaped Comets" <term>Pithos: a thick, rounded comet</term> are produced; but when the ether is caught obliquely, they are "Long-haired Comets" <note>Latin: *Cometae*, from the Greek for "hair"</note>. The Bearded ones fall away more quickly, but even more quickly than these, the Jar-shaped and the "Beam-shaped" <term>Docides: comets that appear long and straight like a wooden beam</term> fall away.

### IN GENERAL 42—45.

42. There are indeed many varieties of flavors, but nine general types: sweet, bitter, acidic, pungent, sub-sweet, harsh, slimy, austere, and salty.

43. If fire increases, a fever arises; it is a daily fever if it comes from air; a tertian <note>recurring every third day</note> if from water; and a quartan <note>recurring every fourth day</note> if from earth. Shivering usually precedes these. For when these aforementioned humors <note>bodily fluids</note> have been made thick by cold (as cold is a property of both water and earth), they cannot be pushed out through the denser parts as they enter through the gaps. Once they fall into these places, they cause constriction and compression; then, when they are driven by heat and dissolved or spread abroad, a necessary disturbance and motion is created—an affliction which is called "shaking and chill."

44. # CONCERNING THE UNIVERSE 50—52.

...they carve him and represent a stretched-out snake in the middle, taking the form of a hawk, as if containing a good spirit <note>original: agathos daimon; a benevolent deity or guiding spirit</note> (or god): and the whole figure is similar to our (that is, the Greek) letter Θ <note>The letter Theta was often associated with death (thanatos) but also represented the cosmos or the "Ennead" in certain esoteric traditions</note>.

51. The number eight <term>ogdoad|In Pythagorean thought, the number 8 was linked to justice and stability, but here it is viewed as "unlucky" regarding gestation</term> is feminine, infinite, and incomplete: for which reason, in the works of Nicomachus <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa, a celebrated Pythagorean mathematician (c. 60–120 AD)</note>, it is also called "born before the proper months" <note>original: ἠλιτόμηνος (ēlitomēnos); refers to a child born prematurely</note>. For the eight-month period of gestation seems to have no mathematical ratio to any of the musical harmonies (or concordant numbers). Therefore, births of eight months are not brought to full maturity; for being in the middle of those numbers that have the power to bring about an end, the number eight itself is found to be incomplete. Indeed, since it partakes of all material power, it has obtained the qualities of matter.

52. They say that lightning <term>fulmina|While often translated as 'lightning bolts,' the ancients viewed these as physical 'stones' or 'fires' hurled from the sky</term> exists when clouds are torn asunder. For when the earthy substance that is mixed with them is set on fire, that part which is ignited is carried down to the Earth with a crash by its own force. And if the clouds happen to be wetter, they are extinguished during the fall itself; but if they are more earthy, the fiery parts are forced out. Furthermore, they say there are two types of lightning, one of which is sharp, rare, and fiery, called "bright lightning" <note>original: κεραυνὸς ἀργής (keraunos argēs)</note>; the other is slow and smoky, called "flaming (or sooty) lightning" <note>original: κεραυνὸς ψολόεις (keraunos psoloeis)</note>. The former, because of its rarity, is carried down with such speed even before it fully ignites that it does not scorch those things which are of a thinner consistency; the slower type, however, is so composed that it con- <note>The text breaks off here; likely 'consumes' or 'burns'</note>

Their bodies were considered sacred or set apart by the gods and were typically buried where they fell or left untouched</term> unburied, as they remained undecayed; for when the moisture within them is snatched away by the fire, they are naturally preserved as if they had been roasted.

53. Thunder occurs when wind is trapped in a thick and rather moist cloud and is violently forced out through it; from this, the continuous masses of the cloud are broken, producing a roar (that is, a sound) and a great crash, which is called thunder—just like air driven forcefully through water. During the rupture of the cloud, the wind catches fire and flashes; this is called lightning.

...[the thunderbolt] is able to stain, as happens with soot, and even ignite certain things that lie in its path. For this reason also, the bodies of those struck by lightning were left unburied by the ancients, as they were seen to remain undecayed; for since the moisture within them is snatched away by the fire, they tend to remain preserved as if roasted. <note>original: extosta; likely a variant of 'extosta' or 'extorris,' referring to being parched or dried out by heat</note>

53. Thunder occurs when a wind <term>spiritus|In ancient meteorology, 'spiritus' or 'pneuma' referred to a pressurized vapor or air force thought to cause weather phenomena</term> is tossed about in a thick and moist cloud and is violently exploded through it. By this action, the continuous, packed-together parts of the cloud are broken apart and produce a roar (or sound) and a great crash, which is called thunder—very much like air that is violently agitated in water. However, if the ignited wind flashes during the rupture of the cloud, it is called lightning.

### IV. ON THE MONTHS IN DETAIL.

---

#### JANUARY.

1. Enough has been said by us regarding how the beginning of the priestly <unclear>year</unclear> was established as the month of January for the Romans by King Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, was credited with reforming the calendar to include January and February.</note>. We must now speak of Janus himself: specifically, who he is and what the ancients believed about him. Labeo <note>Cornelius Labeo, an expert on Roman religion whose works are now lost except for fragments like this.</note> therefore says that he is called Janus Consivius, that is, the Counselor; Janus Caenulus, as if he were "of the feast"; Patricius, as if he were "the native-born"; Clusivius, in place of "the god of the path"; Junonius, that is, "of the air"; and Quirinum,

<note>original: "Κουσίβιον" or "Κονσίβιον"</note> ...while *Kousibion* or *Konsibion*, that is, *Consivius*. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I. 9.: *Janus Consivius, named from sowing [conserendo], that is, from the propagation of the human race, which is sown with Janus as the progenitor.* <note>The scholar argues Janus represents the beginning of human life.</note> Compare Gerard Vossius, *On Idolatry* 11. 16. It is easy to understand, then, why Lydus <note>Joannes Lydus, a 6th-century writer on Roman customs.</note> added the term "counselor" <note>original: "βουλαῖον"</note>. Since the person who produced the Marinian Transcript could not make sense of this, he changed *kousibion* to *kousilion* [counsel]. **Rr.** <note>"Rr." likely refers to the editor, Reifferscheid.</note>

*Janus Caenulus, as if, feasting*] The Paris Codex reads *Janus Caenulus, that is, fond of feasting* <note>original: "εὐωχαστικόν"</note>. Furthermore, I do not find "Janus Caenulus" or "Coenulus" in other

<column-break/>

Latin writers. **Rr.**

*Clusivium — traveler*] The Paris manuscript reads *Clusivium — of the appearance* <note>original: "εἰδιαῖον"</note>. Macrobius, in the place cited above, joins Clusivium with Patulcius <note>Titles meaning "the shutter" and "the opener."</note>, so that this surname of Janus must be derived from the verb "to close" [claudere]. For this reason, Lydus incorrectly interprets it as "traveler" <note>original: "ὁδιαῖον"</note>. Perhaps Lydus is looking back to Cicero’s *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chapter 27, where he derives the name of Janus from "going" [eundo]. **Rr.**

4. As the Sun begins to extend the day, the consul comes forth, and the day is one of festival and truce. For the sake of a good omen, the magistrates appeared on the speaker's platforms <note>original Greek: *bēmata*, the rostra or high platforms in the Forum</note>, and all the armies gathered with their regalia. They also gave laurel leaves, which they called *strena* <term>strena: a ritual New Year's gift, traditionally associated with the goddess Strenia, meant to ensure a prosperous year</term>, in honor of a certain deity of that name, who is the overseer of victories. According to the Greeks, the word *strena* signifies a "good beginning" based on military alertness <note>original: *entrekheia*</note>; for it is not (as the common people think) intended for the sake of games and leisure. # JANUARY.

### 4.
As the Sun, therefore, lengthens the day, the consul begins his duty, and it is a day of festival and rest. For the sake of a favorable omen, the magistrates were on the speaker's platforms and all the armies were gathered with their standards. In ancient times, they used to give each other dried figs, starting the year with sweet food as a symbolic offering. They also gave laurel leaves, which they called *strenae* <term>strena: a ritual New Year's gift, traditionally associated with the goddess Strenia, meant to ensure a prosperous year</term>, in honor of a certain goddess of that name who presides over victories. *Strena* in Greek signifies *euarkhismon* <note>original: εὐαρχισμόν — "a good beginning"</note> (that is, vigor) in military skill; for it is not (as the common people think) given for the sake of mockery or leisure. But Elpidianus, in his book *On Festivals*, is the authority that *strena* is called "health" in the Sabine tongue <note>The Sabines were an ancient Italian people whose language influenced early Rome</note>, which is why laurel leaves were given; for this tree is a producer of health. For neither the "sacred disease" <note>epilepsy</note> nor a troublesome demon will haunt the place where there is laurel, just as lightning will not strike where there is a fig tree, since it has the power to drive away poisons.

---

*...which is given on a religious day for the sake of a good omen from the number, by which a second and third coming of similar benefit is signified, like "trena," with the letter S prefixed, as the ancients used to do in "loco" and "lite" <note>referring to archaic Latin spelling variants</note>. Du Cange, Glossary of Latin on "Strena," which he interprets by the word "good beginning" [euarkhismon]. From a passage of Athenaeus and the interpretation of Du Cange, I have corrected our passage, which had "good dancing" [euorchēsmōn] instead of "good beginning." Moreover, the words "not for... the sake of ease" have some difficulty for me, and I would not dare to contend that my interpretation is right in every part. Rr. <note>Johann Jacob Reiske, 18th-century scholar</note>*

*Elpidianus] This writer seems worth adding to those who wrote about festivals, such as Nicomachus and others. Cr. <note>Friedrich Creuzer, 18th-19th century philologist</note>*

*Sacred disease] that is, epilepsy, the comitial disease <term>comitial disease: epilepsy was so called because its occurrence during an assembly (comitia) was seen as a bad omen, requiring the meeting to be canceled</term>, the falling sickness, the Herculean, or the childish. See Castelli's Medical Lexicon. — Apuleius, Apology 486. p. 509. ed. Leiden. Our people call it not only the "greater" and "comitial" disease, but even the "divine" disease, just as the Greeks truly named it the "sacred disease": namely because it violates the rational part of the soul, which is by far the most holy. Rr.*

5. That laurel leaves were given along with the dried figs is evident from the fact that, even to this day, it is a custom to place laurel leaves in the containers of dried figs. However, the custom has persisted even as it changed due to the increase of wealth;

For this reason, they are named in this way, just as *Tarentina* cakes are named after Tarentum, *Canobica* after Canobus, and *Copta* <note>a "pounded" cake</note> after Coptos. A certain Samian was the first to prepare bread by mixing it with honey, through which he also discovered the so-called sesame in Samos; hence the place has a name related to that of the fruit.

6. In Rome, the emperors used to receive the officials with a kiss, as a tribute to liberty, after the tyrants were driven out by Brutus, the Roman consul <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, the legendary founder of the Roman Republic who overthrew the last king, Tarquin the Proud</note>.

# IV. SPECIFICALLY ON THE MONTHS. 7.

7. On this day <note>referring to the first of January</note>, the Emperor Trajan <note>Roman Emperor from 98 to 117 AD, known for his military conquests and public works</note> dedicated a temple to the Fortune of All. He decreed, according to sacred law, that no one except the person performing the sacrifice should taste the sacrificial meat. — — Fate <note>original: *Εἱμαρμένη* (Heimarmene)</note> is named, as it were, "the threaded thing" <note>original: *εἰρομένη* (eiromenē)</note>, because it requires time and extension so that the connection <note>original: *εἱρμός* (heirmos)</note> of underlying events might be preserved.

> For without God, no mortal is fortunate.
> Alas, how uneven are the fortunes of mortals!
> For some fare well, while others meet misfortunes—
> —though they act piously toward God.

<margin>p. 61.</margin> The Romans, believing that nothing else exists besides human happiness, have come to believe that she [Fortune] alone leads all things. They named her *Fortuna* from the word for "bringing" or "movement" <note>original: *φορᾶς* (phoras). Ancient linguists often linked the name Fortuna to the Latin verb *ferre*, meaning to bring or carry</note>. Now, those who are inclined toward virtue, who keep God in mind, and who anchor better hopes in immaterial and blessed things, look down on the goods of this world. For if Fortune exists, there is no need for God; but if God has power, Fortune is nothing, for the name of Fortune is something random and without essence. Human affairs are like a ladder...

---

->JANUARY.<-

7. On this day, Trajan dedicated a temple to the Fortune of All, after he had decreed by a sacred law that no one, except for the one who had performed the sacrifice, should taste the sacrificial meat. — — Fate <note>original: *Εἱμαρμένη* (Heimarmene)</note> (that is, Necessity) is named, as it were, "the threaded thing" <note>original: *εἰρομένη* (eiromenē)</note>, because time and distance are required so that the connection <note>original: *ὁ εἱρμός* (ho heirmos)</note> of substances may be preserved.

For without God, no mortal is happy. Alas, how unjust are the affairs of mortals! For some manage their affairs successfully, while for others, fates occur—even for the pious—from God.

The Romans, thinking that there was nothing else but that happiness which exists among men, judged that she alone rules the universe, and she was called Fortune <note>original: *Fortuna*</note>—from the word "to bring" <note>original: *ferendo*</note>—a name consistent with its meaning. **Therefore, those who are turned toward virtue and are mindful of God, and who direct their prayers toward things free from matter and the body—the blessed things—these people place little value on those goods which are here (that is, earthly things). For if Fortune exists, there is no need for God; but if God can do anything, Fortune is nothing: for the name of Fortune is something rash and empty.**

---

....of the one who is pious toward God. — Furthermore, these verses are by Euripides, preserved from the *Scyrians*, as it seems to Grotius. Gataker, in his *Posthumous Adversaria* (page 534), attributed them to the *Syleus*. Stobaeus, who himself includes this fragment in Title 105, maintains it was taken from the *Scyrian*. In the fragments of Euripides from Musgrave’s edition (page 471 b), it is read as follows: *Alas, how uneven are the fortunes of mortals. For some fare well, while for others hard calamities are present, even though they act piously toward the gods and live a life of careful thought; they live without shame, though not according to what is just.* Here, indeed, the first verse found in our author is missing,

# JANUARY.

Human affairs tend to be equalized gradually because of their own unequal motion: for in one day, as someone once said, it has swept one man down and raised another up, since none of the things that belong to us are accustomed to remain in the same state, but are turned about in various ways. Do not rulers emerge from private citizens, and private citizens from rulers, the poor from the rich, and the wealthy from the poor, and the famous from the neglected, while the most illustrious emerge from the obscure? Those who desire wealth immoderately turn out worse: for riches are more the servants of depravity than of uprightness, as the orator says <note>original: "pravitatis magis, quam probitatis ministrae sunt" — likely referring to the Greek rhetorician Isocrates</note>: and I believe that with these things in mind, Plato said that no one becomes the master of the greatest wealth unless he had first suffered a loss in his soul.

8. First, therefore, as we said, on the day of the <term>Kalends</term> <note>The first day of the Roman month</note>, the priests proclaimed from the <term>Sibylline oracles</term> <note>A collection of prophetic utterances consulted by the Roman state in times of crisis</note> that for the sake of health everyone ought to taste pure wine <note>original: "merum"</note> early in the morning before any other food, to ward off <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagram" — a painful form of arthritis historically associated with rich diets</note>. It should be known that on the day of the <term>Kalends</term>, the Sun is in its highest state, and the Crown <note>The constellation Corona Borealis</note> sets in the morning.

9. On the following day, which is the fourth day before the Nones of January <note>January 2nd</note>, they held holidays because of the solemnities of the <term>Equiria</term> <note>An ancient Roman festival involving horse races, usually dedicated to Mars</note>. These men, before they went forth to the equestrian contest, performed sacred rites to the <term>Manes</term> <note>The spirits of the ancestors</note> in the presence of the pontiffs; in the streets, however, they distributed <term>miliarisia</term> <note>A silver coin introduced in the later Roman Empire</note>, as they were called among them, to the common people in honor of Scipio <note>Likely Scipio Africanus, the famed Roman general</note>: for he was the first...

10. After this come the <term>Vota Publica</term> <note>original: "βοτὰ πούβλικα" — a phonetic Greek rendering of the Latin for "Public Vows"</note>, which are, as it were, public prayers. 11

He, during the one hundred and ninth Olympiad, because of a shortage of gold, distributed <term>miliaresia</term> <note>A silver coin of the later Roman and Byzantine periods</note> that he had manufactured to the soldiers, while Hannibal was threatening the state's affairs. 10. After that day come the <term>Vota Publica</term> <note>original: "δημόσιαι εὐχαί" — Public Vows or prayers for the well-being of the state</note>. They did this, moreover, in honor of liberty, and the magistrates permitted it, yielding to the custom as if it were law. And the consuls would report on the <term>auguries</term> <note>original: "οἰωνοσκοπίαν" — the practice of divining the future by observing birds or other natural signs</note> to the emperors, from which it was understood what sort of year it was likely to be. 14. ...of February, **Euctemon** <note>A 5th-century BCE Athenian astronomer</note> says that **Cancer** <note>The Crab constellation</note> sets, while **Callippus** <note>A 4th-century BCE astronomer who refined the lunar calendar</note> says that **Aquarius** <note>The Water-Bearer</note> rises—which **Hipparchus** <note>The famous 2nd-century BCE astronomer who discovered the precession of the equinoxes</note> calls **Deucalion** <note>The Greek "Noah" who survived a great flood</note>—amidst the glens and ravines of the mountains. # IV. ON THE MONTHS INDIVIDUALLY. 19—20.

<margin>p. 68.</margin>
> 19. "What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?" says the Lord. "I am full; I do not want burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, nor the blood of bulls and goats, not even if you come to appear before me. For who has sought these things from your hands? You shall no longer tread my court. If you bring fine flour, it is a vain incense, an abomination to me. ### FEBRUARY.

<margin>Cav. I.</margin> 20. The month of February received its name from **Februa**, a goddess addressed by that name; the Romans adopted **Februa** as an overseer of the purification of things. ## FEBRUARY.

20. The name of the month of February was created from **Februa**, a goddess called by that name. The Romans accepted **Februa** as the presiding power who possessed the strength for purifying things. Regarding the sacred rites and holidays of this month, see Sibrandus Siccama, *The Fasti of the Roman Calendar*, chapter 8 (in Graevius's *Treasury*, volume VIII); regarding the name, see Petrus Morestellus, *Philomusus* II. 3. Anysius — *the god of the underworld, etc.* <note>original Greek: ᾿Ανύσιος — τ. καταχθόνιον κ. τ. λ.</note>] I see that Anysius is mentioned by no other ancient writer. — After "underworld," the word "Jupiter" <note>original Greek: Δία (Dia)</note> is to be understood. Book X, line 198, and Creuzer, *Symbolism*, volume II, page 917. They believe the month of February is consecrated to Juno, because to the Natural Philosophers, Juno appears to be the lower air; and purification is clearly appropriate for the air. Not only is it called February, but also *Februatus*, because the goddess who presides over this month is celebrated in sacred rites as both *Februata* and *Februalis*.

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 21.

...month it begins to move, swimming in the womb, and in the ninth month it is completely finished and hastens toward its exit. And if it is female, this happens during the ninth month; but if it is the stronger sex <note>original Greek: "κρεῖττον" (better/stronger), a common ancient designation for the male</note>, it happens at the beginning of the tenth, because the number nine, being female and related to the Moon, is associated with matter, while the number ten is "perfect" and male. Male and female are created according to the mastery of heat: when the heat in the seed is abundant, since the solidification <term>solidification: ancient physicians often compared the formation of an embryo to the "curdling" of milk into cheese</term> happens quickly, it becomes male; and when the heat is overcome, it becomes female. What is solidified more slowly is also formed more slowly. That this reasoning is true is shown by the fact that males who are miscarried <margin>p. 70</margin> even within forty days fall out already formed, whereas females even after forty days are still fleshy and unshaped. After the pregnancy, they say the infant is released from its swaddling clothes on the third day after birth; on the ninth day it grows strong and can endure being touched; and on the fortieth day it begins to smile and recognize its mother. During the reversal of its elements <note>referring to the process of bodily dissolution or death</note>, nature observes these same numbers again in reverse, and through the same stages by which the body was composed,

---

the thirty-sixth, and is completed in its limbs from the fifty-first day. — Asclepiades <note>a Greek physician who practiced in Rome in the 1st century BCE</note> says that for males, differentiation <term>differentiation: the process where the embryo's organs and limbs become distinct</term> occurs from the twenty-sixth day and is completed within fifty parts; for females, they differentiate in two months and are completed in four months. Compare Aristotle, *History of Animals* VII. 3. and Empedocles in Sturz’s edition, p. 438 and following, where more is said. Rr. <note>original: "Rr." refers to the scholar Johann Jakob Reiske</note>

The child becomes female or male depending on whether the power of heat is greater or lesser: indeed, when the heat in the seed prevails—since the "curdling" <term>coagulatio: ancient physicians often compared the formation of an embryo to the way milk curdles into cheese</term> is accelerated—it is rendered male; but where the heat is suppressed, it becomes female. Furthermore, that which is curdled more slowly is also formed more slowly. 

That we speak the truth is indicated by this fact: that male offspring, even within forty days, if they are expelled through a miscarriage, fall out already formed, whereas females, even after forty days, are still fleshy and unshaped. <margin>Chapter IV.</margin> 25. The Romans call a public servant a *vernaculus* <note>original: "Βέρνακλον," a term for a slave born within the master's household rather than purchased</note>. ### IV. ON THE MONTHS IN DETAIL. 27.

...taking up and destroying <note>original Greek: *aireseōs kai anaireseōs*</note>, as they say he was named, but rather from "to help" <note>original Greek: *arēgein*</note> and to assist in circumstances of violence and battle; or as "arctic" <note>original Greek: *arktikos*</note> and the cause of change (they assign Capricorn to him as his exaltation); or Ares, the one honored by "males" <note>original Greek: *arrhenōn*</note> alone; or from the word "to fight" <note>original Greek: *marnasthai*</note>.
<margin>p. 75.</margin>
Mars was the discoverer of bronze and iron. The natural philosophers sometimes join Aphrodite <note>Venus</note> to him, and sometimes to Hephaestus <note>Vulcan</note>; this hints that generation proceeds from the moist and the hot, as it were, by joining the fiery substance to the moist substance. Or also, it is because Scorpio is common to them: Mars rules the "sting," while Aphrodite rules the "claws" <note>in ancient astrology, the "claws" of the Scorpion were the sign now known as Libra, the sign of balance ruled by Venus</note>. But Aphrodite turns away from Mars, just as in the myth, because winter follows the specific atmosphere of Mars, whereas Aphrodite is temperate. Thus they are opposed to one another in a general sense; yet they seem to be joined to each other in the sequence of the seasons, for after winter, spring is brought back. Mars is worshiped with the sounds of weapons and trumpets, and for this reason the Romans performed his first festival, calling it the *Armilustrium* <note>original: *Armiloustrion*</note>, which is to say, a "purification of weapons," so that neither winter nor any other circumstance might hinder the movement of weapons on the Field of Mars <note>original Greek: *Areos pediō*</note>. His name according to the Egyptians is *Pyroeis* <note>meaning "The Fiery One"</note>, hence he is also called *Xanthikos* <note>meaning "The Golden" or "The Fair"</note> among the Macedonians; but the Greeks, as has been said, called him Ares from his deeds. # MARCH.

(that is, from "removal") and destruction <note>original Greek: *anaireseōs*</note> they say he was named, but rather from "helping" <note>original Greek: *arēgein*</note> and providing aid in the perils of force and battle; or perhaps as "originating" <note>original Greek: *arktikos* — here suggesting the start of a movement</note> and the author of change (they also assign to him his exaltation <note>term: *hypsōma* — the astrological sign where a planet's influence is most powerful</note>, that is, his highest point or summit, in the sign of Capricorn). Others say he is Ares because he is worshiped by males <note>original Greek: *arrhenōn*</note> alone, or from the word for "fighting" <note>original Greek: *marnasthai*</note>.

Mars was the inventor of bronze and iron. Natural philosophers <note>term: *Physici* — ancient thinkers who explained mythology through the laws of nature</note> link Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> sometimes with him, and sometimes with Vulcan <note>Hephaestus</note>; they do this to obscurely signal that generation <note>the creation of life</note> comes from a moist and hot nature, joining a fiery essence to a moist one. Or perhaps it is because the sign of Scorpio is common to them both, since the "sting" belongs to Mars, while the "claws" <note>original: *forcipes* — ancient astronomers often viewed the constellation Libra as the "Claws" of the Scorpion, and Libra is ruled by Venus</note> belong to Venus. However, as it happens in the myth, Venus turns away from Mars, because winter accompanies the specific nature of Mars, whereas Venus represents a well-tempered climate. Thus they are opposites, yet not entirely: for they seem to be joined by the steady progression of the seasons; for after winter, spring arises. Mars is worshiped with the clashing of arms and trumpets, and for this reason the Romans held his first festivals in this month, calling them the *Armilustrium*, which is a purification <note>original: *lustratio*</note> of weapons, held when neither winter nor any other event prevented the handling of arms in the Field of Mars <note>original: *Campus Martius*</note>. Among the Egyptians, his name is *Pyroeis* <note>meaning "The Fiery One"</note>, from which also comes the name *Xanthikos* <note>meaning "The Golden" or "Yellow-Red"</note> among the Macedonians; but the Greeks, as was said, called him Ares after his deeds. For no one...

# IV. SPECIALLY CONCERNING THE MONTHS. 29.

<columns>

Diogenes <note>This refers to an author cited by Joannes Lydus, though modern scholars debate which Diogenes is meant</note> says that both human beings and beans arose from the same state of decay. He provided clear evidence for this: if someone chews a bean and grinds it with their teeth, then places it in the warmth of the sun's rays for a short time, then steps away and returns shortly thereafter, they would find it smelling of human slaughter. 

<margin>p. 77.</margin> Furthermore, if one were to place a tiny bit of the flower, while it is blooming, into a ceramic vessel, put a lid on it, and bury it in the earth for ninety days, and then after those ninety days were to dig it up and remove the lid, they would find that in place of the bean, there had formed either the head of a child or the private parts of a woman. 

Therefore, according to **Pythagoras** <note>The famous Greek philosopher and mathematician who famously forbade his followers from eating beans</note>, one must abstain from the bean, just as one must abstain from the so-called "golden-vegetables" <note>likely orache or mountain spinach</note>, since their origin is also from the menstrual blood of women. For this reason, beans are thrown into tombs for the sake of the salvation of human beings. Experience also proves that the bean (*kyamos*) is named after blood (*haima*); for if someone soaks a bean for a full day and night, they will find the water inside it has become like gore <note>original: *lythron*—the dark, clotted blood of a wound</note>.

### IV. ON THE MONTHS INDIVIDUALLY. 32—34.

<columns>

...just as we regard **Asclepius** <note>original: *Ἀσκληπιόν*—the Greek god of medicine and healing</note>. It would be the same thing; for just as we, taking the **Sun** <note>original: *Ἥλιον*</note> to be Asclepius after its setting, when night comes on, [consider] him the cause of sleep and night and rest, the cause and giver of health — — so they tell the myths. But the man of **Chaeronea** <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD), the famous Greek biographer and philosopher who lived in Chaeronea</note> wishes **Isis** to be the **Earth**, and **Osiris** the **Nile**, and **Typhon** the **sea**, into which the Nile falls and disappears.

33. The Greeks depict **Fortune** <note>original: *Τύχη* (Tyche)—the personification of luck and fate</note> with the face of a cow; but I think she is the liquid essence <note>moisture or water</note>, which is why it is the custom for the Romans to call her **Aequa** <note>original: *ἀκουὰν*—the author is phonetically rendering the Latin *aqua* (water) or *aequa* (equal) into Greek. He is linking the Roman goddess of "Equality" or "Fairness" to the nature of water</note> from **equality** <note>original: *ἰσότητος*—the Greek *isotes* mirrors the Latin *aequitas*</note> (for water is uniform and equal in nature). <margin>page 79</margin> And she is rightly named *Aequa* by them, since they name equality, or uniformity, by derivation from the word for water.

# IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 38.

<column-break/>

...ruled over Asia, from whom the Cabiric initiation rite <note>The mysteries of the Cabiri, ancient and secretive deities worshipped in Samothrace</note> is derived. The fourth was the son of **Zeus** and **Semele**, for whom the **Orphic mysteries** were performed, and by whom wine was first mixed with water. The fifth was the son of **Nisus** and **Thyone**, who established the triennial festival <term>trieteris; a festival held every third year according to ancient reckoning, though it actually occurred every two years</term>. These are the traditions of the **Greeks**. However, the **Romans** say that **Dionysus** is the "Reveller of **Cithaeron**" <note>original: "Bakcheuten tou Kithaironos"</note>, as if he were a reveller running up toward the heavens; they named him **Cithaeron** after the harmony of the seven stars <note>referring to the seven classical planets: the Sun, Moon, and five visible planets</note> which resembles a cithara <note>a stringed instrument like a lyre</note>. This is why, in the myths, **Hermes** gives the lyre to **Apollo**—it signifies **Reason** <note>original: "Logos"</note> providing the **Sun** <note>original: "Helios"</note> with the harmony of the entire universe. Dionysus’s mysteries were performed in secret because the Sun's connection to the nature of the whole is hidden from everyone. They included phalluses in his rites as symbols of the generative organs, and a mirror to represent the clear sky, and a sphere to represent the **Earth**. For as **Plato** says in the <margin>p. 83.</margin> ***Timaeus***: "Earth indeed possesses the spherical form." Likewise, **Pythagoras** says that souls are sown within the ten spheres in this same way. They called him "Fire-born" <note>original: "Pyrigenea"</note> and "All-powerful" <note>original: "Pankrates"</note> in the rituals because the Sun is fiery by nature and commands and rules over everything. They also associate the panther with him...

...they create the name to be receptive, as if the **Earth**, which is **all-hunting** <note>original: "πάνθηρον" (pantheron). They consider **Dionysus** to be, as it were, the **Mind** of **Zeus** <note>original: "tōn tou Dios noun"</note>, or the **Soul of the World**; for we find in many places that the whole universe is named **Zeus** because it is ever-living and without end. And they describe him as being nourished in the thigh of **Zeus**, as if he were hiding in the secret parts of the universe. He is called **Dithyrambus** and **Dimetor** <note>"Dimetor" means "Twice-born" or "having two mothers"</note> because he obtained two progressions: the eastern one toward the South in winter, and the northern one toward the West in summer.

Such is the tradition of antiquity regarding the **Dionysia**. The **Chaldæans** <note>A people from Mesopotamia famous for their astrology and occult wisdom</note> call the god **Iao**—meaning "intelligible light."

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 43—44. 208

Metrodorus <note>an Epicurean philosopher or possibly the grammarian Metrodorus of Scepsis</note> says that in **April**, the **Hyades** <note>a star cluster associated with rain</note> rise along with the South Wind. On the eighth day before the Kalends <note>March 25th</note> occurs the spring equinox.

->A P R I L.<-

<margin>Chapter I.</margin> 44. Since the first month, as we were saying, was dedicated to the honors of the **intelligible beings** <note>spiritual or divine entities perceived by the mind rather than the senses</note> because of the excellence of the **Monad** <note>the number One, representing unity and the source of all things</note>, it follows that the one after it—that is, the second, which the Romans call **February** in their native tongue—was set apart for Pluto and the gods of the underworld according to the infinity of number. They call him **Hades**; for the **Dyad** <note>the number Two</note> is formless and indefinite, which is why he is said to be the king of the unseen things and of those who have departed from the divine realms. Correctly, therefore, **Philolaus** <note>a Pythagorean philosopher</note> says that the Dyad is the consort of **Cronus** <note>Saturn</note>, whom one might clearly call Time. The Dyad is joined with Time as the cause of corruption. She happens to be the mother of flowing substance <note>the material world of change and decay</note> for him.

<margin>p. 87.</margin> But the third, that is, **March**, they assigned to this order of number either according to the first odd number <note>three is the first odd number, as the Pythagoreans did not count one as a number but the father of numbers</note>, or as a native god. For the **Triad** <note>the number Three</note> is the beginning of number; thus they couple **Mars** with **Venus** not without philosophy. For when the Monad joins with the Dyad, the first number was born, which is called "perfect" by some, because—

...the first [number, the triad] signifies all things, and was the first to show a beginning, a middle, and an end <note>original: "πρῶτος τὰ πάντα σημαίνει, καὶ πρῶτος ἔδειξεν ἀρχήν, μέσα, τέλος"</note>. <header>IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 44.</header>

...in May, when the birds already begin their spring songs; and they say that he <note>Adonis, the youth loved by Venus who represents the cycle of vegetation</note> was killed by Ares, who had transformed into a boar—symbolizing, as it were, the spring being destroyed by the summer. For the nature of the boar is hot, and the myth-makers use it to represent the heat of summer. Or, as it seems to others, Adonis represents the fruit of the earth, while Ares represents the boar; for this animal is an enemy to crops, just as the ox is their savior. Because of this, even now, the Egyptians generally abstain from eating oxen, but make the greatest use of swine for food. 

Euripides, however, claims that Aphrodite herself was named after the "foolishness" <note>Greek: *aphronas*</note> that she produces in those who are in love. <margin>p. 89.</margin> But Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his detailed logic and etymologies</note> argues that she should be called not Dione, but "Didone," from her "giving" <note>Greek: *epididōnai*</note> the pleasures of procreation. He says she is called "Cypris" because she provides "conception" <note>Greek: *kyein*</note>, and "Cythereia" for a similar reason: because she grants the power of conception not only to humans, but also to wild beasts. 

For this reason, Hermes in his *Cosmopoeia* <term>Cosmopoeia: a lost work or tradition regarding the "Creation of the World"</term> teaches that the parts of Aphrodite above the waist are male, while the parts below are female; which is why the Pamphylians <note>A people from the southern coast of Asia Minor</note> once honored an Aphrodite who even possessed a beard. They also claim she was born from the genitals of Kronos—that is, from Time <note>Greek: *aion*; a common philosophical pun on the similarity between the names of the titan Kronos and *Chronos*, time</note>—while she...

...that is, in May, when even the birds begin their spring season: and they say that he <note>Adonis, the youth representing the cycle of vegetation</note> was killed by Mars, who had turned into a boar—symbolizing, as it were, the spring being destroyed by the summer. For the nature of the boar is hot, and the myth-makers use it to represent the heat of summer. Or, as it seems to others, Adonis represents the fruit of the earth, while Mars represents the boar; for this animal is an enemy to crops, just as the ox is their savior. Because of this, even now, the Egyptians generally abstain from oxen, but make the greatest use of swine <note>original: "suillis (carnibus)"</note> for food.

Euripides, however, claims that she was named Aphrodite <note>original: "Ἀφροδίτην"</note> because she makes lovers foolish <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ ἄφρονας τοὺς ἐρῶντας ἀποτελεῖν", literally: "from the fact that she renders lovers insane"</note>. But Chrysippus <note>A Stoic philosopher known for his logic and interest in the origins of words</note> argues that she should be named not Dione, but "Didone," because she grants <note>original: "ἐπιδίδωσι" (epididōsi)</note> the pleasures of procreation. He says she is called Cypris <note>original: "Κύπριν"</note> because she provides conception <note>original: "παρὰ τὸ κύειν παρέχειν"</note>, and "Cythereia" for a similar reason: because she grants the power of conception <note>original: "τὸ κύειν ἐπιδίδωσι"</note> not only to humans, but also to wild beasts. 

For this reason, Hermes in his <term>Cosmopoeia</term> <note>original: "Κοσμοποιΐᾳ", a work or tradition regarding the creation of the world</note> teaches that the parts of Venus above the hip are masculine, while the parts behind it are feminine; which is why the Pamphylians <note>A people from the southern coast of Asia Minor</note> used to worship a bearded Venus in ancient times. They also claim she was born from the genitals of Saturn—that is, from time <note>original: "ex aevo", a pun on the Greek Chronos (Time) and Kronos (Saturn)</note> or eter...

<margin>Chapter III</margin> ...to produce [life] because she is a provider of physical bodies. People used to sacrifice geese and partridges to her; geese because they delight in the waters (as she is **Aphrodite of the Sea**), and partridges because the males are captured when they are lured by the calls of the females. Such were the opinions held by the ancients regarding Aphrodite, according to both mythical and natural perspectives.

The philosophers, however, say that **Dione** is Aphrodite, representing the nature that pervades all existing things. They say she was born from the genitals <note>original: "μηδέων," referring to the myth of Uranus's castration</note> of **Uranus** <note>The Sky</note> and the **Sea**, which is to say, she arises from even and odd numbers. The odd number represents the *Form* <note>The active, celestial principle</note>, while the even number comes from the *Sea*, which represents infinite *Matter* <note>The passive, formless substance of the universe</note>.

**Cincius**, the Roman scholar <note>Lucius Cincius Alimentus, a historian and lawyer who lived during the Second Punic War</note>, says that Aphrodite was born from foam <note>original: "ἀφροῦ" (aphros), the Greek etymology for her name</note>, as if to suggest that **Spring** is born from the snowy air and the cold essence of winter. So much for the Greek views on Aphrodite.
