# IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN DETAIL. 44—46.

44. They claim that **Astarte**, their <term>city-guardian<note>original Greek: "πολιοῦχον"; a deity who serves as the special protector of a specific city</note></term>, (as if to say, the "starry one," or the "excellence of the city") is actually **Aphrodite**. For from Lebanon (which is a mountain there, named after the city near Lebanon) two rivers flow out into the sea; the larger and clearest of these is called **Adonis**, while the smaller and more earthy one is called **Ares**. Since the Adonis flows entirely into the open sea, it is thought that he is especially beloved by Aphrodite—which is to say, by the Sea.

<margin>p. 92</margin>
45. Therefore, on the **Kalends of April** <note>April 1st, the first day of the month</note>, the honorable women honored **Aphrodite** for the sake of harmony and a modest life. However, the women of the common people used to bathe in the men's baths, crowned with myrtle in her honor—either because myrtle is beneficial for infants (as it strengthens the bodies of the newborn, and happens to be the most fragrant of all evergreen plants), or because it is the only plant that delights in the sea. **Aphrodite** was honored with the same rites as **Hera**; and in **Cyprus**, they would sacrifice a sheep covered in its fleece to Aphrodite (this style of priesthood in Cyprus once came over from **Corinth**). Furthermore, they also sacrificed wild boars to her because of the plot against **Adonis**, on the fourth day before the Nones—that is, the second day of April.

# IV. SPECIFICALLY ON THE MONTHS. 46.

<margin>v. 93.</margin>
[Hercules] was honored as a victor, as a giver of health. There was also a law for the Romans to abstain from **radishes** during this month. **Nicomachus** <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa was a mathematician and philosopher who often linked numbers and gods</note> states that **Hercules** is Time, but indeed he is also the **Sun**, speaking in this way: "Hercules is the one who effects the refraction <note>original Greek: κλάσιν (*klasin*), meaning a breaking or bending, though editors suggest it should be 'mixing'</note> of the air by the turning of the seasons; that is, he is the **Sun**." For this reason, in his mysteries, they dress the males in women's clothing, as if the seminal birth—beginning from the wildness and barrenness of winter—is being "feminized" <note>made fertile and soft</note> at the start of spring. These rites were performed in the spring. He holds three **apples** <note>a reference to the golden apples of the Hesperides</note> in his left hand as a symbol of the division of time through him; the apple is used because of its "sympathy" <note>the Greeks often used etymological puns; here, *mēlon* (apple) is linked to the harmony of the seasons</note> with the season, and the spring equinox is the beginning of time. Furthermore, there are three apples because time is tripartite <note>divided into three: past, present, and future</note>. He is also said to bring up the **three-headed dog** <note>Cerberus</note> from the Underworld because time is both a guardian and a destroyer, just like a dog. Its three heads represent the time that has passed, the time that is present, and the time that is to come. And in another way, the three apples should be understood...

### APRIL.

[Hercules, the Victorious] was worshipped as a giver (or author) of health. It was also the custom for the Romans to abstain from **radishes** during this month. Furthermore, **Hercules** was called "Time" by **Nicomachus** <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa, a Neo-Pythagorean who saw mathematical and divine order in the universe</note>, and indeed also the **Sun**, stating: "**Hercules** is therefore he who effects the refraction <note>original Greek: κλάσιν (*klasin*), a breaking or bending</note> of the air by the turning of the seasons; that is, he is the **Sun**." It is undoubtedly for this reason that in his mysteries they dress the males in women's clothing, since after the wildness and barrenness that prevails in winter, the seminal seed begins to soften <note>The author views the transition from winter's "harsh" sterility to spring's "soft" fertility as a metaphorical feminization</note>. These attributes were assigned to the spring. Moreover, he holds three **apples** <note>A reference to the Golden Apples of the Hesperides</note> in his left hand as a symbol of the division of time that occurs through him; the apple is used because of its harmony with the season, and the spring equinox marks the beginning of time. Furthermore, there are three apples because time is divided into three parts. He is also said to lead the **three-headed dog** <note>Cerberus</note> out of the Underworld, which is a characteristic of Time—it both guards and destroys, much like a dog. Its three heads represent the past, the present, and the future. Additionally, the three apples are to be understood in the case of Hercules according to the opinion of the phi[losophers]...

**Hercules** <note>original Greek: Ἡρακλῆς</note>] Nicomachus wishes to interpret this name, as do those praised by Creuzer in *Dionysius* (page 142), the Scholiast on Hesiod's *Theogony* (page 136), who interprets it as "glory of the air" <note>original Greek: ἀέρος κλέος (*aeros kleos*)</note>, and Macrobius in *Saturnalia* I. 20, as "glory of Hera" <note>original Greek: Ἥρας κλέος (*Hēras kleos*)</note>. — RR.

**In his mysteries**] The Paris manuscript incorrectly reads "in his thighs." — RR.

**Since indeed from wildness and barrenness**] For the word "barrenness" <note>original Greek: ἀγονίας (*agonias*)</note>, the Paris Codex and the Roman Codex incorrectly read *agorias*. By a slight change of the letter *r* to *n*, I believe I have corrected this passage. In the same way, winter is called "inert" by Horace in *Odes* IV. 7. line 12: *"the inert winter returns."* Friedrich Jacobs also reads "since indeed from wildness and barrenness" in his notes on the *Palatine Anthology* (page 503). See the same in Philostratus's *Images* (page 220). — Cr. The Codex reads: "since indeed from wildness and [agorias]." I have removed the error and retained the correction "from wildness." — Sch.

<column-break/>

**These things in the spring**] I suspect the text should read "these things for him in the spring." — RR.

**Symbol of division**] See Plutarch’s *On Isis and Osiris* (page 506, Wyttenbach edition). — Cr.

**Time is destructive**] Our author in *On the Magistracies* (page 218) says: "**time, being destructive by nature**." — RR.

**And otherwise the three apples**] I have restored the word "apples" <note>original Greek: μῆλα (*mēla*)</note> from the Codex.

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN PARTICULAR. 46.

<columns>

...according to philosophical doctrine, it is held that Hercules, having completed the three periods of the practical life, is considered perfect. For this reason, he is also called "of three evenings" <note>original Greek: τριέσπερος (*triesperos*)</note> according to Lycophron, who says:

> Of the lion of three evenings, whom once the sharp-toothed
> dog of Triton crushed with his jaws.

The idea that Hercules was conceived over three nights is a mythical tradition. The story gives him Hebe "of the beautiful ankles" as a wife, which signifies the creative power and the beauty found within the material world. The crown is a sign of perfection; for this reason, it was originally given to gods, kings, and priests. However, <margin>p. 94.</margin> when Fortune took the crown away from Virtue, the priests thereafter began shaving their hair, creating a circle of hair on their heads to serve as a crown <note>This refers to the "tonsure," the practice of shaving the top of the head as a sign of religious devotion</note>. Furthermore, they say he is "of twelve labors" because the Sun runs through the twelve signs of the zodiac. He is also said to have restored Alcestis to life for her husband Admetus; this represents the Sun restoring the life-giving nature of the world after it has been struck dead by the winter. In this allegory, Admetus represents the World, named for being untiring and ever-living <note>A Greek pun: *Admetos* sounds like *akamas* (untiring)</note>. He is also said to have destroyed Augeas; this means that the rising Sun scatters the morning time, which most people call the "dawn" <note>original Greek: αὐγή (*augē*), sounding like Augeas</note>. Finally, Hercules is commanded by Eurystheus to perform the twelve labors; this signifies the Sun, who, by the command of the great God and despite the opposition of Hera (representing the atmospheric sphere), passes through the twelve signs of the zodiac in the heavens. Thus speak the philosophers.

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN DETAIL. 49–50.

<columns>

...at the sacrifice of the **Fordicalia** <note>A festival where pregnant cows were sacrificed to Tellus (Earth)</note>. Indeed, they called the way-stations "milestones" <term>milliaria<gloss>markers at intervals of 1,000 paces</gloss></term> in their ancestral tongue, from the word for a thousand <note>Greek: χιλιάδος / chiliados</note>. From this also comes the name for soldiers among them, "milites"; for **Romulus** organized only one thousand shield-bearers, and called them *milites* from that number (as if to say, "the thousand"), though they were previously called *sabellites* <note>The text reads σαβέλλιτας/sabellitas, but scholars suggest this is a corruption of "satellites," meaning guards or attendants</note>. For antiquity counted the multitude in thousands (not tens of thousands), just as **Homer** himself says:
> As loud as nine thousand or ten thousand men cry out in battle.
For the number ten thousand <note>Greek: μυρία / myria, the root of "myriad"</note> is capable of expressing an indefinite amount.

50. On the eleventh day before the **Kalends of May** <note>April 21st, the traditional date of the founding of Rome</note>, **Romulus** founded the city of **Rome**. He summoned all those living nearby <margin>p. 98.</margin> and commanded them to bring a clod of earth from their own lands, as an omen that **Rome** would thus rule over every land. He himself, taking up a priestly trumpet (which it is the ancestral custom of the **Romans** to call a *lituus*, from the word for "supplication" <note>Greek: λιτῆς / litēs</note>), proclaimed the name of the city, having led every priestly rite. There are three names for the city: the ritual, the sacred, and the political. The ritual name is **Eros** <note>Greek: Ἔρως / Erōs, meaning Love. This is a mystical anagram of "Roma" (R-O-M-A / A-M-O-R)</note>, so that everyone might be held by a divine love for the city. Because of this, the **Poet** <note>Virgil, in his Eclogues</note>, speaking riddlingly in his pastoral verses, calls the city **Amaryllis**. The sacred name is **Flora**, as if to say, "The Flowering One," which is why during this time the festival of the Flowers—

...at the sacrifice of the **Fordicalia** <note>A festival involving the sacrifice of pregnant cows to the Earth goddess, Tellus</note>. They called the way-stations "milestones" in their native tongue <term>milliaria<gloss>from the Latin 'mille,' meaning a thousand paces</gloss></term>; and from this, the soldiers among them took their name <note>Latin: *milites*</note>. For **Romulus** established only one thousand bodyguards, and he called them "soldiers" from that number (as if to say, "the thousanders"), whereas previously they were called *satellites* <note>Attendants or guards</note>. In ancient times, the people counted a large multitude in terms of thousands (not tens of thousands), as **Homer** himself wrote:

> As loud as nine thousand or ten thousand men cry out in battle.

For the number "ten thousand" <note>Greek: *myria*, the root of the English word "myriad"</note> allows for the concept of infinity.

50. On the eleventh day before the **Kalends of May** <note>April 21st, the traditional date of the Parilia and the founding of Rome</note>, **Romulus** founded **Rome**. He himself, taking up a priestly trumpet (which the **Romans** are accustomed to call a *lituus* in their native tongue, from the Greek word *litē* <note>λιτή</note>, meaning "prayer" or "supplication"), announced the name of the city, having performed every priestly initiation. Now, there were three names for the city: the secret, the sacred, and the political. The secret name was *Amor* <note>Latin for "Love"</note>, so that all might be held by a divine love for the city—which is why the poet <note>Virgil</note> refers to the city through riddles as "Amaryllis" in his pastoral poem; the sacred name was **Flora**, meaning "blooming," which is why the festival of the **Floralia** is held on this day;

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN DETAIL. 50—51.

After the ceremony for the naming of the city, **Romulus** yoked a bull with a heifer and circled the wall, yoking the male on the side facing the fields and the female on the side facing the city, so that the males might be terrifying to those outside, and the females might be fertile for those within. ### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 51–52.

If, therefore, he is shown to be mind and speech, the Egyptians represent him as a long-tailed monkey <term>cercopithecus</term>, since it is the most intelligent of all animals and is capable of understanding and knowledge. # MAY

2

There are, however, those who say that **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; the Roman name for the Greek god *Hermes*</note> is the son of **Jupiter** <note>original: *Jovis*</note> and **Maia** by way of allegory. They suggest that Jupiter represents reason <term>ratio</term>, while Maia represents the mind <note>original: *mentem*; likely referring to intelligence or prudence</note>, and Mercury, the eloquent <note>original: *facundum*</note> son born from both, is represented through these symbolic riddles. They fashioned him as the youngest of all the gods, because speech <term>oratio</term> does not grow old; furthermore, they made him the swiftest, equipped with wings, signifying the quickness of reason and the speed of speech through such artistry. Thus the poet <note>Homer</note> says:

-> --- Winged words --- <-

Next, the Greeks represent him in a square shape <note>Referencing the *Herma*, a squared stone pillar topped with a head</note>, providing the strongest evidence that he represents speech, and specifically true speech. For there are different types of speech: lying and deceptive speech are many-angled <note>meaning they are unstable or complex in a dishonest way</note>, but true speech is equal to itself in all its parts. Wherever it is turned, it is firmly established on all its bases, which is clearly the nature of the square figure. If, therefore, it has been demonstrated that he represents reason and speech, the Egyptians make the long-tailed monkey <term>cercops</term> his image <note>original: *simulacrum*</note>, since it is more prudent than all other animals and possesses skill and art. <columns>

<margin>p. 103</margin> We know that the bird <note>The ibis</note> is dedicated to him <note>Mercury/Thoth</note>; for it resembles the heart, its body being white while it is blackened on both sides. This represents the form of speech <term>logos</term> proceeding from the intellect; for before it is spoken, speech is dark, but as it is being spoken, it is illuminated, and once uttered, it vanishes into the unseen. The animal feeds near water, just as in us the heart draws its power from a moist substance. Yet, of all birds, the ibis alone does not know how to swim, and it is most helpless when dragged down into a greater depth. The same thing should be observed regarding the heart; for when liquid drink is introduced in a balanced measure, the heart is naturally strengthened and firmly established in its reasonings, remaining in its own proper seat—which they call the diaphragm <term>phrena</term>—and staying sober. However, when it is flooded with tremors, it produces its own internal agitation throughout the entire body. People suffer these things from drunkenness, having preferred the unmixed wine over their own natural strength. Both the ibis and the long-tailed monkey <term>cercops</term> <note>original: *κέρκωψ* (kerkopops)</note> are said to be in sympathy with the Moon <note>original: *Selene*</note>. The ibis is similar to her in its very shape, being dark at the extremities but white in the middle, just like the ethereal moon. Indeed, when the sky is moonless, the ibises do not even see; they close their eyes during this time and endure without food, waiting for their kindred element. The monkey <term>cercops</term> has even more obvious reactions: for when the Moon waxes, the circle of its eyes then widens, but when she wanes, the circumference of its eyes contracts.

243 MAY.

<columns>
2

We know that the ibis, a bird, is consecrated to him <note>Mercury or Thoth</note>; for its white body is similar to the heart, while it is black on either side. This is indeed the figure of speech <term>logos</term>, as it is conceived: for before it is uttered, it is obscure, but when it is brought forth, it is illuminated, and once spoken, it vanishes. This animal lives near the waters, just as in us the heart receives its power from a moist essence. However, of all birds, the ibis alone does not know how to swim, and any of them that are very weak are pulled down into a greater depth. One may observe the same thing in the heart; for when a liquid drink is taken in moderation, the heart is usually strengthened and confirmed in its thoughts, not leaving its seat—which they call the diaphragm <term>praecordia</term>—and remaining sober. But when it has overflowed, it causes its own motion through palpitations throughout the whole body. This happens to people through drunkenness, who have preferred unmixed wine over their own strength. It is also likely that the ibis and the long-tailed monkey <term>cercops</term> <note>original: *cercopem*</note> are in harmony with the Moon. The ibis itself is similar to her in appearance, being black at its extremities but white in the middle, just like the ethereal Moon. For when the Moon does not appear in the sky, the ibises do not see either, but they close their eyes at that time and remain without food, waiting for their kindred element. In the long-tailed monkey, the power of this thing is even more apparent: for when the Moon waxes, the circle of its eyes dilates, but when she wanes, the circle of its eyes contracts.

# IV. ON THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 53–54.

...the month for protection against the disease of arthritis <note>specifically gout, often associated with the month of May in ancient medical lore</note>. Merchants used to pray to **Maia** and **Hermes** <note>Mercury</note> that their profits might be free from danger. For all profits, it seems, spring up in and from matter, and in it they are found as if they were "windfalls" <term>Hermaia</term> <note>original: *Hermaia*, meaning a lucky find or stroke of luck attributed to Hermes</note> and are distributed, as they say, according to merit. **Mummius** the **Roman** <note>likely referring to Numinius, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher</note> wishes **Hermes** to be the "progressive word" <term>prochoritikos logos</term>; for he says that a babe would not utter a sound before it touched the Earth, so that the common people rightly understood **Maia** as the Earth. According to another sacred teaching, **Frontinus** <note>an author on Roman rituals and land surveying</note> says that the Earth must be honored on the **Kalends of May** <note>May 1st</note>, because the Earth, bubbling up its innate heat to the surface—to exult as if to leap—being led forth, generally creates tremors during the month of **May**. Therefore, they honor **Maia** at this time, serving her as the Earth. They call the act of celebrating the festival *maioumidzein*, from which also comes the term *maiouman* <note>referring to the Maiouma, a popular and sometimes controversial spring festival involving water and theater</note>. — *The beginning of generation is the **Moon**.*

### MAY.

...as a precaution against arthritis <note>specifically gout, which ancient writers often linked to the seasonal changes of spring</note>. Moreover, merchants used to offer supplications to **Maia** and **Mercury**, so that their business dealings might be profitable and free from danger. For all profit exists within physical matter and arises from it, and within it, profits are found like **windfalls** <note>original: *Ἕρμαια* (Hermaia), meaning "gifts of Hermes" or unexpected strokes of luck</note> (that is, unexpected gains). **Mummius the Roman** <note>likely referring to Numenius, the Neo-Pythagorean philosopher</note>, however, suggests that **Mercury** represents "speech in progress"; for he says that an infant cannot produce a voice until it has touched the Earth, implying that the common people correctly understood **Maia** to be the Earth. According to another sacred tradition, **Frontejus** <note>Frontinus, a Roman author known for his work on rituals and land measurement</note> says that it is necessary to worship the Earth on the **Kalends of May** <note>May 1st</note>, because the Earth pushes its innate heat upward to the surface—to **well up, to exult,** and **to leap**—and by bringing this heat forth, it causes earthquakes most frequently in the month of May. They therefore worship Maia in this month, venerating her as the Earth. They use the terms **to celebrate the Maiouma** or **to keep holiday** (meaning to observe festive days), from which also comes the word **to keep the Maiouma festival** <note>The *Maiouma* was a famous, and sometimes scandalous, water festival celebrated in the late Roman Empire</note>. *The beginning of generation is the **Moon**.*

# IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN PARTICULAR. 54–56.

...second: a son of the Nile, whom the Egyptians call **Ptah** <note>original Greek: *Φθάν* (Phthan)</note>; third: the son of Cronus and Hera, the Lemnian, the blacksmith; fourth: Hephaestus the prophetic, the Sicilian, from whom come the **Hephaestian islands** <note>The Lipari or Aeolian Islands, known for volcanic activity</note>. ### 56. (Continued)
...it is fitting for the state to be managed, as **Plato** says. And it appears he assigns the number six to this month for good reason; for this number is life-generating <note>original: "ζωογονικὸς" (zoogonikos); a term used in Neopythagorean math to describe numbers that relate to the biological creation of life</note>, starting from the monad <note>the number one</note>, from which it is completed through the triad <note>the number three</note>, being sufficient unto itself; and for this reason **Pythagoras** dedicated this number to the first of the **Fates** <note>original: "Μοιρῶν" (Moiron); the goddesses who spin the thread of destiny</note>.

### 57.
On the **Kalends of June** <note>June 1st</note> there is a festival of **Juno** <note>original: "Ἥρας" (Hera); the Roman Juno was the protector of the state and of women</note> and prayers are offered in the **Capitol**, while all **Romans** together taste cold water at dawn to guard against every kind of disease, especially gout <note>original: "ποδαλγικῆς" (podalgikes); literally 'foot-pain'</note>, as the oracle commanded, and also so that births might not result in twins or monstrous deformities. This custom was introduced in the time of **Hadrian**, after an **Egyptian** woman was brought to him who recounted that she had given birth to four children at unequal intervals over four days, and after forty <margin>p. 107.</margin> days, a fifth child, according to **Aristotle**, who says—

---

**Plato**] While these are not his exact words, similar ideas are found in Plato’s *Republic*, Book III, page 412: <note>original: "Ὅτι μὲν πρεσβυτέρους τοὺς ἄρχοντας δεῖ εἶναι, νεωτέρους δὲ τοὺς ἀρχομένους κ. τ. λ."</note> *“That the elders must be the rulers, and the younger the ruled...”* and on page 414: <note>original: "Ἆρ' οὖν ὡς ἀληθῶς ὀρθότατον καλεῖν τούτους μὲν φύλακας παντελεῖς — τοὺς δὲ νέους — ἐπικούρους τε καὶ βοηθοὺς τοῖς τῶν ἀρχόντων δόγμασιν; κ. τ. λ."</note> *“Is it not then most correct to call these men 'perfect guardians'—and the young men 'auxiliaries' and 'helpers' to the decrees of the rulers?”* — Note by Roether.

**For this number is life-generating, etc.**] This passage does not seem to be complete. Lydus explained the same doctrine more fully above in Book II, section 10: <note>original: "τῶν γὰρ ἀπὸ μονάδ. κ. τ. λ."</note> *“for of those [starting] from the monad...”*, for which reason I think the article "the" should be inserted before "from," and the word "alone" after "monad," or at least "alone" before "from." — The words **from which until** 

<column-break/>

**the triad** are to be understood as: *from the one, the two, and the three.* Instead of the phrase **from itself**, one should read **from the same [parts]**, as it appears above in the cited passage, or it should be understood as if it were written **equally**. — Unless perhaps instead of **from which** we should read **successively**, as it appears above in II. 8: *“continuously up to the four,”* where the Paris manuscript reads “from which.” Also in III. 10: *“the squares in succession from the monad,”* where the Paris manuscript likewise has “from which.” (*“Since from the monad it is filled up in a continuous line as far as the triad...”*) Similar things can be seen in the *Theology of Arithmetic*, page 40. — Nokk agrees with me, noting on this passage: “Read: **for this is life-generating, starting from the monad successively up to the triad, being filled up from its own parts.**” For one, two, and three are the sides or parts of the <term>senarius</term> <note>the number six; Lydus is explaining that 1+2+3=6, making it a 'perfect' and 'life-generating' number</note>.

...**Plato**, it is fitting [for the state] to be administered. Indeed, it appears that the number six was assigned to this month by him not without reason: for this number—the first from the monad <note>original: "monade"; the number one, seen by Pythagoreans as the source of all numbers</note>—possesses the power of procreation. It is completed through the triad <note>the number three</note> and is sufficient unto itself; for this reason **Pythagoras** dedicated this number to the first of the **Fates** <note>original: "Parcarum"; the goddesses who spin the thread of human destiny</note>.

### IV. ON THE MONTHS INDIVIDUALLY. 68.

<margin>p. 112.</margin>
**It looks toward the etymology of the Nile.** Regarding the increase of the waters in summer, **Anaxagoras** <note>A Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BC) who was among the first to offer a physical explanation for the Nile's flood.</note> says that the melting snows of **Ethiopia** send forth the Nile. And **Aeschylus**, **Sophocles**, and **Euripides** <note>The three great Athenian tragedians, showing that this "snow-melt" theory was common in Greek literature.</note> are of this same opinion. But the greatest among Roman philosophers, **Seneca**, speaks against this, saying—that Ethiopia (where even the bodies of the **Troglodytes** <note>A name used by ancient Greeks for various "cave-dwelling" peoples, often located in Ethiopia or near the Red Sea.</note> are scorched, who, not enduring the sun, live under the earth; where silver in that place turns to the color of lead, and no timber fails to melt away) is too hot for snow; and besides, there are many rivers exposed to the South Wind, of which we see none flooding, even though mountains lie above them...

...bringing in the year, and from this the Nile is named. <note>original: "ἔτους ἐπάγοντα" (bringing in the year). This likely refers to the "epagomenal" or extra days added to the Egyptian calendar to align with the solar year, which coincided with the rising of the Nile.</note> See the *Gudian Etymon* under the entry "Kutilos," page 350. [Initialed RR].

**It looks toward the etymology]** Compare Jablonski’s *Egyptian Words*, Supplement page 443, collected on page 473, and there the passages from ancient and more recent writers. Compare the same author’s *Egyptian Pantheon*, Book IV, chapter 1, pages 142—148—161. [Initialed CR].

**Regarding the [increase] in summer etc.]** These words and those that follow as far as the words "But Herodotus" are excerpted and translated into Greek from Seneca’s *Natural Questions*, Book IV, chapter 2, page 725 and following in the edition by Lipsius. I shall transcribe the relevant parts here. "But now," Seneca says, "I shall proceed to inspect the causes for which the Nile grows in summer, and I shall begin with the most ancient. Anaxagoras says that snows loosened from the heights of Ethiopia run down all the way to the Nile. All antiquity was of the same opinion. This is what Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides hand down. But it is clear from

<column-break/>

many arguments that this is false. First, the scorched color of the men indicates that Ethiopia is extremely hot, as do the **Troglodytes**, who have subterranean houses. — silver turns to the color of lead — no experiment remains of wood placed on top [due to the heat]. — And yet the rivers of these mountains swell in spring and early summer. — **Euthymenes of Marseille** <note>A Greek explorer from roughly the 6th century BC who explored the coast of Africa and believed the Nile was connected to the Atlantic Ocean.</note> gives testimony: 'I sailed,' he says, 'the Atlantic sea. From there the Nile flows larger, as long as the **Etesian winds** <note>Annual summer winds in the Mediterranean; Euthymenes incorrectly theorized that these winds pushed the Atlantic ocean into the mouth of the Nile.</note> keep their time: for then the sea is driven out by the pressing winds. When they subside and the sea becomes quiet, the power of the Nile departing from there is less. Furthermore, the taste of the sea is sweet, and there are beasts similar to those in the Nile.' — — At that time there was room for lies, since foreign places were unknown. It was permitted for those men to put forth fables. But now the entire coast of the outer sea is brushed by the ships of merchants, none of whom now report a blue Nile or a sea of [sweet] taste."

# JULY. 261

The Nile seems to have been named from *ilys* <note>original: "ἰλύος" — meaning mud or slime, suggesting the river is named for the fertile silt it deposits.</note> (that is, from "new mud"); this refers to its etymology. ...mountains, flooding <note>original: "πλημμυροῦντα" — the text includes a [sic] note in the original, likely because the Greek grammar is irregular here.</note> in the summer. **Euthymenes of Massalia** <note>A Greek explorer from the 6th century BCE who sailed out of the Mediterranean into the Atlantic to explore the African coast.</note> says that he sailed the **Atlantic** Sea, and from there he saw the **Nile** flowing out; it swells more, he claims, when the so-called **Etesian winds** <note>Annual northern winds that blow across the Mediterranean in late summer. He adds that the water of the Atlantic Sea is almost sweet, and that it contains beasts similar to those found in the Nile. <margin>page 113.</margin> But **Seneca** <note>The Roman Stoic philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca, who discussed the Nile in his "Natural Questions."</note> argues against this opinion as well, saying that the sweet and light water is snatched up by the **Sun**, and that in every way all sea-water is salty, and there is no truth in this claim. For if this were the case, the Nile would also increase in the winter—and even more so, as the force of the winds is more violent then. Furthermore, the river appears more silty than dark blue, which is a characteristic foreign to sea waters. Along with these views, **Diogenes of Apollonia** <note>A philosopher who believed the earth was a living system with "veins." # JULIUS.

[*sic*] ...mountains lie above, which rivers swell in the summer. However, **Euthymenes of Massalia** <note>A Greek explorer from the 6th century BCE who explored the Atlantic coast of Africa.</note> says that he sailed the **Atlantic** sea, and from there he saw the **Nile** flowing out; it swells most at that time, he claims, when the so-called **Etesian winds** <note>Annual northern winds that blow across the Mediterranean; Euthymenes believed they pushed sea water into the Nile's mouth.</note> blow. For then, he says, the sea is driven inland by the winds; when they subside, it becomes calm. He adds that the water of the Atlantic sea is almost sweet nearby, and its aquatic beasts are similar to those of the Nile.

But **Seneca** <note>The Roman philosopher Lucius Annaeus Seneca, who wrote extensively on natural phenomena.</note> speaks against this opinion as well, saying that sweet and light water is snatched up by the **Sun**, and that in every way all sea water is salty; therefore, there is no truth in this claim. For if this were the case, the **Nile** would also overflow in winter, and all the more so, the more violent the force of the winds was then. Furthermore, the river appears more turbid and silty than dark blue, a characteristic that is inconsistent with sea waters.

In agreement with these views, **Diogenes of Apollonia** <note>A 5th-century BCE philosopher who believed the earth functioned like a living organism with "veins."</note> says that as the **Sun** draws moisture to itself, the **Nile** is drawn from the sea by the parched earth. Because the earth is porous and perforated by nature, it attracts moisture to itself; the more arid the land of **Egypt** is, the more fully it draws moisture into itself, just as oil flows more abundantly in lamps where it is being consumed by the flame.

**Herodotus** <note>The famous Greek historian who traveled to Egypt in the 5th century BCE.</note>, however, says that the **Sun** draws moisture from all rivers while traversing the southern zone <note>original: "zonam Noti"</note> of the **Earth** nearby; but toward summer, as the Sun inclines toward the **North**, it calls forth (or draws up) the **Nile**, and for this reason the river overflows...

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 68—69.

A part [of the water] falling from various parts into its own bed takes the appearance of a river. This would be the **Nile**, which, winding through various climates, passes through places that are wooded and impassable. From there, it pours out into a plain, and is gathered again into a riverbed; thereafter, it becomes navigable and is carried toward **Meroe** <note>An ancient city-state on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan</note> through the uninhabited parts of the South, and flowing around this area, it forms an island (for the land is entirely level). And from there, being for the most part enclosed, it turns toward the east and toward **Egypt**, and from there it reaches the sea when a more violent wind blows upon it; for by the force, as has been said, of the northern wind <note>The Etesian winds, which blow from the north in the summer</note>, the river is pushed back and, being spread out further, it floods all of **Egypt**. But when the **East Wind** <note>original: Eurus</note> blows from the east against the **Etesian winds**, or the **South Wind** from the midday region pushes the **Nile** out, the river naturally runs down to the sea (the North Wind having gently abated <margin>p. 116</margin>).

And this is proof that the river does not increase from the melting of snows: that its water is not cold, but warm. Because of this, when the water recedes, certain animals are found upon the mud, partially formed, and in part strange beasts <note>original: knodala; refers to unidentifiable or monstrous creatures believed to be spontaneously generated from the mud</note>. Such things are naturally brought to life by heat and moisture, which is not the case with other waters; for they contain only fish. And while others speak by conjecture, I (says **Chrestus** <note>Likely an otherwise obscure geographical source or traveler cited by the author</note>) have been at the promontory of **Maurusia** <note>The northwestern coast of Africa, near the Strait of Gibraltar</note> at the mouth of the **Ocean**."

->### JULIUS.<-

...because, falling into narrow places and partly from diverse directions into its own channel, the stream takes on its proper form. This is essentially the **Nile**, which rolls over various slopes through rough and pathless regions. From there it pours out into a plain and is again contracted into a riverbed, and is navigable; then it is carried toward **Meroe** <note>An ancient city-state on the east bank of the Nile in modern-day Sudan, which the ancients often described as an island because it was surrounded by the Nile and the Atbara rivers</note> through the uninhabited southern regions, and by flowing around this area, it forms an island (for the land is entirely level). And from there further on, while it is mostly enclosed, it turns toward the east and toward **Egypt**, and from there into the sea when a more violent wind blows upon it; for by the force, as has been said, of the **North Wind** <note>original: septentrionalis</note>, while the river is turned back and more widely poured out, it floods all of **Egypt**. But when the **East Wind** <note>original: Eurus</note> blows from the east against the **Etesian winds** <note>Annual summer winds from the north that were thought to "hold back" the Nile's flow, causing the flood</note>, or the **South Wind** <note>original: Notus</note> from the south pushes the **Nile** along, it is natural that the stream (once the **North Wind** <note>original: Boreas</note> has paused a little) should run down into the sea. And this indeed is proof that it is not increased by the melting of snows: that it is not cold, but lukewarm. For this reason, when the water recedes, certain animals are found in the mud—some fully formed, others creeping creatures <note>original: reptilia; this refers to the ancient theory of "spontaneous generation," where life was thought to spring directly from warm, moist earth</note>. Such animals are accustomed to be born from warmth and moisture, which does not happen in other waters, which contain only fish. Others speak by conjecture; but I (says **Chrestus**) saw it myself after I was at the promontory of **Mauritania** <note>The northwest coast of Africa</note> at the mouth of the **Ocean**."

The Romans, according to the native meaning of the word, call him "Augustus" who is consecrated and brought forward (or chosen) by the augury <note>The Roman practice of divining the will of the gods by observing the flight or behavior of birds</note> of the gods [as a testimony].

73. There are nine types of comets, as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose work 'Meteorologica' served as the standard text on atmospheric phenomena for centuries</note> teaches, but according to **Apuleius the Roman** <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 AD), a philosopher and author known for his Platonist works</note>, there are ten: the *Hippias* (Horse-comet), *Xiphias* (Sword-comet), *Pogonias* (Bearded-comet), *Docias* (Beam-comet), *Pithus* (Jar-comet), *Lampadias* (Torch-comet), *Cometes* (Hairy-comet), *Disceus* (Disk-comet), *Typhon*, and *Cerastes* (Horned-comet). The *Hippias* is so named for its speed and movement; it scatters thin and slanted rays. The *Xiphias* appears stretched out like a sword or a long spear, but it is pale and misty. The *Pogonias* does not scatter its mane from its head, but downwards like a beard. Zopyrus was a Persian noble who mutilated himself to gain the trust of the Babylonians and betray them to King Darius</note> and the **Sinon of Virgil** <note>original: "Σίνωνος τοῦ Οὐεργιλιανοῦ." Sinon was the Greek spy who pretended to be a deserter to convince the Trojans to bring the Wooden Horse into their city</note>, burned the ships by which he had been transported along the Euphrates, so that the Persians would certainly not have the freedom to use them. Since the army carried only a moderate amount of provisions, he followed the deceivers; but they, having led him into a dry and waterless wasteland, revealed their trick. They themselves perished (for what more was there to gain?), while the Emperor, finding he could neither proceed further nor turn back for the future, was miserably destroyed. When the greater part of the army had fallen, the Persians came upon him in his weakened state; and though they were repulsed, they attacked again against him who now had not even twenty thousand men, though he had previously led seventeen <note>original: "ἑπτακαίδεκα" (seventeen). In this context, it refers to 17 myriads, or 170,000 soldiers</note>. Julian fought most bravely; but one from the Persian phalanx, of those called **Saracens** <note>The term used by late Roman authors for nomadic Arab tribes of the desert</note>, recognizing the Emperor by his purple robe, cried out in his native tongue, "**Malchan**" <note>original: "Μαλχάν." ### IV. ON THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 76—78.

<margin>p. 121.</margin> Of the **Aparctias** <note>The North wind</note>, the wind adjacent to the **Apeliotes** <note>The East wind</note> is called **Caecias** <note>The North-East wind</note>, while the one adjacent to the **Aparctias** itself is called **Boreas** <note>A more general name for the North wind</note>. Among those winds originating from a great beginning, the one that arises from a small movement of a cloud is called an **Eknephias** <note>A storm wind that "bursts from a cloud"</note>; the one coming from certain bays and through narrow gorges is a **Kolpias** <note>A "gulf wind," from the Greek word "kolpos" for bay</note>; and the one coming from the earth and a whirlwind of air is a **Gnophias** <note>A "darkening" or "gloomy" wind</note>. For breezes themselves are also "natures of air," and they are not without reason called "winds" when they are carried from lakes or rivers. Similar to these are the land-breezes; hence, quite reasonably, when the air is still, the condition is called **nenemia** <note>original: "νηνεμία" — a dead calm, literally "no-wind"</note>.

77. During the month of August, the oracle decrees that those who wish to have healthy joints must abstain from eating **mallow** <note>Mallow was often used as a laxative or emollient in antiquity, but here it is restricted to prevent joint pain or gout</note>.

<margin>Chapter I.</margin> 78. We were speaking the truth when we said that the Romans established the month of March as the beginning of the year, as can be understood from the name of the present month; for they named it **September**, as being the seventh month from spring—that is, from the month of March. It is on the twenty-fourth day of March that the **Sun**, entering **Aries** <note>The Ram, the first sign of the zodiac</note>, allows the nature of spring to begin. Therefore, there will be no need to speak at length regarding the names of the months that follow. For the eighth month <note>October</note> follows the **Auxiphotia** <note>original: "Αὐξιφωτίων" — a term referring to the "Increase of Light," a name used here for August</note>—The number of the ninth <note>November</note> is **Divine**, being completed by three triads <note>3 times 3 equals 9</note>, and preserving the heights of **Theology** according to the **Chaldean philosophy** <note>A mystical tradition involving the *Chaldean Oracles*, much admired by late antique Neoplatonists</note>, as **Porphyry** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonic philosopher and scholar</note> says.

### IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 79—82.

<margin>p. 122.</margin> 79. On the first of the month <note>original: "νεομηνίᾳ" (neomēnia), the New Moon or the Calends</note>, Metrodorus <note>an ancient Greek grammarian and philosopher</note> says that the constellation **Andromeda** rises, and while the other winds cease, the **East Wind** <note>original: "Εὖρον" (Euron)</note> prevails.

80. On the fourth day before the Nones of September <note>September 2nd</note>, **Augustus** defeated the Egyptians along with **Antony** and **Cleopatra** near the Leucadian promontory <note>the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE, which marked the start of the Roman Empire</note>. For this reason, he introduced the cycle of the so-called **Indiction** <note>a fifteen-year tax and calendar cycle</note>, to be counted from the beginning of the month of September. On this same day, **Democritus** <note>the famous natural philosopher</note> says a change of winds occurs and a prevalence of rain follows.

<margin>Chapter II.</margin> 81. According to Apollonius <note>likely Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher</note>, the varieties of **humors** <note>the bodily fluids that ancient medicine believed governed health</note> are many, but there are nine general types: **sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, fatty** <note>original: "βριγχή" (bringchē)</note>, **astringent, mucous, puckering** <note>original: "σύστηρά" (systēra)</note>, and **salty**. Therefore, during this ninth month, the Romans used to offer prayers for health.

82. On the eighth day before the Ides of September <note>September 6th</note>, Eudoxus <note>a 4th-century BCE astronomer</note> notes that the constellation of the **Horse** <note>Pegasus</note> sets, and the **West Wind** <note>original: Zephyrus</note> or the **North-West Wind** <note>original: Argestēs</note> blows. We know of a worm that grows on cabbage called a *kampē* <note>a caterpillar</note>. When the cabbage dries up in the spring, this creature is born to transform into a winged worm, like an ant but larger—

The East Wind blows, and the winds are changed.”* Compare also Ptolemy, *On the Significance of the Fixed Stars*, page 57, edition by Petavius. **Re.** <note>Reiske, the editor</note>

### SEPTEMBER.

79. At the **New Moon**, **Metrodorus** <note>an ancient Greek grammarian and philosopher</note> says that **Andromeda** rises and, as the remaining winds cease, the **East Wind** <note>Latin: Eurus</note> gains strength.

80. **On the fourth day before the Nones of September** <note>September 2nd</note>, **Augustus** defeated the **Egyptians** along with **Antony** and **Cleopatra** at **Leucate** <note>referring to the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE</note>: for which reason he ordained that the cycle of the so-called **indiction** (that is, a period of time) should be numbered from that point, starting from the beginning of the month of **September**. On this day, **Democritus** <note>the philosopher of the atomic theory</note> says a change of winds occurs and rain increases.

81. There are indeed many varieties of flavors according to **Apollonius**, but nine general types: sweet, bitter, acid, sharp, sub-sweet, harsh, mucous, austere, and salty. — This is evidently why the **Romans** offered prayers for health in this ninth month.

### 288 IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS SPECIFICALLY. 89—91.

...others say that a gate was created and so named in **Troy**, through which the **Greeks** <note>original: *Hellenes*</note> entered.

89. **On the day before the Ides of October** <note>October 14th</note>, **Euktemon** <note>an Athenian astronomer who helped develop the Metonic cycle</note> considers it to be the **very middle of autumn**. **On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November** <note>October 18th</note>, **Metrodorus** <note>an Epicurean philosopher and scientist</note> says the **Hyades** <note>a star cluster in the constellation Taurus, traditionally associated with the arrival of rain</note> rise in the evening, along with a **violent wind**.

<margin>p. 125</margin> 90. Three different men named **Asclepius** <note>the Greek god of medicine and healing</note> are said to have existed: the first was the son of **Apollo** (son of **Hephaestus**), who invented the **medical probe** <note>original: *mēlēn*</note>; the second was the son of **Ischys** (son of **Elatus**) and **Coronis**, who was buried in the territory of **Cynosura**; the third was the son of **Arsippus** and **Arsinoe** (daughter of **Leucippus**). This third one invented **surgery** <note>original: *tomēn*; literally "cutting"</note> and the **tooth-extractor** <note>original: *odontagran*; a specialized forceps</note>, and his tomb is located in **Arcadia**. Astronomers, however, claim that he is the constellation **Ophiuchus** <note>the Serpent-Bearer</note> who stands upon the **Scorpion**.

91. **On the day before the Kalends of November** <note>October 31st</note>, **Varro** <note>the famous Roman scholar and antiquarian</note> says the **Lyre** <note>the constellation Lyra</note> rises along with the **Sun**.

I have given "gate" <note>original: *pylēn*</note> instead of "city" <note>original: *polin*</note> based on Hasii’s conjecture, in the location cited above. In exactly the same way, I see this passage corrected by **Friedrich Jacobs** in the **Palatine Anthology**, volume III. Why he treats the **Trojan horse** in this place will be understood from **Festus** in his entry on the "**October Horse**" <note>a Roman ritual sacrifice of a chariot horse to Mars on October 15th</note> on page 302, and also from **Plutarch’s** *Roman Questions* 97. It can be gathered from these that this passage by **Lydus** <note>the author of this work</note> is fragmentary, but it can be filled in using Festus and Plutarch.

90. **Cicero**'s *On the Nature of the Gods* <note>original: *De nat. deor.*</note>, Book III, chapter 22, page 612 in the edition by Moser and Creuzer: Of the **Aesculapii** <note>the Latin form of Asclepius</note>, the first is the son of **Apollo**, whom the **Arcadians** worship; he is said to have invented the **medical probe** <note>original: *specillum*</note> and was the first to bind a wound. The second is the brother of the **second Mercury**; he is said to have been struck by lightning and buried at **Cynosura**. The third is the son of **Arsippus and Arsinoe**; he was the first to discover the **purging of the bowels** and the **pulling of teeth**, as they say; his tomb and a sacred grove are shown in **Arcadia**, not far from the river **Lusius**. <header>IV. CONCERNING THE MONTHS IN PARTICULAR. 92—94.</header>

## N O V E M B E R.

92. **Cincius** <note>a Roman historian and antiquarian</note> says in his work **On the Festivals** that **November** was called *Merchedinus* <note>original: *Μερχηδῖνον*; likely a reference to the Roman intercalary month *Mercedonius*, derived from *merces* meaning "wages" or "merchandise"</note> among the ancients, as if it were a "wage-payer" <note>original: *μισθοφόρον* (misthophoron)</note>. For in this month, the hired laborers brought in the returns to the landowners for the past cycle, while other crops were beginning to come in again. It was later named **November** from its number; for it is the ninth month counting from **March**.

<margin>p. 126.</margin>
93. On the seventh day before the **Kalends of December** <note>November 25th</note>, **Democritus** <note>the Greek "laughing philosopher," here cited for his astronomical observations</note> says the Sun enters **Sagittarius**. The **Romans** used to call the year *Phaba* <note>original: *Φάβα*; related to the Latin word for "bean"</note>, after the **West Wind** <note>original: *Ζεφύρου* (Zephyrou)</note>, because when it begins to blow, this is the first crop that naturally sprouts. This West Wind is called *Favonius* <note>original: *Φαβώνιος* (Phabonios)</note> among them. For this reason, **March** is also called *Zephyrites*, just as **January** is called *Monias* from the unit <note>original: *μονάδος* (monados); the number one</note>, and **October** is called *Sementilius* from the sowing <note>original: *σπόρου* (sporou); referring to the autumn planting</note>, as antiquity has handed down.

<header>NOVEMBER. DECEMBER.</header>

### N O V E M B E R.

92. **Cincius** <note>Lucius Cincius Alimentus, a celebrated Roman historian and antiquarian</note> says in his book **On the Festivals** that the ancients called **November** *Mercedinum* (or *Mercedonium*), as if to say it was "the bringer of wages." For in that month, the hired laborers used to pay their tributes to their masters for the time that had passed, just as other crops were once again being harvested. Later, it was named **November** from its number; for it is the ninth month counting from **March**.

93. On the seventh day before the **Kalends of December** <note>November 25th</note>, **Democritus** <note>likely referring to the Greek philosopher's astronomical calendar</note> says the Sun is in **Sagittarius**. It seemed to the Romans that the bean <note>original: *fabam*</note> was called *the pulse* <note>original: *τὸ ἔτνος* (to etnos)</note> after the **West Wind** <note>original: *Zephyrus*</note>, because when it begins to blow, this crop is usually the first to sprout. Among them, the West Wind is called **Favonius**. For this reason, **March** is called *Zephyrites*, just as **January** is called *Monias* from the unit <note>original: *monade*, the number one</note>, and **October** is called *Sementilis* from the sowing, as ancient tradition has handed down.

95. **Dionysus** is the spirit that comes into being in fire—that is, the heat. For this reason, he was called **"fire-born"** <note>original: πυρίτοκος (pyritokos)</note>, **"thigh-nursed"** <note>original: μηροτραφὴς (merotraphês)</note>, and **"male-female"** <note>original: ἀρσενόθηλυς (arsenothêlys)</note> by the Greeks. For he is the warm spirit that is deposited from the seed of every living creature into the process of generating life and the growth of all things in the cosmos. He was called **"thigh-nursed"** because <margin>p. 127.</margin> this substance of every living being—from which all things are composed—is settled in the membranes <note>the meninges of the brain or spinal cord</note>, the reproductive organs, and the veins in the thighs. He was called **"male-female"** because the seeds of both sexes are two—male and female in nature—and one cannot beget another unless they come together and give life to the creatures crafted by this spirit. People have also supposed that he is dissolved and born again, because the things generated from him are likewise consumed without ceasing and then brought back to life.

The first, because of its thinness, is carried down with such speed that it passes through before it can ignite, so that it does not burn even those materials of loose texture; but the slower one is so composed that it can stain, as happens with soot, and harm some of those things lying beneath it. However, bulbs, fig trees, seals, and hyenas remain unharmed <note>Ancient naturalists believed these specific plants and animals possessed a natural immunity to lightning</note>, which is why it is said that the masts of ships are covered with these skins to protect against thunderbolts.

The learned men among the Hebrews divide the method of foreknowledge into two categories: **signs** and **wonders** <note>original: σημεῖα (semeia) and τέρατα (terata); i.e., portents and miracles</note>. They maintain that signs are those things that exist in the air, while wonders are those things on earth that appear contrary to nature. Such is the event reported concerning Moses himself in the so-called Exodus of the Hebrews: "And he saw that the bush was burning, and the bush was not consumed." And again: "Moses threw his staff upon the ground, and it was turned into a serpent." And again: "Moses put his hand into his bosom, and it became..." <note>The text cuts off, referring to the miracle where Moses' hand becomes leprous, as described in Exodus 4:6</note>

And not only these things, but yet another more fearful wonder: the transformation of all the Egyptian water into gore <note>original: λύθρον (lythron)</note>, and the multitude of frogs, and those called gnats, and the gadflies which they themselves call "dog-flies," and the destruction of the livestock, and the dusty sores, the blisters and locusts—all these might rightly be called wonders <note>original: τέρατα (terata); miraculous events that occur on the earth</note>. Signs <note>original: σημεῖα (sēmeia)</note>, however, are those appearing from the upper regions, such as that reported in the same scripture: "And the Lord rained hail upon all the land of Egypt," <margin>p. 129</margin> and there was indeed hail, and fire flaming within the hail. And again: "And Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness, gloom, and a storm over all the land of Egypt." Such, then, is the account of signs among the Hebrews; from which, I believe, the other nations also decided to call these portents "signs from Zeus" <note>original: διοσημίας (diosēmias); weather omens</note>. For Zeus is said by the natural philosophers to be the air, because he is life-giving; thus, a "sign from Zeus" is a sign of the air, which <note>original: sic</note> is fair when it is gentle and calm...

## EXCURSUS <note>A scholarly term for a detailed discussion or appendix added to a text to explore a specific point in depth.</note>

->concerning two passages from Joannes Laurentius Lydus <note>A 6th-century Byzantine administrator and scholar whose works preserve many fragments of lost ancient texts</note>, in one of which a fragment of Aristotle is presented, containing a principal tenet of his ethics; in the other, a doctrine concerning the intellect by the same philosopher—or certainly his followers—is recorded.<-

*John Lydus, On the Months [De Mensibus], pages 252 and following of this edition:*

> Aristotle [says]: If there is virtue, there is no chance; for the affairs of chance toss up and down in human matters, particularly regarding wealth and, most notably, injustice. But those who hold fast to virtue and are mindful of God, and who anchor better hopes in blessed and immaterial things, look down upon the [fleeting] beauties of this world. <note>original: "Ἀριστοτέλης· Εἰ ἔστιν ἀρετή, οὐκ ἔστι τύχη· ἄνω γὰρ καὶ κάτω τὰ τῆς τύχης ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρωπίνοις γυμνάζεται πράγμασι πλούτῳ τε καὶ διαφερόντως ἀδικίᾳ. οἱ δὲ πρὸς ἀρετὴν ἔχοντες καὶ θεοῦ μεμνημένοι, καὶ κρείττονας ἐπὶ τῶν μακαρίων καὶ ἀΰλων πραγμάτων ἐλπίδας σαλεύοντες, καταφρονοῦσι τῶν τῇδε καλῶν."</note> \*)

**T**he dialogues written by Aristotle are praised here and there among the ancients (see Buhle, *On the Lost Books of Aristotle*, in the *Commentaries of the Göttingen Society* <note>original: "Commentatt. societat. Gotting."</note>, volume 15, historical and philological class, pages 130 and following): from the shipwreck of which time—

### EXCURSUS.

...one might suspect that through the help of John Lydus, this elegant fragment has escaped the ravages of time safe and sound; in which certainly the style of speech appears suited to imitate a living voice <note>A reference to the "dialogue" style for which Aristotle's lost popular works were famous in antiquity.</note>. Regarding the first short clause of this fragment, a more careful consideration of its logic reveals that the sentence is not entirely complete in every respect, but rather is disconnected from the flow of the speech and, as it were, torn away from its context. And indeed, at the words *If there is virtue* <note>original: "Εἰ ἔστιν ἀρετή"</note>, I would wish you to supply in the place of the predicate: *the cause for us of living well*, or *that through which happiness comes about*. Clearly, in Aristotle’s view, virtue contributes as much as possible to living well and blessedly; indeed, it is properly the sole cause of happiness, since he places the highest good <note>term: "summum bonum" — the ultimate goal of human existence</note> in the *activity of the soul according to virtue* <note>original: "ἐνεργείᾳ κατ’ ἀρετὴν"</note>. \*) For a person focused and intent upon this end, the gifts of fortune—external conveniences (*external goods* <note>original: "τὰ ἐκτὸς ἀγαθά"</note>, or *matters of chance* <note>original: "τὰ τῆς τύχης"</note>)—are certainly not entirely superfluous: since *it is impossible, or at least not easy, to perform noble deeds if one is unprovided with resources*. \*\*) Although the randomness of fortune is by no means to be called the actual producer of a blessed life: \*\*\*) nor unless

---

\*) See Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* Book I, chapters 7 and following. Having made a distinction between things desirable for their own sake and those chosen for some further end, the author explains that "highest good" (that is, happiness)—which is always sought for itself and never for any other reason—and beautifully defines the proper function of a living being endowed with reason. From this "work" or type of life assigned to humanity by nature (which he places in the activity of the soul consistent with reason), he judges where human happiness resides. He also establishes that an honorable life is pleasant in itself, and does not require pleasure as a mere "appendix." See also Book X, chapter 5 and following, as well as the preceding chapter 4, regarding the general discussion of the sensation of pleasure or delight that is joined with any perfected action.

\*\*) *Nicomachean Ethics* Book I, chapter 8. Compare Cicero, *Academia* I, 6: *Therefore, all that ancient philosophy held that a happy life is placed in virtue alone; yet not the most happy, unless there were added both bodily goods and those other things mentioned above, which are suitable for the exercise of virtue.*

\*\*\*) *For it is not in these [fortunes] that well-being or ill-being lies, but...* <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ ἐν ταύταις (ταῖς τύχαις) τὸ εὖ ἢ κακῶς, ἀλλὰ προσ-"</note>

# ERNEST ANTON LEWALD

...interpreters of these matters arose. I see that these men, who were sometimes more ingenious in organizing his doctrines, brought forward this same opinion concerning the threefold intellect—which was known to them—having explained it in such a way that the individuals were hardly consistent with themselves, nor did they agree with one another. The material for this inquiry is taken entirely from chapters 4 and 5 of the third book of Aristotle's *On the Soul*—in which he deliberately discussed the intellect or the rational part of the soul—calling to his aid, it seems, a passage from *On the Generation of Animals* (Book II, ch. 3), in which the intellect is said not to be born along with the body of the living creature like the lower parts of the soul, but, arriving from the outside, to enter into it. 

In the aforementioned books *On the Soul*, after he had taught that the mind or intellect is distinct from sensation and from the faculty of imagination, he now proceeds to show in what way the intellect is said to be simple and <term>impassive</term> <note>original: ἀπαθής (apathēs); meaning it cannot be altered or "suffered" by external things</note>. However, since notions of things are formed within it, the intellect seems to be affected in some way by these things, or to be confused with them. Therefore, he declares that its power must be distinguished as twofold: one for receiving the forms of things,*) the other for acting. He declares this in these words (see chapter 5, beginning): "Since, just as in the whole of nature there is something which is the <term>matter</term> <note>original: ὕλη (hylē)</note> for each genus (that is, what is potentially all those things **)), and another which is the cause and productive because it makes all things—as art is related to its material—it is necessary that these differences also exist in the soul. And there is one mind of such a sort that it becomes all things; and another that makes all things, as a kind of disposition, like light; for in a certain way..."

---

...revealing his opinion to us, compare his *Politics* (Book VII, ch. 15, edited by Göttling, page 256): "For every art and education wishes to fill up what is lacking in nature." <note>original Greek: πᾶσα γὰρ τέχνη καὶ παιδεία τὸ προσλεῖπον βούλεται τῆς φύσεως ἀναπληροῦν.</note>

*) In the same work, chapter 4, near the end, he compares the intellect to wax on which nothing has yet been written. <note>This refers to the famous "blank slate" or *tabula rasa* concept.</note>

**) Naturally, the material principle of things contains nothing except the <term>potentiality</term> <note>original: δύναμις (dynamis)</note> of being. See *On the Soul* (Book II, 1): "Matter is potentiality, but form is <term>actuality</term> <note>original: ἐντελέχεια (entelecheia)</note>." Compare also *Metaphysics* (Book VIII, ch. 1).

*...and light makes colors that exist potentially into colors in actuality.* <note>original: καὶ τὸ φῶς ποιεῖ τὰ δυνάμει ὄντα χρώματα ἐνεργείᾳ χρώματα</note> [*One power of the intellect is this: that it can be transformed, as it were, into every form, so that it is able to transfer to itself and make kindred to itself whatever things are supplied to it by sensation and imagination; the other, however, is engaged in acting—which can be compared with a state of the soul.* \*) *It is similar to light, by which the eye is affected, in that it makes those things which were previously in the soul only potentially to now exist in it actually; for when light arrives, colors also become colors in actuality, which before they appeared to the eyes were colors only potentially.*] *And this intellect is separate* [*not attached to the organs of the body*], *and unmixed and impassive, being in its essence an activity* <note>original: ἐνεργείᾳ (energeia)</note> [*because its very substance is action*]; *for that which acts is always more honorable than that which is acted upon, and the principle is more honorable than the matter.* <note>original: ἀεὶ γὰρ τιμιώτερον τὸ ποιοῦν τοῦ πάσχοντος, καὶ ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς ὕλης</note> He adds that only this superior part of the mind is immortal and eternal, though it will lack memory of past events, for the very reason that it is free from all emotion. — From this it will also be clear that what was said about the intellect in general in the books *On the Generation of Animals*, Book II <note>OCR says "l. ...intellect, which encompasses the matter of thinking, whereas "the external" <note>original Greek: τὸ θύραθεν (to thyrathen)</note>, that is, the extraneous or adventitious, is its more excellent power, active by nature. The question of where to refer "the habitual" <note>original Greek: τὸ καθ' ἕξιν (to kath' hexin)</note> is somewhat more obscure; this is the species of mind which, in our Lydus, is placed in the middle between those other two. But perhaps we can make some progress here by offering a conjecture that is not entirely improbable. For we have seen, in the cited place from the books *On the Soul* <note>original Latin: de anima</note>, that the role and continuous function of the active intellect was compared by Aristotle with a "state" or "habit" <note>original Latin: habitu</note>: a fact which could cause difficulty for interpreters of that passage who are less attentive to the particular reasoning and connection of thoughts; for in itself, the action of the mind should by no means be confused with a habit. \*) Therefore, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> wishing to preserve the distinction between these notions here as well, turned to their own use—as one may suspect—those passages of the master in which he, systematically discussing the matter and form of things in general, adds a third element to these: that which consists of both joined together. \*\*) Thus they were led to the point that, besides that part of the intellect which receives forms—the **power of thought** <note>original German: Denkvermögen</note>, or the **receptivity of the understanding for the separate forms of things** <note>original German: Empfänglichkeit des Verstandes für abgesonderte Formen der Dinge</note>—and that nature and power of the mind which is seen in constant and perpetual act—the **force of thought** <note>original German: Denkkraft</note>, or the **principle of the self-activity of the understanding** <note>original German: Princip der Selbstthätigkeit des Verstandes</note>—they [added] some...

***

> \*) What difference there is between "disposition" <note>original Greek: ἕξιν (hexin)</note> and "activity" <note>original Greek: ἐνέργεια (energeia)</note> you may learn from a passage in the *Ethics*, where Aristotle warns that it is consistent for a moral habit to sometimes be void of function and effect; as in one who is sleeping, or otherwise resting from labor and work: but "activity" <note>original Greek: ἐνέργειαν</note>, that is, the action itself, can by no means be idle. See *Nicomachean Ethics* I, 8.

> \*\*) See *Metaphysics* VIII, 1. *On the Soul* II, 1: "We say that substance <note>original Greek: οὐσίαν</note> is one kind of the things that exist; and of this, one part is as matter <note>original Greek: ὕλην</note>, which by itself is not a 'this,' another is shape and form <note>original Greek: μορφὴν καὶ εἶδος</note>, according to which it is already called a 'this,' and the third is that which is from these [two]."

### EXCURSUS. 307

...what they might imagine was composed of both of these: I mean the active intellect, operating with a certain and finite reason upon the matter which the passive [intellect] provided to it <note>original German: *selbst-thätiger Verstand in concreto, in seiner Richtung auf bestimmte Objecte*, or "self-active understanding in the concrete, in its direction toward specific objects"</note>: this persistent operation could be quite appropriately called a **habit** <note>original Greek: ἕξις (hexis), meaning a stable disposition or state</note>. Nor does it seem entirely wrong to refer the idea of **learning** <note>original Greek: τῆς μαθήσεως (tēs mathēseōs)</note> to the perfection of this combined function—that is, the idea of discipline, or the knowledge of things to be acquired by practice and art. This is because **nature** <note>original Greek: φύσις (physis)</note> properly belongs to the passive intellect, while **exercise** <note>original Greek: ἄσκῃσις (askēsis)</note> belongs to the active intellect; for a good natural disposition is required to correctly shape the perceived images of things with a concept. However, for the highest power of the mind to be cultivated, nothing is needed but exercise, or the frequent repetition of its own function.

But let us set these matters aside, lest we seem to justly exceed our limits and measure in scrutinizing things that cannot be brought to perfect clarity. Let us now hear from those who—having received from others older than themselves the opinion of Aristotle regarding the three-fold intellect—have handed it down to us, amplified by their own explanations and discussions. I speak of **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, the celebrated Peripatetic <note>a follower of Aristotle's school</note>, and **Plutarch**, the son of Nestorius, an eclectic philosopher <note>Plutarch of Athens, a Neoplatonist</note>. ...the second meaning of the **mind** <note>original Greek: τοῦ νοῦ (tou nou)</note> <unclear>is the mind according to</unclear> **habit** <note>original Greek: ἕξιν (hexin), referring to a stable state or disposition</note>, such as that found in mature humans. For mature humans, possessing a logical knowledge of things, are said to have the mind according to habit. The third meaning of the mind is the **intellect in activity** <note>original Greek: ὁ ἐνεργείᾳ νοῦς (ho energeia nous)</note>, which is the **intellect from without** <note>original Greek: ὁ θύραθεν (ho thyrathen); a famous Aristotelian concept of an intellect that enters the human from an external, divine source</note>. This is the all-perfect intellect, which exists neither by habit nor by potentiality, so that it may be simple, being always in activity; it is that which governs the universe. **) These are the three meanings of the mind according to **Alexander**. **Plutarch**, however, does not accept these, but describes the meanings of the mind differently. For he says that the first meaning of the mind is the **mind according to habit**, such as exists in children. For Plutarch wishes, following Aristotle, for children to possess the rational principles of things, and for the logical soul to know all things, and that learning is not strictly "learning," but rather **recollections** <note>original Greek: ἀναμνήσεις (anamnēseis); the Platonic theory that all learning is actually remembering knowledge the soul possessed before birth</note>. The second meaning of the mind is that which is at once both in habit and in activity, just as the mind is in mature humans. For in these people, it exists both according to habit and according to activity; for such a person has already learned and known things, and as it were—

---

—about to explain more fully, he adds: "But if the **mind** [is in potentiality <insert>in children</insert>], it is clearly according to its aptitude; it has no form, but is matter only. For everything that is first in potentiality is in matter. The mind, therefore, is matter, and has no form, so that it might not be clouded by its own form and lean toward the knowledge of its own specific form, thereby failing to know the forms contrary to it. For just as that which is **transparent** <note>original Greek: τὸ διαφανὲς (to diaphanes)</note> is colorless, so that it may serve the colors without bias, so also the mind, he says, is **formless** <note>original Greek: ἀνειδεός (aneideos)</note>, so that it may know all things that exist." These are the views of Alexander.

### EXCURSUS.

...was reminded through learning. \*) The third meaning is the **mind in activity alone**; such is the **perfect intellect from without**. These are the three meanings of the mind according to **Plutarch**. — We see that none of those points included in the division handed down by **Lydus** <note>Johannes Lydus, a 6th-century Byzantine author</note> were passed over in silence by **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle</note>. However, Alexander does not acknowledge these as mere individual parts or powers and functions of our mind. Instead, he intends them to represent different types of minds, differing both in their level of perfection and in their very nature and kind.

In terms of perfection, the intelligence that only flourishes in a person of mature age differs from a mere natural disposition for thinking, such as that found in an infant. However, there is also a natural difference between the human intellect and that **external intellect** <note>original Latin: extraneum illum [intellectum]</note>. Alexander so closely identifies or merges this external intellect with God (that is, the supreme mind) that he cannot conceive of it as being truly joined to a living being. \*\*) Indeed, this wise man should be said to act more as a critic here, or perhaps to be philosophizing on the logical consequences of Aristotelian principles, rather than acting as a completely faithful interpreter of his master's original meaning.

**Plutarch**, being a man from the school of the **eclectics** <note>Philosophers who selected the best parts of various systems rather than adhering to just one</note>, could not bring himself to adopt **Alexander’s** reasoning in its entirety. He altered at least the first part of it slightly so that it would openly align with the view of **Plato**, who had taught that there are certain innate notions of things in our souls, which—

---

\*) I have thus corrected the spelling *passion* <note>original Greek: παθήσεως (pathēseōs)</note>, which was an error caused by the laziness of the scribes, to *learning* <note>original Greek: μαθήσεως (mathēseōs)</note>.

\*\*) He reveals this opinion of his in the two books he wrote *On the Soul*. However, it would be a long task to examine and explain each of his reasons and arguments. **Brucker** <note>Johann Jakob Brucker, author of a massive history of philosophy</note> provides several points that suit our purpose in his *Critical History of Philosophy*, Volume II, page 481.

### A LITTLE BOOK ON THE JUICING OF HERBS. 315

...just as the effluxes <note>original: ἀπόῤῥοιαι (aporrhoiai). It is perfectly clear, then, that the Sun, being the king of all the stars, is exalted <note>original: ὑψοῦται (hypsoutai). ### OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

...and 40 <term>ounces|The symbol ℥ represents an ounce, a unit of weight roughly equal to 27 grams</term> of fermented [material]; 2 ounces of cedar oil <note>171</note>: taking up the dry ingredients with the liquids, use it. The herb itself and its leaves, when drunk, act against reptiles <note>original: "herpeta", often referring to venomous snake bites or creeping skin diseases</note>. When boiled whole with wine, it breaks away the scabs in the tonsils, and the juice, gargled with hyssop <note>173</note> and boiled wine, helps spreading ulcers in the mouth. It is said that when the infusion is sprinkled at banquets, it makes the guests more jovial <note>The transcription reads "adiēgyoterous," likely a corruption of the Greek word for "well-behaved" or "pleasant" used in Dioscorides</note>. It is given to those with tertian fevers to drink the third node [of the plant], and to those with quartan fevers, the fourth node. Hung in a house, it is beneficial; and placed in a workshop, it provides success.
Just as Artemisia <term>Artemisia|Mugwort or wormwood; a plant associated with the goddess Artemis and used in women’s medicine</term> provides the same benefits. It is called the **sacred herb** because it is useful for many things; and it is surprisingly effective for everything, such as scrofula <term>scrofula|A swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, usually tubercular</term>, swellings of the parotid glands, tumors of the neck, and buboes when applied as a plaster. Its juice treats hemorrhoids when used as an enema with natron <term>natron|A naturally occurring mineral salt used for cleansing and as a drying agent</term> and honey, and many other things.

Gather this from the 15th of December. <note>174</note>

# LITTLE BOOK ON THE USE OF HERBS

->The herb of Sagittarius is the pimpernel;<- of this there are two kinds: the red and the blue. It is only the leaves that provide usefulness. The juice of the blue variety, when taken up and mixed in equal parts with honey and instilled into the nostrils, draws out phlegm from the head and from the chest; similarly, it relieves the pains of the teeth. If you mix the juice with rose oil and anoint your face, <note>Note 180: The Augustanus manuscript omits "your" and suggests "you will be seen."</note> you will be gazed upon forever with pleasure by all people. <note>Note 181: This suggests a cosmetic or even magical charm to increase the user’s attractiveness.</note> 

If you give the juice to a woman to use <note>Note 184: The Augustanus manuscript specifies "to smear on."</note> mixed with honey, Indian lycium <term>Indian lycium|A medicinal extract, likely from the plant Berberis lycium, imported from India and used for eye diseases</term> <note>Note 182: The original Greek text literally says "Indian wolf," but the editor notes it should be "lycium," a common correction in botanical texts.</note> and the sharpest vinegar, it brightens the eyes and makes them firmer. <note>original: "tetanoteras," meaning stretched or tight, perhaps referring to reducing puffiness or sagging around the eyes.</note>
