# OF HERMES TRISMEGISTUS

Madness <note>original: *mania*</note> occurs without fever; but epilepsy <note>original: *epilepsia*</note> occurs with fever. These conditions develop in this way: for example, when from a cooling of the meninges <note>the membranes enveloping the brain</note> the vessels are constricted; when the fluid is too plentiful, some pneuma <term>pneuma|In ancient Greek medicine, the "vital breath" or spirit believed to circulate through the body to facilitate movement and thought</term> is squeezed out, and while it should have a straight path through the pores, it necessarily produces a disturbance of the mind. Therefore, the aforementioned power [of the herb], being naturally sharp and thinning, when it is applied, dilates the pores and draws out the blockage of fluid; thus, as the pneumatic pores are restored to their natural state, the ailment finds its cure. 

From this same herb an ointment is also prepared, which treats freckles and moles, as well as pimples and recent dark skin spots <note>likely referring to *alphos*, a type of scaly skin condition or vitiligo</note>.
- Alcyonium <term>alcyonium|A substance traditionally made from calcified sea foam or the remains of sea organisms, used for its cleansing and abrasive properties</term> — 4 units
- Burnt pumice, ground — 8 units
- Immature gallnuts — 12 units
- Indian lycium <term>Indian lycium|A medicinal extract from the plant Berberis lycium, highly valued in antiquity for treating skin and eye diseases</term> — 11 units
- Illyrian iris — 12 units
- Honey — 6 units
- The juice [of the herb] — 15 units
Mix these in a tin vessel; after cleansing the area with soda <note>original: *nitrasas*, referring to natron or soda used as a soap substitute</note>, rub the mixture on and you will be cured. 

If you mix equal parts of the juice with honey and Indian lycium and anoint the "stalk of the member" <note>a euphemism for the penis</note>, you will be more ready for intercourse and will provide pleasure to the woman you approach.

Gather this herb starting from the 16th of January.

# OF VETTIUS VALENS OF ANTIOCH
## THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANTHOLOGIES <note>Note 1: These words were written by a more recent hand, likely that of Marcus Meibom, a 17th-century scholar who studied these manuscripts.</note>

To find the <term>Midheaven<note>original: Μεσουράνημα (*Mesouranema*). In astrology, this is the highest point of the zodiac at the moment of a birth or event, representing one's public life or career.</note></term> <note>Note 2: The scribe originally omitted the first letter; it should read *Mesouranema*.</note> by hand: take the degrees <note>Note 3: Throughout this text, the scribe uses a specific shorthand symbol for "degree."</note> from the setting degree according to the <term>ascensions<note>original: ἀναφοράς (*anaphoras*). This refers to the time it takes for a sign of the zodiac to rise above the eastern horizon.</note></term> of the <term>clime<note>original: κλίματος (*klimatos*). A geographical zone or latitude. Ancient astronomers divided the world into seven "climes" to account for how the sun and stars appear to move differently at different latitudes.</note></term> until the degree opposite them. Take half of this total and count it out from the western [setting] degree. Wherever it falls, that will be the Midheaven.

For example: let the <term>Ascendant<note>original: ὡροσκόπος (*hōroskopos*). The degree of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time.</note></term> be the 15th degree of Capricorn <note>Note 4: In the original manuscript, the names of the zodiac signs marked with asterisks are written as symbols (sigla) rather than full words.</note> in the second clime. I take from the setting degree of the 15th degree of Cancer until the 15th degree of Capricorn. The ascensions total 214. Half of these is 107. Adding these to the 15th degree of Cancer, I counted forward from that same point; it ended <margin>le r <note>Note 5: A brief marginal notation of uncertain meaning, possibly a cross-reference or textual variant.</note></margin> at the 2nd degree of Libra. That is where the Midheaven is located. The process is similar for the other signs.

If you wish to determine this according to the length of the hours of the day, always add the differences from the degree of the Sun until the degree opposite it. By taking a 15th part of this total, you will know the length of the hour. For example: using the aforementioned setting 15th degree of Cancer...

### Concerning the Rising Times of the Zodiac Signs <note>Note 8: This heading was written by the same more recent hand [likely Meibom's] that added notes to the previous page.</note>

To know how many hours each sign takes to rise <note>Note 9: The original text is missing a letter; it should read "Of how many" (Posōn).</note>, it must be understood from the ascension of each. For example, since Aries rises in 20 [equatorial times]—and one hour contains 15 <term>equatorial times<note>original: χρόνους ἰσημερινοὺς (chronous isēmerinous). These are degrees of the celestial equator. Since the sky turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, 15 degrees is equal to one hour of time.</note></term>—if you subtract 15 from 20, the remainder is 5, which is a third part of 15. Therefore, Taurus will rise in one hour and a third. 

To know how much time each degree is worth, you will know it this way: double the ascension of each sign. These [multiplied] six times become 240. [In this calculation], one degree equals 8 months. 

To know how much of an <insert>addition</insert> <note>Note 11: The original scribe wrote "proposal," but the editor suspects it should be "addition" (prosthesin).</note> or subtraction each sign has in its ascension <note>Note 10: The original text had a minor grammatical error in the word "how much."</note>, it should be known as follows: since Aries rises in 20 and Leo rises in 40, to complete the sum of 60, whichever sign is diametrically opposite will follow <note>Note 12: The scribe originally wrote "following," but corrected it to "will follow."</note> to complete that 60. And regarding how many hours each sign takes: the diametrically opposite sign [is used] to complete 4 hours. And for the number of days and months: the diametrically opposite sign will govern for two years. For just as each sign exceeds [a certain value], the one diametrically opposite falls short—

(Key) Wonders/Signs <note>original: "מַפְתֵּחַ מוֹפְתִים" (maphteach mophtim); likely an index entry for "key signs"</note> God of Hosts <note>original: "אֱלֹהִים צְבָאוֹת" (Elohim Tzevaoth)</note>, God of Hosts <note>original: "אֱלֹהֵי צְבָאוֹת" (Elohei Tzevaoth)</note> 295. a. 204. a. 299. b.
One <note>original: "אַחַת" (achath), feminine form</note> 295. a.
Baal, Baalat <note>original: "בַּעַל" (lord/master), "בַּעֲלַת" (lady/mistress)</note> 26. a.
Jehovah <note>original: "יְהוָֹה" (Yahweh), the sacred name of God</note> 203. b. 204. a. 298. b.
To throw or to teach <note>original: "יָרָה" (yarah); the root for the word Torah</note> 239. a.
Canaanites <note>original: "כִּנְעָנִים" (Kena'anim)</note> 8. b.
To number or count <note>original Syriac: "ܡܢܳܐ" (mena)</note> 239. a.
Water <note>original: "מַיִם" (mayim)</note> 239. a.

Ashtoreth <note>original: "עַשְׁתֹּרֶת"; a goddess of fertility and war</note> 129. b.
*ravey* instead of *roy* <note>original: "רָוֵי pro רוֹי"; a correction of Hebrew orthography</note> 239. a.
Drunkard or saturated <note>original Syriac: "ܪܰܘܳܐ" (rawwa)</note> 239. a.

### CORRECTIONS <note>original: "CORRIGENDA"</note>.

Page 28. b. last line. After the word **Accent** <note>original: "Accentum"</note> delete the parenthesis mark.
->and in place of a simple period, put a semicolon.<-
- 42. line 11. for **Helios** <note>original: "Ηλιος", lacking the breathing mark</note> read **Hēlios** <note>original: "Ἥλιος", with the correct rough breathing mark</note>.
- 259. - 5. after **of Aeneas** <note>original: "Aeneae"</note> delete **and** <note>original: "et"</note> and supply **sons** <note>original: "filii"</note>.

<meta>This page follows the index of subjects and corrections, moving into supplementary material regarding the fragments of Vettius Valens of Antioch, a 2nd-century Hellenistic astrologer. It provides a visual and linguistic comparative table of zodiac signs.</meta>

<header>Notes on the Fragments of Vettius Valens of Antioch <note>Vettius Valens was a professional astrologer in the 2nd century CE whose "Anthology" is a primary source for ancient astrological practice.</note></header>

## Symbols of the Twelve Zodiac Signs <note>original: "Σημεῖα τῶν ιβ' ζῳδίων" (Sēmeia tōn dōdeka zōdiōn)</note>.

| Du Cange <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange (1610–1688), a renowned philologist whose work cataloged medieval Greek and Latin.</note> | | The Creuzer Codex <note>Likely referring to a manuscript from the collection of Georg Friedrich Creuzer (1771–1858), a scholar of ancient mythology.</note> |
| :--- | :---: | :--- |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Aries: a stylized ram's horn, the letter 'p', and 'v'.</image-desc> | Aries <note>original: "Κριός" (Krios), the Ram.</note> | <image-desc>Variants of the Aries symbol with dots above.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Taurus: a character resembling a cursive 'u' with a tail, a 'z' with a bar, and two versions of the standard Taurus glyph ♉.</image-desc> | Taurus <note>original: "Ταῦρος" (Tauros), the Bull.</note> | <image-desc>Four variants of the Taurus symbol, resembling inverted arches or the letter 'u' with decorative dots and lines.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Gemini: two sets of wavy horizontal lines and the Roman numeral II.</image-desc> | Gemini <note>original: "Δίδυμοι" (Didymoi), the Twins.</note> | <image-desc>Two horizontal double-bar symbols, one with small circles above.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>A horizontal symbol for Cancer resembling a flattened figure-eight or infinity sign.</image-desc> | Cancer <note>original: "Καρκίνος" (Karkinos), the Crab.</note> | <image-desc>A symbol resembling two crossed loops.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Leo: a cursive 'o' shape and the standard Leo glyph ♌.</image-desc> | Leo <note>original: "Λέων" (Leōn), the Lion.</note> | <image-desc>Two variants: an 'Λ' shape and a Leo glyph with a circle above.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Virgo: a cursive 'ux' shape and the standard Virgo glyph ♍.</image-desc> | Virgo <note>original: "Παρθένος" (Parthenos), the Virgin.</note> | <image-desc>Four variants of the Virgo glyph, stylized as the letter 'y' or 'm' with varying tails and dots.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>The standard Libra glyph ♎.</image-desc> | Libra <note>original: "Ζυγός" (Zygos), the Scales or Balance.</note> | <image-desc>Two variants of the Libra glyph with dots above.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Scorpio: a cursive 'm' with a long tail and the standard Scorpio glyph ♏.</image-desc> | Scorpio <note>original: "Σκορπίος" (Skorpios), the Scorpion.</note> | <image-desc>Four hook-like symbols resembling the number 9 or stylized tails with dots.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Sagittarius: three variants of arrows and crosses.</image-desc> | Sagittarius <note>original: "Τοξότης" (Toxotēs), the Archer.</note> | <image-desc>Two variants of an arrow/cross symbol with dots.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Capricorn: symbols resembling 'p x' and two variants of the Capricorn glyph ♑.</image-desc> | Capricorn <note>original: "Αἰγόκερως" (Aigokerōs), the Goat-Horned.</note> | <image-desc>Four variants of the Capricorn glyph, stylized with loops and dots.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Aquarius: two sets of horizontal wavy lines.</image-desc> | Aquarius <note>original: "Ὑδροχόος" (Hydrochoos), the Water-Bearer.</note> | <image-desc>A symbol of horizontal wavy lines with a dot above.</image-desc> |
| <image-desc>Astrological symbols for Pisces: two variants of the Pisces glyph ♓.</image-desc> | Pisces <note>original: "Ἰχθύες" (Ichthyes), the Fish.</note> | <image-desc>Three variants of the Pisces glyph, some with bars across the vertical lines.</image-desc> |

<summary>This page presents a comparative chart of the astrological symbols for the twelve zodiac signs, contrasting the versions recorded by the scholars Du Cange and those found in the Creuzer Codex. These illustrations serve as technical appendices to the fragments of the ancient astrologer Vettius Valens.</summary>
